api.error.food_gone: The food diary is gone — I took it out. Everything you logged before is still there, in your full diary export.
api.error.ai_consent_required: I don't pass your data to the AI without your OK — so I can't answer yet. Tap “I agree” on the coach screen or turn it on in Settings.
api.error.ai_model_gone: There's no coach model switch anymore — I answer with one model, nothing to switch.
api.error.bad_request: I couldn't read that request — update the app and try again.
api.error.not_found: Can't find that — the screen's stale. Go back and open it again
api.error.rep_range: No such range. Pick one of five: 3–6, 5–12, 8–12, 8–15 or 12–20
api.error.invalid_gender: Didn't catch the gender. Pick Male, Female or Not set.
api.error.internal_error: Something broke on my side — try again in a bit.
api.error.unauthorized: You got signed out — sign in to the app again.
api.error.invalid_apple_token: Apple didn't confirm the sign-in — try again.
api.error.invalid_credentials: Wrong username or password — check them and try again.
api.error.rate_limited: Too many attempts in the last few minutes. Wait a bit and try again.
api.error.already_linked: This account is already linked to Telegram.
api.error.not_configured: That's not available right now — try again later.
api.error.name_taken: That name's already taken — pick another one.
api.error.name_too_long: That name's too long — keep it under {max} characters.
api.error.feedback_limit_exceeded: That's enough messages to the developer for today — write again tomorrow.
api.error.timeout: I didn't answer in time — ask again.
api.error.shutting_down: I'm restarting — give me half a minute and ask again.
api.error.answer_failed: Couldn't answer — try again in a minute.
api.error.factcheck_failed: Couldn't check that post — try forwarding it again.
api.error.delivery_failed: Couldn't deliver your message — try again later.
api.error.setup_stale: That question isn't current anymore — reopen the coach chat.
api.error.routine_limit: Your programs already have as many days as fit. Delete the extra ones and try again.
api.error.workout_finished: That workout's already finished — start a new one.
api.error.workout_active: Finish the workout first — only a finished one can be edited this way.
api.error.no_ai_comment: This workout has no AI coach review yet — nothing to discuss.
api.error.workout_not_finished: The workout's still going — I'll break it down once you finish.
api.error.active_workout_exists: Finish or discard your current workout first.
api.error.no_exercises: That workout has no exercises — nothing to repeat.
api.error.unit_conversion_in_progress: Already converting your weights to the new unit — give it a minute.
api.error.invalid_csv: There's an error in the file. Fix the file and send it again.
api.error.csv_too_large: That file's too big — send a smaller one.
api.error.unrecognized_columns: Couldn't recognize the file's columns — I need date, exercise, weight and reps. Check the headers and send it again.
api.error.text_import_failed: Couldn't parse the text — try again in a minute.
api.error.not_in_program: That day isn't part of any program.
api.error.already_standalone: That day's already on its own, outside any program.
api.error.already_in_program: That day's already in a program.
api.error.empty_program: That program has no exercises — nothing to share yet.
api.error.empty_routine: That day has no exercises — nothing to share yet.
api.error.out_of_range: That number's out of range — check it and try again.
api.error.unsupported_media_type: That file format won't work — send a regular photo, video or voice note.
api.error.target_archived: That exercise is archived — restore it first.
api.error.invalid_exercise_mapping: Couldn't find that exercise among yours. Pick one of your own and send it again.
api.error.active_workout: One of those exercises is in your current workout — finish it first.
api.error.own_card: This is your own card — no need to add it.
api.error.set_not_last: I've already logged another set after that one — refresh and try again.
api.error.weight_negative: Weight can't be negative — write 0 or more.
api.error.number_negative: This can't go below zero — write 0 or more.
api.error.number_too_big: That's too much — {max} at most. Check the number and send it again.
api.error.progression_invalid: Couldn't read that progression rule. The step must be a number above zero and not huge. Check it and send it again.
api.error.text_too_long: That's too long — keep it under {max} characters.
ai.comment.first_workout_note: This is the athlete's first workout in the log. A newcomer gets support only: say the start is made, give one tip for next time, and don't list under-trained groups or mistakes.
ai.digest.first_week_note: it's their first week in the log, there's no previous week. A newcomer gets support only: one tip for next week, don't list under-trained groups
ai.comment.workout_not_found: Can't find that workout — open your history and pick it again.
ai.factcheck.empty: Couldn't make it out — try forwarding it again.
ai.language_tail: Reply ONLY in English — never switch to Russian, Ukrainian, or any other language, not even one word inside an English sentence. Terms the user themselves used in another language (an exercise name from the catalog, a unit, a technique term) are normal gym vocabulary, not a violation — keep them as given. Speak of yourself as “I”, never “the bot”: “I'll cut the sets myself”, “I don't put weights into the program”.

import.intro:
📥 Send me a CSV file with columns "date, exercise, weight, reps".

Where to get the export:
• Hevy — Settings → Export & Import Data, the CSV file arrives by email.
• Strong — Profile → Settings → Export Workouts, the file saves to your phone.

Send either one as is — no need to tidy it up by hand.

📝 Kept your workouts in notes? Paste them here as text — I'll read them myself.

mcp.code_screen: 🔗 Connection code {code} Enter it on the confirmation page the app opens. The code is one-time and valid for {ttl} — missed it, hit “New code”. If the page isn't open yet: add a connector in the app at this address {address}— it'll prompt you to confirm access itself. Step by step on the “Claude in browser”, “ChatGPT” and “Claude Desktop” screens.
mcp.disabled: 🔌 MCP is switched off right now — there's no public address for it. All your data is still right here, in the bot.
mcp.guide.chatgpt: 🤖 ChatGPT ChatGPT hides connectors behind developer mode. 1. Settings → Connectors → Advanced → turn on Developer mode 2. Back in Connectors → Create 3. MCP Server URL: {address}4. Authentication — OAuth, then Create 5. On the confirmation page enter the code: {code}6. Tap “Allow” — done Checking it worked: in a chat turn the connector on via "+" and ask "show my recent workouts". OpenAI shuffles menu names now and then — search for Connectors and Developer mode. The code is one-time and lasts {ttl}. Expired — “🔄 New code” below.
mcp.guide.claude: ☁️ Claude — browser and app Same steps either way: the connectors section exists on claude.ai and in Claude Desktop alike, and it's called the same thing. 1. Settings → Connectors 2. Add custom connector 3. Paste the address: {address}4. Claude opens a confirmation page. Enter the code there: {code}5. Tap “Allow” — done Checking it worked: in a new chat ask "show my recent workouts" — Claude will ask permission to call the tool and hand back data. The code is one-time and lasts {ttl}. Expired — “🔄 New code” below. No Node.js, no mcp-remote needed: the app connects the connector itself. The bridge is only left for builds without a connectors section — if that's your case, say so and I'll give you the command.
mcp.guide.claude_code: 🖥 Claude Code (terminal) 1. Add the server — no token needed: {add_command}2. Run claude, type /mcp → training-log → Authenticate 3. A browser opens with a confirmation page. Enter the code: {code}4. Tap “Allow” — /mcp shows connected -s user makes the server available across every project, not just the current folder. Claude Code stores and refreshes its own tokens without you. No browser handy: claude mcp login training-log --no-browser prints a link — open it on your own machine. {tail}
mcp.guide.claude_code.tail_no_token: If there's no browser at all (scripts, cloud sessions) — you'll need a token: issue one with the “Issue terminal token” button on the connection screen.
mcp.guide.claude_code.tail_with_token:
With a token in the header — for scripts and cloud sessions with no browser to open:
{command}
mcp.intro: 🔌 Your data in Claude and ChatGPT Connect once — and ask about your training right there: "what's my bench looked like over the last six months", "build a split from my history". Reading covers everything: workouts and sets, exercise progress, volume by muscle group, bodyweight, programs. Writing covers logging weight, removing a wrong weigh-in, adding an exercise, duplicating a program. Renaming anything from outside isn't possible — same as chatting with the AI coach, that's only here, in the bot.

onboarding.text: HEY ATHLETE! 💪 One rule: log a set in one line — 100 8. Weight and reps. Logged. Records, volume, progress — that's on me. The iron's on you. Not sure what to do today? Open 🤖 AI coach and tell me what you want — I'll build a program and split it into days. I see your whole history too: ask "am I stronger than 3 months ago?" and I'll answer with numbers, not vibes. Hit 🏋️ and let's go 👇

Deadlifts get a single work set of five — they're the heaviest lift here and take the most out of you. No isolation on purpose — the whole point is adding a little weight to the bar every session, for as long as it keeps going up.

push.newbie_nudge.3: HEY ATHLETE! I'm here, the log's open, and it's still at zero workouts. Start with anything — I'll count the rest.
push.newbie_nudge.4: HEY ATHLETE! The log's waiting for its first entry. Doesn't have to be perfect — just first.
push.newbie_nudge.5: HEY ATHLETE! You're signed up, no workouts yet. Fix that today?
push.newbie_nudge.6: HEY ATHLETE! The first set doesn't have to be heavy — it has to be logged. Everything else builds from there.
push.newbie_nudge.7: HEY ATHLETE! Every chart in this app starts from a single point. Put yours down today.
push.newbie_nudge.8: HEY ATHLETE! An empty log is like a bar with no plates on it. Let's load the first workout?
push.newbie_nudge.9: HEY ATHLETE! Every monster at your gym had a first log entry once. Yours is one set away.
push.plateau.1: HEY ATHLETE! {exercise}, third session at the same weight — and over 12 reps every time. That's not a plateau — the weight's just been sitting there too long. Add weight.
push.plateau.2: HEY ATHLETE! {exercise}: 12+ reps, three sessions straight, same weight. Your body's ready for more — time to load it.
push.plateau.3: HEY ATHLETE! {exercise}'s clearly gotten easier — three workouts over 12 reps, same weight the whole time. Your body's ready for more.
push.plateau.4: HEY ATHLETE! {exercise} has held steady for three sessions straight at 12+ reps. Time to move the weight.
push.plateau.5: HEY ATHLETE! Three workouts of {exercise} with reps to spare — your body's asking for more load.
push.plateau.6: HEY ATHLETE! {exercise}: weight's frozen, reps past 12 — three sessions straight. The next step's obvious, you just have to take it.
push.plateau.7: HEY ATHLETE! By the numbers, {exercise} is too light for you now: three workouts at 12+ on the same weight. Try the next one up.
push.plateau.8: HEY ATHLETE! {exercise}: three sessions on the same weight, over 12 reps every time. You've mastered this weight — time for the next step.
push.plateau.9: HEY ATHLETE! You've outgrown {exercise}: 12+ reps, three sessions straight, same weight. The plates on the rack are waiting.
push.rank_near.1: HEY ATHLETE! {missing} to the rank “{rank}”. You're closer than you think. Finish it.
push.rank_near.2: HEY ATHLETE! Next rank is “{rank}”, and it's {missing} away. That kind of gap gets closed, not stared at.
push.rank_near.3: HEY ATHLETE! {missing}, and “{rank}” shows up in your profile. A solid target for the next few days.
push.rank_near.4: HEY ATHLETE! “{rank}” is already in sight from where you're standing: {missing}, and it's yours.
push.rank_near.5: HEY ATHLETE! {missing}, and “{rank}” moves into your profile. I'll handle the move.
push.rank_near.6: HEY ATHLETE! I ran the numbers: {missing} left to “{rank}”. Numbers like that don't close themselves — but you will.
push.skip_10.1: HEY ATHLETE! Day ten with no workout. That's not a pause anymore, that's a habit of not showing up. Breaking it today?
push.skip_10.2: HEY ATHLETE! Ten days with no gym. A couple more, and you'll have to relearn how to walk in.
push.skip_10.3: HEY ATHLETE! Day ten of downtime. Not rushing you — just pointing out the door's open.
push.skip_10.4: HEY ATHLETE! Ten days of silence. The weights didn't grow, but they didn't run off either — right where you left them.
push.skip_10.5: HEY ATHLETE! Day ten. Starting over is always harder than continuing — don't push it to day twenty.
push.skip_10.6: HEY ATHLETE! Ten days off is a vacation at this point. Vacation's over.
push.skip_10.7: HEY ATHLETE! Ten days. I've got your schedule memorized: empty, empty, empty. Let's rewrite it.
push.skip_10.8: HEY ATHLETE! Day ten. The bar's standing right where it was and remembers your grip. Out of the three of us, you're the only one not showing up.
push.skip_10.9: HEY ATHLETE! Ten days with no gym. Muscle memory's reliable, but it never signed up to wait forever.
push.skip_14.1: HEY ATHLETE! Two weeks. I'm not lecturing, I'm counting days. The gym's still here. Where are you?
push.skip_14.2: HEY ATHLETE! Fourteen days of silence. Enough already — come in, we'll sort it out there.
push.skip_14.3: HEY ATHLETE! Two weeks without a single workout. Past this point it's not a pause anymore, it's a new habit. Which one do you want?
push.skip_14.4: HEY ATHLETE! Two weeks with no gym. The first set after a break matters more than any other. It's waiting.
push.skip_14.5: HEY ATHLETE! Day fourteen. I'll be honest: your form's started packing its bags. Stop it.
push.skip_14.6: HEY ATHLETE! Two weeks is the line. Past it, people either come back or disappear. You're a come-back — I've seen your log.
push.skip_14.7: HEY ATHLETE! Two weeks. I'm already telling the newbies about you like you're a legend. Show up before I start exaggerating.
push.skip_14.8: HEY ATHLETE! Fourteen days. The log opens in two taps, the gym in one door. Check both.
push.skip_14.9: HEY ATHLETE! Two weeks of silence. I get it — life happens. But life's easier when your back can hold it. Come back.
push.skip_3.1: HEY ATHLETE! Day three with no gym. Rest or excuses — you sort that out. I just count the days.
push.skip_3.10: HEY ATHLETE! Three days of silence. The membership runs even when you don't.
push.skip_3.2: HEY ATHLETE! Three days of silence. Not lecture-worthy yet — but I noticed.
push.skip_3.3: HEY ATHLETE! Three days without the bar. Not a tragedy, but not champion mode either.
push.skip_3.4: HEY ATHLETE! Day three. The gym didn't move — you just didn't show up.
push.skip_3.5: HEY ATHLETE! Day three. Two days is rest, three is a decision. Make the right one.
push.skip_3.6: HEY ATHLETE! Three days and the log's gone quiet. Muscles are still fine. The habit's getting nervous.
push.skip_3.7: HEY ATHLETE! Third day I'm staring at a blank page. Put a warm-up on it, at least.
push.skip_3.8: HEY ATHLETE! Three days, no entries. The bar asked about you — I said you were busy. Don't make a liar out of me.
push.skip_3.9: HEY ATHLETE! Day three. The couch counts as equipment too, but you won't build progress on it.
push.skip_5.1: HEY ATHLETE! Day five with no gym. Muscles still remember how this works. The habit's starting to forget.
push.skip_5.10: HEY ATHLETE! Day five with no gym. Some newbie's already eyeing your favorite bench. Come back — I'll get it for you.
push.skip_5.2: HEY ATHLETE! Five days of silence in a row. Time to break it, not get used to it.
push.skip_5.3: HEY ATHLETE! Five straight days with no gym. A bit more, and skipping becomes the habit.
push.skip_5.4: HEY ATHLETE! Five days isn't a collapse, but it's a trend now. Stop it today.
push.skip_5.5: HEY ATHLETE! Five days straight, no entry. Your form outlasts your motivation — but not forever.
push.skip_5.6: HEY ATHLETE! Five days past the gym. The road there hasn't grown over — check for yourself.
push.skip_5.7: HEY ATHLETE! Five days of rest, closed out. Open a working one — today's a good day for it.
push.skip_5.8: HEY ATHLETE! Day five. Muscles are still calling this rest. By day six they'll call it something else.
push.skip_5.9: HEY ATHLETE! Five days straight, not one entry. I checked — the log works fine. So it's not the log.
push.skip_7.1: HEY ATHLETE! A full week off. The bar won't take it personally — it's iron. Your form will, and fast.
push.skip_7.10: HEY ATHLETE! A week's gone. Good news: I'm still waiting for you. No bad news — just come in.
push.skip_7.2: HEY ATHLETE! Exactly a week of silence. No lecture — just a reminder where the gym door is.
push.skip_7.3: HEY ATHLETE! A week without a single set. Form doesn't wait — it's the first thing to go.
push.skip_7.4: HEY ATHLETE! Seven days quiet — a full week. Time to bring the conversation back to the gym.
push.skip_7.5: HEY ATHLETE! A week with no entries. Strength fades slow, habit fades fast. Get both back.
push.skip_7.6: HEY ATHLETE! Seven days — a whole week. Good news: one workout and the counter resets.
push.skip_7.7: HEY ATHLETE! A week ago you trained. Remember that feeling after? Still free of charge.
push.skip_7.8: HEY ATHLETE! A week with no gym. I wiped the dust off your bar. Twice. Your turn now.
push.skip_7.9: HEY ATHLETE! A week of silence. Your last record's already telling the gym it's in charge. Come argue with it.

push.streak_at_risk.10: HEY ATHLETE! You built that {weeks} streak one workout at a time, and it resets all at once. Time left: {days_left}. Don't hand it over.
push.streak_at_risk.2: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} without a miss — and it's all hanging by a thread right now. One workout keeps the chain going. Your call.
push.streak_at_risk.3: HEY ATHLETE! One day left before the streak turns into "used to train." {weeks} is nothing to joke about.
push.streak_at_risk.4: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} straight is a schedule now, not luck. Zero workouts this week. Time left: {days_left}. Close it out.
push.streak_at_risk.5: HEY ATHLETE! Time left: {days_left}, and the streak ({weeks}) still isn't extended. One workout decides everything.
push.streak_at_risk.6: HEY ATHLETE! You showed up every week — {weeks} straight. This one's still empty. Time left: {days_left}. Don't let the counter reset.
push.streak_at_risk.7: HEY ATHLETE! Your streak is {weeks}. One workout is all it takes to make it longer. Time left: {days_left}.
push.streak_at_risk.8: HEY ATHLETE! A {weeks} streak is riding on one workout — the one you haven't done yet. Time left: {days_left}.
push.streak_at_risk.9: HEY ATHLETE! I don't fudge the numbers: {weeks} straight, zero this week. Time left: {days_left}. Your move.
push.streak_milestone.1: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} straight without a single skip. That's not motivation anymore — that's character. Respect.
push.streak_milestone.2: HEY ATHLETE! The streak just hit “{weeks} straight”. That's what regulars look like around here. Keep the pace.
push.streak_milestone.3: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} straight — milestone hit. I don't see streaks like this often, so I logged it separately.
push.streak_milestone.4: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} without a skip. Discipline is when you stop counting. I still count, though — and I'm proud.
push.streak_milestone.5: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} straight. I've seen plenty of guys in this basement: the ones who show up like this end up complaining their shirts got tight.
push.streak_milestone.6: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} straight. Motivation comes and goes — you just keep showing up. That's worth more.
push.streak_milestone.7: HEY ATHLETE! {weeks} without a single skip. Weather changed, excuses were right there — and you showed up anyway. That's how it's forged.

push.weekly_digest.2: HEY ATHLETE! This week: {week_count}. Come in, let's see what's grown.

push.weekly_digest.5: HEY ATHLETE! Monthly tonnage: {tonnage}, and this week added up to {week_count}. Come in, see the whole picture.

push.weekly_digest.7: HEY ATHLETE! Monthly total: {tonnage}. You lifted those kilos, I just kept the log. Come in for the details.
push.weekly_digest.8: HEY ATHLETE! {tonnage} this month. Movers get paid for that kind of work — for you it just goes into a chart. Come take a look.
push.weekly_digest.9: HEY ATHLETE! This week gave you {week_count}. I logged it, broke it down, and did the math — all that's left is for you to look.
push.win_back.1: HEY ATHLETE! The break ran long — and that's fine. Everyone knows how to come back from one. No excuses needed — come in, keep it light today, no heroics.
push.win_back.10: HEY ATHLETE! The best day to come back was yesterday. The second best is today. There's no third on that list.
push.win_back.11: HEY ATHLETE! A warm-up and two lighter sets, and you're back in the game. I'll do the counting, like always.
push.win_back.2: HEY ATHLETE! Your last record is still here, waiting for you to come beat it. It's patient.
push.win_back.3: HEY ATHLETE! Start light. The first step back after a break is the one that counts most. Let's warm up together.
push.win_back.4: HEY ATHLETE! A long break isn't a life sentence. Come in for even 20 minutes, no plan needed.
push.win_back.5: HEY ATHLETE! Coming back doesn't call for heroics. Lighter weight, fewer sets — just start.
push.win_back.6: HEY ATHLETE! The log remembers all your workouts, not just the break. Add a fresh one?
push.win_back.7: HEY ATHLETE! Nobody's going to ask where you were. The gym doesn't ask questions — just open the door.
push.win_back.8: HEY ATHLETE! Today's plan is simple: show up. Everything else is details, we'll sort it out there.
push.win_back.9: HEY ATHLETE! The bar doesn't remember how long you were gone. It only remembers your grip. That hasn't gone anywhere.

export.readme.intro:
This is your whole diary — everything you logged yourself. Every file is a CSV table: it opens in Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets.
Times are in the time zone from your settings, weights are in {unit}.
export.readme.workouts: workouts.csv — workouts, one row per set. Workout and exercise notes are in the workout_note and exercise_note columns. A workout that's still going is marked status = active.
export.readme.bodyweight: bodyweight.csv — body weight: date and weight.
export.readme.programs: programs.csv — programs, one row per exercise in a day: program, day, exercise, target and progression scheme.
export.readme.exercises: exercises.csv — your exercises: muscle group, notes, description and the other names I know them by (aliases).
export.readme.food: food.csv — old food diary entries (the diary is gone, nothing new gets added): what you ate, calories, protein, fat and carbs.
export.readme.coach_comments: coach_comments.csv — your coach's comments on your workouts.
export.readme.outro: AI coach replies and photos don't go into the archive.

workout.format_hint: 💡 Weight and reps in one line: 100 8
workout.help_full: 💡 HOW LOGGING WORKS A SET: • 100 8 = 100x8 = 100-8 — 100kg × 8 reps • 100 8 3 = 100x8x3 — 3 sets at once • 8 — just reps, weight carries over from the last set • +20 8 — same as 20 8; the "+" is for you, if you think of it as extra on your bodyweight • 100x8@9 — RPE, how hard the set was, 1-10 • several sets at once — comma, ";" or a new line WHILE AN EXERCISE IS OPEN: • - — delete the last set • = — repeat the last set • !shoulder hurts — a note on the exercise • 2: 100 8 — fix logged set #2 • ? or /help — this cheat sheet e1RM — your estimated one-rep max: the weight you could probably lift once. I calculate it from the weight, reps and RPE of every set — nothing to test in the gym. RPE is not decoration here: @9 means one rep left in the tank, so the set counts as one rep longer. It's for comparing: 100×8 and 110×5 are roughly the same level, and weight alone doesn't show that. Change the formula in ⚙️ Settings. Got history from Hevy, Strong, or another app? Upload it as a CSV — ⚙️ Settings → 📥 Import CSV.
workout.help_short: 💡 HOW TO LOG A SET 100 8 — 100kg × 8 reps 100 8 3 — 3 sets like that at once 8 — just reps, weight carries over from the last set 100 8, 100 7, 95 8 — several sets at once - delete the last one · = repeat the last one

ai.screen.actions_hint: 💡 By the way, I don't just answer: I can log your weight, add an exercise, or copy a program myself. Just say the word.
ai.screen.build_program_intro: 🤖 OKAY, BUILDING THE PROGRAM. I'll ask you a couple of questions — answer them, and you'll walk away with a ready plan.
ai.screen.build_program_seed: I want to put together a training program. First ask me clarifying questions about the inputs you can't see from my history — through ask_setup_questions, one at a time — and only build the program after I've answered.

ai.screen.program_stage.split: Working out the split by day
ai.screen.build_workout_intro: 🤖 BUILDING TODAY'S WORKOUT. I'll check what's recovered, ask you a couple of things — and then we go straight into it.
ai.screen.build_workout_seed: Put together a workout for me for today — just one, I'm heading straight to the gym after this. First check get_muscle_recovery and decide what makes sense to load today and what hasn't recovered yet. Then ask me through ask_setup_questions no more than two short questions (how much time I have and how I'm feeling) and only after I answer call propose_program with exactly one day.
ai.screen.import_cta_question: Have I gotten stronger this year, judging by my history?
ai.screen.video_hint: 🎥 LET ME SEE. Send me a video of your set right here — I'll check the technique and tell you what to fix first. How to shoot it so I actually see something: • from the side, not from behind — that shows the bar path and your back • the whole set: from the first rep to the last • up to {seconds} seconds, one set No sound needed, I'm only watching the picture.
ai.screen.program_superseded: That's the old version — I've already reworked it. The fresh button is under my latest answer, hit that one.
ai.screen.program_gone: This offer isn't current anymore. If you saved it, the program's already in “🗂 Programs”; if not, ask the coach to put one together again.

ai.screen.setup_hint_with_choices: Tap an option or write your own. Don't know — just say so, we'll sort it out.
ai.screen.setup_hint_text_only: Answer in words. Don't know — just say so, we'll sort it out.
ai.screen.setup_answers_frame: These are the person's answers to your clarifying questions. If instead of answering they asked a counter-question or said they don't know, respond to that in your text, and if the program can't be built without this data, call ask_setup_questions again with ONLY the questions that are still open. If you have enough to go on, don't ask again — pick a sensible default and say so out loud. And in any case, except for asking again, on this same step BUILD the program by calling propose_program: without calling the tool, the person won't see the composition or a save button — your text alone isn't a program.
ai.screen.setup_enough_frame: No more follow-ups — I won't ask the person anything else. Build the program on sensible defaults and say them out loud: what you assumed about days, time, experience, and equipment. “Build” here is literal: call propose_program, or the person's left with text instead of a program.

coach.ai.system_all:
You're the coach from the basement gym, helping a human coach run their athletes. Below is their clients' diary data: this week's workouts, days since the gym, fresh records, assigned programs, recent workouts with their sets (weight×reps, like 62.5×9) and the verdicts I already computed from those sets: an overall verdict per athlete and one line per exercise with the first and last best set, e1RM and the change. Talk to the coach directly, first person singular only: "I'd add", never "we".
Give one short line per athlete:
- the overall verdict word exactly as given — progressing, mixed, dropping or flat. Never relabel it, never soften or upgrade it. "Progressing", "improved", "went up" only where the verdict says progressing or an exercise line says up; a drop is a drop, flat is flat, even with more reps at a lighter weight. A record line earns a word of support, but never changes the verdict;
- back it with one or two exercise lines, numbers copied as given, like 60×8 → 62.5×9, e1RM 76 → 81kg (+7%);
- away: 7+ days without a workout or behind on an assigned program — say so, the coach should nudge them.
Don't compare sets yourself and don't name a trend for an exercise without a verdict line. No verdicts for an athlete — say in a few words how the week is going.
End with one line: the one concrete thing the coach should do next — who to message and about what, or what to change in the program.
Say only useful facts. Don't talk about your inputs: no "I see no…", "no records listed", "no data on…", "no nudge needed". Nothing to say on a point — skip it silently.
State facts only: no question marks, no guesses, no "maybe", "probably", "seems", "might", "likely". Write exercise names exactly as in the data — don't translate, explain or comment on them.
Don't guess gender from a name: no "he", "she", "him", "her", "his" or "hers" — use the name or "they", "them", "their". Use names exactly as in the data. Only say what the data shows, never make it up. Jabs are only for skipped workouts; records, drops and light weights get support only. No tables, no headings.

coach.ai_chat.mode_prompt: Right now you're building a program not for the person writing to you, but for their athlete, {name}. The one writing is the athlete's human coach: they answer your questions on the athlete's behalf and decide themselves whether to assign the program. Talk to the coach as usual, and about the athlete in the third person. The read tools (get_training_overview, list_recent_workouts, get_full_workout_history, get_exercise_progress, get_weekly_volume_by_group, get_muscle_recovery, get_stalled_lifts, compare_periods, get_bodyweight_history) return the ATHLETE's diary and change nothing in it. You can't see the athlete's profile — goal, experience, equipment, injuries — and neither can the coach, so there's no profile field on purpose. Ask the coach for all of that through ask_setup_questions, phrased about the athlete ("How many days a week can the athlete train?"), and don't make anything up. The question about the athlete's goal goes first in the questionnaire on its own — don't add your own. There's nowhere to remember the answers: save_athlete_profile isn't available here. The program from propose_program goes into the COACH's programs as a new one, and the athlete only gets it when the coach taps "Assign" — don't say the athlete already has it. Don't pass replaces_program here. The athlete's weights are in {unit}.

These are tool arguments, not your reply, so the reply-language rule doesn't apply to them. Keep talking to the coach in English.

These are tool arguments, not your reply, so the reply-language rule doesn't apply to them. Keep talking to the coach in English.

seo.import.hevy.description: Step by step: export a CSV from Hevy and load your history into the bot or the app. I don't double up, I ask about names I'm unsure of, and you can undo the import.
seo.import.hevy.lead: Hevy hands over your history as a CSV file, and I read it as is — nothing to fix by hand.
seo.import.hevy.export.h: Step 1. Export a CSV from Hevy
seo.import.hevy.export_html:
1. In Hevy, open Profile and go to Settings.
  2. Pick Export & Import Data → Export Data → Export Workouts.
  3. Hevy builds a CSV file with all your workouts — save it or share it right away.

Log in pounds in Hevy? No problem: I recognize the weight_lbs column and convert it to your diary's units. Hevy marks warm-up sets itself, and I skip them.

Menu path per the Hevy help center as of October 2026; newer versions may name things differently.
seo.import.strong.title: How to move your workouts from Strong: CSV import — Athlete Diary
seo.import.strong.description: Step by step: export your Strong data as a CSV and load your history into the bot or the app. I skip duplicates, and you can undo the import.
seo.import.strong.lead: Strong saves your history as a CSV file. I recognize its columns myself: date, workout name, duration, exercise, set order, weight, reps and notes.
seo.import.strong.export.h: Step 1. Export a CSV from Strong
seo.import.strong.export_html:
1. In Strong, open Profile and tap the settings gear.
  2. Scroll down and pick Export Strong Data.
  3. Strong saves a CSV file to your phone — then send it to me.

I recognize the columns by their English headers. If your Strong is in another language, the bot asks about the columns one by one, and the app needs a file with English headers — switch Strong to English before you export.

Menu path per public guides as of October 2026; newer versions of Strong may name things differently.
seo.import.csv.title: Import workouts from CSV and Excel — Athlete Diary
seo.import.csv.description: Load your training history from any spreadsheet: date, exercise, weight, reps. I work out the delimiter, date format and weight units myself.
seo.import.csv.lead: Kept your training in a spreadsheet — Excel, Google Sheets or another app? Send me a CSV file and I'll move the history into your diary.
seo.import.csv.export_html:
I need four columns: date, exercise, weight and reps. Set number and RPE are optional.

  • Headers in English or Russian: date, exercise, weight, reps — I recognize them myself.
  • Delimiter: comma, semicolon, tab or pipe. Excel and Google Sheets save differently, I figure it out.
  • Dates: 2025-09-12, 12.09.2025 and other common formats. If a date can be read two ways, I tell you how I read it.
  • A unit in the header — "Weight (lbs)" or weight_lbs — gets converted to your diary's units. No unit means I treat the weight as yours.
  • No header row? In the bot I ask about the columns by number and show you the first row.
  • The extension is .csv. In Excel: File → Save As → CSV. In Google Sheets: File → Download → CSV.

Notes instead of a spreadsheet? Paste them into the bot or the app as text — the AI coach reads them, and I show you the result before logging anything.
seo.import.bot.h: Step 2. Load it into the bot
seo.import.bot_html:
1. Open the bot and go to {settings} → {import_btn}. While your diary is empty, the {import_history} button sits right in the main menu.
  2. Send the CSV file as a document — as is, no edits.
  3. Check what I read and tap {upload}. Until then I log nothing.
seo.import.app.h: Or load it into the iPhone app
seo.import.app_html:
1. In the app, open Settings → Import CSV and pick the file. From Hevy it's shorter: pick Athlete Diary in the Share window.
  2. I show a preview: workouts, sets, units and the exercises I didn't recognize.
  3. All good — run the import.
seo.import.what.h: What I do with the file
seo.import.what_html:
• Split it into workouts by start time and title — two workouts on one day stay two.
  • No doubling up. A workout that's already in your diary (same start minute, or the same exercises on the same day) gets skipped, and I tell you how many.
  • Match the names against the catalog and your own exercises. Where I'm unsure, I ask where it goes and don't import until you pick.
  • Explain what I skip. Warm-ups, cardio, timed exercises and sets with no weight on a loaded exercise don't go in — but I say how many and why, with examples.
  • Carry notes over for exercises and for workouts.
  • Let you undo it. Landed wrong? "↩️ Undo import" removes exactly what I loaded: workouts, sets, the exercises it created and the badges they unlocked. You can undo within {days, plural, one{# day} other{# days}}.
seo.import.cta: Bring your history over — and keep going from where you were.

seo.tool.1rm.title: 1RM Calculator: one rep max for bench, squat, deadlift — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.1rm.description: Work out your estimated one-rep max from weight and reps — Epley or Brzycki, with an RPE adjustment — plus a percentage table for working weights.
seo.tool.1rm.lead: Weight and reps from one set — and I'll work out your estimated one-rep max (e1RM) with the same formula the diary uses.
seo.tool.1rm.too_many: A set longer than {max, plural, one{# rep} other{# reps}} is no good for estimating a max — go heavier.
seo.tool.1rm.how_html:
By default it's the Epley formula: weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30). Brzycki is weight × 36 ÷ (37 − reps); it runs high on long sets, so past 10 reps I switch to Epley — at 10 reps the two give the same number.

RPE says how many reps you had left: @9 is one, @8 is two. The formula gets the reps to failure, but I cap the reserve at five. Sets longer than {max, plural, one{# rep} other{# reps}} don't count: the formulas are fitted to low reps.

In the diary you pick the formula in {settings} — I use it for your records and charts.
seo.tool.1rm.cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll count your estimated max, tonnage and records myself.
seo.tool.wilks.title: Wilks, DOTS and IPF GL calculator — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.wilks.description: Work out your IPF GL, DOTS and Wilks score from your powerlifting total or bench and bodyweight to compare strength across weight classes.
seo.tool.wilks.h1: Wilks, DOTS and IPF GL calculator
seo.tool.wilks.lead: Your squat, bench and deadlift total (or a bench alone) plus bodyweight — and I'll work out the scores lifters of different weights are compared by.
seo.tool.wilks.how_html:
IPF GL (Goodlift) is the score the IPF has used to pick best lifters since 2020: result × 100 ÷ (A − B·e−C·bodyweight). A, B and C differ for men and women, powerlifting and bench, classic and equipped — I use the published IPF table as recorded by OpenPowerlifting and check it against the IPF's own examples.

DOTS is the formula OpenPowerlifting and a number of federations use: total × 500 ÷ a fourth-degree polynomial of bodyweight.

Wilks uses the classic coefficients from before the 2020 revision: a fifth-degree polynomial. The revised Wilks gives different numbers — here I count the classic one.

I keep bodyweight within the same limits the standard tables use: for DOTS that's 40–210 kg for men and 40–150 kg for women. My strength standards are built on DOTS too.
seo.tool.wilks.cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll collect your squat, bench and deadlift records myself.

seo.ex.barbell_squat.lead: The back squat is the main leg lift: quads, glutes and the whole posterior chain, with your back and abs holding the torso.
seo.ex.barbell_squat.setup: Set the rack so the bar sits just below shoulder height. Duck under, put the bar on top of your traps, pull your shoulder blades together and grip a little wider than your shoulders. Unrack, take two or three steps back, feet shoulder-width or a bit wider, toes slightly out. Breathe into your belly and brace before you start down.
seo.ex.barbell_squat.mistakes:
Knees cave in on the way up — push them out along your toes.
Heels come off the floor — keep the weight mid-foot and check your ankle mobility.
Hips shoot up faster than your shoulders and the squat turns into a good morning — lead with your chest so hips and shoulders rise together.
Cutting depth — easy to do with heavy weight; check it on a side-angle video.
seo.ex.barbell_bench_press_medium_grip.l: The barbell bench press is the base lift for chest, front delts and triceps, and the main yardstick of upper-body strength.
seo.ex.barbell_bench_press_medium_grip.s: Lie down with your eyes under the bar. Pull your shoulder blades back and down, chest up, a slight arch in the lower back, feet planted. Grip a little wider than your shoulders, wrists stacked over elbows. Unrack and bring the bar over your shoulders.
seo.ex.barbell_bench_press_medium_grip.m:
Elbows flared out at 90 degrees to the torso — keep them around 45–70 degrees, your shoulders will thank you.
Shoulder blades drift apart on the press — set them before you unrack and keep them there the whole set.
Bouncing the bar off your chest — lower it under control, touch, then press.
Butt coming off the bench — it stays down from the first rep to the last.
seo.ex.barbell_deadlift.lead: The deadlift lifts the bar off the floor with your legs and back: glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors, traps and grip.
seo.ex.barbell_deadlift.setup: Stand with the bar over mid-foot, feet hip-width. Hinge down and grip just outside your legs. Drop your hips until your shins touch the bar, back flat, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar. Breathe in, brace your abs and lats, pull the slack out of the bar — then pull.
seo.ex.barbell_deadlift.mistakes:
Back rounds as the bar breaks the floor — take the slack out and lock your lats before it leaves the ground.
Bar drifts away from your legs — drag it up your shins and thighs, the bar path is a vertical line over mid-foot.
Hips shoot up first — legs and back straighten together, not one after the other.
Leaning back at lockout — standing tall is enough, no need to hyperextend.
seo.ex.romanian_deadlift.lead: The Romanian deadlift is a hinge with nearly straight legs: hamstrings and glutes under stretch while your back holds a flat position.
seo.ex.romanian_deadlift.setup: Take the bar from the rack at hip height or lift it off the floor and stand tall. Shoulder-width grip, knees soft and barely changing angle from there. Shoulder blades back, abs braced.
seo.ex.romanian_deadlift.mistakes:
Squatting instead of hinging — push your hips back, don't drive your knees forward.
Back rounds at the bottom — go only as low as you can keep it flat.
Bar drifts away from your legs — keep it in contact with your thighs.
Chasing weight — this lift is about stretch and control more than kilos.
seo.ex.standing_military_press.lead: The standing overhead press works the delts and triceps while your legs, glutes and abs hold the torso as one piece.
seo.ex.standing_military_press.setup: Take the bar from the rack at chest height, grip a little wider than your shoulders, bar resting on your front delts, elbows slightly in front of the bar. Feet hip-width, glutes and abs tight, ribs down.
seo.ex.standing_military_press.mistakes:
Big arch in the lower back — squeeze glutes and abs, the torso stays straight.
Bar travels forward in an arc — pull your head back and press straight up, then bring your head back under the bar at the top.
Using leg drive — that's a push press; for a strict press the knees stay straight.
Short lockout — finish with straight arms overhead.
seo.ex.bent_over_barbell_row.lead: The bent-over barbell row is a base back lift: lats, rhomboids and rear delts, with the erectors holding the hinge.
seo.ex.bent_over_barbell_row.setup: Grip the bar a little wider than your shoulders and stand tall. Bend your knees, push your hips back and lean forward to nearly parallel with the floor, back flat. Arms hang straight under your shoulders.
seo.ex.bent_over_barbell_row.mistakes:
Torso rises with every rep — hold the angle, otherwise momentum does the work, not your back.
Pulling with your arms — start each rep by pulling your shoulder blades together, elbows drive the bar to your waist.
Back rounds — drop the weight and keep the hinge flat.
Short range — let your arms straighten at the bottom and touch your stomach at the top.
seo.ex.pullups.lead: The pull-up lifts your own bodyweight to the bar: lats, biceps and the muscles between your shoulder blades.
seo.ex.pullups.setup: Grab the bar with an overhand grip a little wider than your shoulders and hang with straight arms. Pull your shoulders away from your ears, brace your abs and glutes, legs together — that keeps the body from swinging.
seo.ex.pullups.mistakes:
Swinging and kicking — every rep starts from a still hang.
Partial reps — straight arms at the bottom, chin over the bar at the top.
Shoulders shrug up to your ears — set the shoulder blades down first, then pull.
Can't do one yet — start with negatives and band-assisted reps; I'll track your progress by reps.
seo.ex.dips_chest_version.lead: Dips press your own bodyweight: chest, triceps and front delts. Leaning forward puts more on the chest.
seo.ex.dips_chest_version.setup: Get up on straight arms, shoulders down, torso leaning slightly forward, legs crossed if you like. Elbows point back, not out.
seo.ex.dips_chest_version.mistakes:
Going too deep from day one — use the depth your shoulders are fine with and add gradually.
Shoulders shrug up at the bottom — keep them down the whole set.
Bouncing at the bottom — lower under control, no rebound.
Elbows flaring out — keep them closer to your body.
seo.ex.leg_press.lead: The leg press trains quads and glutes on a machine: your back is supported, so you can load the legs without a bar on your spine.
seo.ex.leg_press.setup: Sit in the machine, lower back and hips pressed into the pad. Feet shoulder-width in the middle of the platform. Release the safeties, legs nearly straight but knees not locked.
seo.ex.leg_press.mistakes:
Hips peel off the seat at the bottom — lower only as far as your lower back stays down.
Locking your knees at the top — keep a slight bend.
Knees caving in — keep them in line with your toes.
Short reps for a big number — fewer plates and full range beats that.
seo.ex.wide_grip_lat_pulldown.lead: The lat pulldown pulls a handle from overhead to your chest: lats and biceps, a good stand-in for pull-ups and a step toward them.
seo.ex.wide_grip_lat_pulldown.setup: Sit down and lock your thighs under the pads. Grab the bar wider than your shoulders, arms straight. Lean back slightly, chest up.
seo.ex.wide_grip_lat_pulldown.mistakes:
Leaning back more and more and using your body — the lean is small and stays the same.
Pulling behind your neck — pull to your upper chest, it's safer on the shoulders.
Pulling with your arms — drive your elbows down and in, think shoulder blades.
Letting the weight fly up — return the bar under control to straight arms.
seo.ex.seated_cable_rows.lead: The seated cable row is a horizontal pull: mid-back, lats and rear delts.
seo.ex.seated_cable_rows.setup: Sit down, feet braced, knees slightly bent. Grab the handle, back straight, torso upright or leaning just a little forward.
seo.ex.seated_cable_rows.mistakes:
Rocking back and forth — your back does the pulling, not a pendulum; the torso barely moves.
Shoulders shrug up — drop them and squeeze your shoulder blades at the end of the pull.
Back rounds as your arms extend — let the shoulder blades spread, but keep the lower back flat.
Pulling to your chest — bring the handle to your lower stomach.
seo.ex.dumbbell_bench_press.lead: The dumbbell bench press works the chest through a bigger range than the barbell: each arm works on its own, so a weak side can't hide.
seo.ex.dumbbell_bench_press.setup: Sit on the end of the bench, dumbbells on your thighs. Lie back and kick them up with your knees to straight arms over your chest. Shoulder blades back and down, feet on the floor.
seo.ex.dumbbell_bench_press.mistakes:
Dumbbells wobble and drift apart — lower slowly with vertical forearms.
Going too deep — lower to where your shoulders are comfortable, usually just below chest level.
Dropping the dumbbells at the end — bring them to your thighs and sit up, it's better for your shoulders and the floor.
Elbows flared to 90 degrees — keep them at 45–70 degrees to your torso.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_press.lead: The incline dumbbell press puts the emphasis on the upper chest and front delts.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_press.setup: Set the bench at 30–45 degrees. Sit with the dumbbells on your thighs, lie back and bring them over your shoulders. Shoulder blades back, chest up, feet on the floor.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_press.mistakes:
Bench too steep — past 45 degrees it's a shoulder press.
Dumbbells come down toward your neck — lower them to your upper chest.
Hips lift off the seat — your butt stays on the bench.
Banging the dumbbells together at the top — stop just short and keep the tension.
seo.ex.barbell_incline_bench_press_mediu: The incline barbell bench press shifts the bench press toward the upper chest and front delts.
Bench at 30–45 degrees. Lie with the bar over your eyes, shoulder blades back and down, feet on the floor. Grip a little wider than your shoulders.

Bar comes down to mid-chest — on the incline it touches higher, near the collarbones.
Shoulder blades spread — keep them pinned the whole set.
Bouncing off the chest — controlled touch, no rebound.
Hips lift off the bench — that turns the incline into a flat press.
seo.ex.seated_dumbbell_press.lead: The seated dumbbell press works the delts and triceps overhead, with a backrest that protects your lower back.
seo.ex.seated_dumbbell_press.setup: Set the backrest upright or nearly so. Sit back against it, bring the dumbbells to your shoulders, palms forward. Feet on the floor, abs braced.
seo.ex.seated_dumbbell_press.mistakes:
Arching off the backrest — that turns it into a chest press and loads the lower back.
Dumbbells coming down too low — at the bottom they're at shoulder level or just below.
Elbows pulled far back — keep them slightly in front of your torso.
Banging the dumbbells at the top — bring them together under control.
seo.ex.side_lateral_raise.lead: The lateral raise isolates the side delts — that's where shoulder width comes from.
seo.ex.side_lateral_raise.setup: Stand tall, dumbbells by your thighs, elbows slightly bent and locked at that angle. You can lean forward a touch, shoulders down.
seo.ex.side_lateral_raise.mistakes:
Swinging your body — if it won't go up without a heave, it's too heavy.
Shrugging to your ears — that's traps, not delts; keep the shoulders down.
Dumbbells above shoulder height — shoulder level is enough.
Dropping them on the way down — lower slower than you lift.
seo.ex.barbell_curl.lead: The barbell curl is the base lift for the biceps and brachialis.
seo.ex.barbell_curl.setup: Stand tall, bar hanging in your hands with an underhand shoulder-width grip. Elbows tucked to your sides, shoulder blades back, knees soft.
seo.ex.barbell_curl.mistakes:
Swinging with your back — the torso stays still, only the elbows move.
Elbows drifting forward — keep them at your sides.
Not straightening your arms at the bottom — full range gives you more than an extra plate.
Dropping the weight — lower it under control.
seo.ex.hammer_curls.lead: The hammer curl is a neutral-grip curl: brachialis, brachioradialis, biceps and forearms.
seo.ex.hammer_curls.setup: Stand tall, dumbbells at your sides, palms facing each other. Elbows tucked to your body.
seo.ex.hammer_curls.mistakes:
Rotating your wrist — the grip stays neutral the whole rep.
Swinging your body — drop the weight.
Elbows drifting forward and up — keep them at your sides.
Short range — arms go fully straight at the bottom.
seo.ex.triceps_pushdown.lead: The triceps pushdown isolates the triceps, simple to learn and easy on the elbows.
seo.ex.triceps_pushdown.setup: Face the cable, grab the handle, elbows tucked at your sides and bent to about 90 degrees. Lean forward slightly, abs braced.
seo.ex.triceps_pushdown.mistakes:
Elbows moving back and forth — only the forearms move.
Pushing with your bodyweight — if you have to lean into it, it's too heavy.
Not finishing the rep — straighten your arms fully and hold for a second.
Handle flying back up — return it slowly, to about 90 degrees.
seo.ex.ez_bar_skullcrusher.lead: The EZ-bar skull crusher extends the arms from behind the head and loads the long head of the triceps well.
seo.ex.ez_bar_skullcrusher.setup: Lie on a bench with the EZ bar on straight arms over your chest, narrow grip. Tilt your arms slightly back toward your head so the triceps stay loaded at the top.
seo.ex.ez_bar_skullcrusher.mistakes:
Elbows flaring out — keep them pointing up and narrow.
Upper arms moving with the forearms — only the elbow bends.
Dropping the bar toward your forehead — lower it slowly to the top of your head or just behind.
Going too heavy — elbows hate it; more reps is the better trade.
seo.ex.dumbbell_lunges.lead: Dumbbell lunges train the legs and glutes one leg at a time, with balance work on top.
seo.ex.dumbbell_lunges.setup: Stand tall, dumbbells hanging at your sides, feet hip-width. Torso upright, abs braced, eyes forward.
seo.ex.dumbbell_lunges.mistakes:
Step too short — the knee shoots far past the toes and the heel lifts; step longer.
Front knee caving in — keep it over your foot.
Torso falling forward — chest up.
Slamming your knee into the floor — lower to a touch or just short of it, under control.
seo.ex.split_squat_with_dumbbells.lead: The Bulgarian split squat is a one-leg squat with the back foot on a bench: quad and glute of the front leg, lots of work with little weight.
seo.ex.split_squat_with_dumbbells.setup: Stand with your back to a bench and put the top of your rear foot on it. Place the front foot far enough out that your shin is nearly vertical at the bottom. Dumbbells hanging at your sides.
seo.ex.split_squat_with_dumbbells.mistak:
Front foot too close to the bench — the knee drives forward and the heel lifts; move the foot out.
Pushing off the back leg — it's only there for balance, the front leg does the work.
Knee caving in — track it over your toes.
Losing balance — start without dumbbells and hold on to a rack.
seo.ex.goblet_squat.lead: The goblet squat is the easiest squat to learn proper depth and a flat back with.
seo.ex.goblet_squat.setup: Hold a kettlebell or dumbbell with both hands at your chest, elbows down. Feet shoulder-width or a bit wider, toes slightly out.
seo.ex.goblet_squat.mistakes:
Weight drifting off your chest — hug it in, or your torso tips forward.
Heels lifting — weight on mid-foot and heels.
Knees caving — push them out with your elbows at the bottom.
Back rounding at the bottom — only go deeper as long as it stays flat.
seo.ex.front_barbell_squat.lead: The front squat puts the bar on your front delts: a more upright torso, more work for the quads and upper back.
seo.ex.front_barbell_squat.setup: Set the bar on your front delts against your neck, elbows high and forward. Grip with your fingertips at shoulder width or cross your arms. Unrack, feet shoulder-width.
seo.ex.front_barbell_squat.mistakes:
Elbows dropping — the bar rolls forward; keep them high the whole set.
Holding the bar with your hands — it sits on your shoulders, fingers only steady it.
Torso tipping forward — the front squat needs an upright back, start lighter.
Heels lifting — weight mid-foot, check your ankle mobility.
seo.ex.barbell_glute_bridge.lead: The barbell glute bridge drives your hips up from the floor: glutes lead, hamstrings help.
seo.ex.barbell_glute_bridge.setup: Sit on the floor, roll the bar over your hips and pad it. Lie back, knees bent, feet flat at hip width, heels not far from your butt.
seo.ex.barbell_glute_bridge.mistakes:
Arching your lower back at the top — the glutes lift, ribs down, pelvis tucked.
Feet too far out — the hamstrings take over; bring your heels closer.
Knees flaring or caving — keep them over your feet.
No pause at the top — hold a second and squeeze your glutes.
seo.ex.hyperextensions_back_extensions.l: The back extension bends and straightens the torso on a bench: spinal erectors, glutes and hamstrings.
seo.ex.hyperextensions_back_extensions.s: Set the pad so it sits under your hips and your torso can bend freely. Hook your heels, cross your arms on your chest or put your hands behind your head.
seo.ex.hyperextensions_back_extensions.m:
Hyperextending at the top — come up to a straight line, no higher.
Jerking and swinging — move smoothly both ways.
Pad set too high — it digs into your stomach and blocks the hinge; drop it under your hips.
Grabbing a plate right away — get 15–20 clean reps without weight first.
seo.ex.standing_calf_raises.lead: The standing calf raise trains the calves.
seo.ex.standing_calf_raises.setup: Stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of the machine platform or a step, heels hanging off. Shoulders under the pads, knees nearly straight.
seo.ex.standing_calf_raises.mistakes:
Bouncing at the bottom — drop into the stretch and hold a second.
Short range — rise all the way onto your toes.
Bending your knees to help — they stay at the same angle.
Going too fast — calves respond better to control and pauses.
seo.ex.one_arm_dumbbell_row.lead: The one-arm dumbbell row is a supported row: lats and mid-back, one side at a time.
seo.ex.one_arm_dumbbell_row.setup: Put one knee and the same-side hand on a bench, the other foot on the floor. Back flat, nearly parallel to the floor. The dumbbell hangs under your shoulder in the free hand.
seo.ex.one_arm_dumbbell_row.mistakes:
Twisting your torso to get the dumbbell higher — shoulders and hips stay square to the floor.
Pulling to your chest — drive the elbow back, dumbbell to your hip.
Yanking up and dropping down — pull and lower under control.
Shoulder shrugging to the ear — set the shoulder blade down first, then pull.
seo.ex.good_morning.lead: The good morning is a hinge with the bar on your back: hamstrings, glutes and spinal erectors.
seo.ex.good_morning.setup: Put the bar on your traps like for a squat. Feet hip-width, knees slightly bent. Shoulder blades back, abs braced.
seo.ex.good_morning.mistakes:
Back rounding — go only as low as you can keep it flat; often that's above parallel.
Squatting instead of hinging — push your hips back, knees barely change angle.
Using squat weights — good mornings take a lot less.
Jerking up — come up smoothly, driving your hips forward.
seo.ex.pushups.lead: The push-up presses your own bodyweight: chest, triceps and front delts, with your core holding a plank.
seo.ex.pushups.setup: Hands on the floor a little wider than your shoulders, fingers forward. Body in a straight line from heels to head, glutes and abs tight.
seo.ex.pushups.mistakes:
Hips sagging or piking up — keep the body in one line the whole set.
Elbows flared to 90 degrees — keep them closer to your body.
Partial reps — go down until your chest nearly touches the floor.
Head reaching for the floor — your neck continues the line of your back.
seo.ex.plank.lead: The plank is a static hold for your abs and core: it teaches you to keep the body straight under load.
seo.ex.plank.setup: Forearms and toes on the floor, elbows under your shoulders. Body in a straight line from heels to head. Squeeze your glutes, tuck your pelvis, ribs down.
seo.ex.plank.mistakes:
Lower back sagging — squeeze glutes and abs; if you can't hold it, end the set.
Hips up high — that makes it easier and stops it working.
Holding your breath — breathe steadily without losing tension.
Holding for five minutes — once 60 seconds is easy, pick a harder variation instead of adding time.
seo.ex.hanging_leg_raise.lead: The hanging leg raise trains the abs and hip flexors, and your grip along the way.
seo.ex.hanging_leg_raise.setup: Hang from the bar with straight arms, shoulders down. Legs together, body still.
seo.ex.hanging_leg_raise.mistakes:
Swinging — start every rep from a calm hang.
Only lifting the legs — curl your pelvis toward your chest at the top, that's where the abs work.
Dropping your legs — lower them slowly.
Can't lift straight legs — start with bent-knee raises.

seo.faq.what.q: What's a good workout log app with an AI coach?
seo.faq.what.a_html: Athlete Diary is a workout diary with an AI coach, in Telegram and as an iPhone app. You type a set in one line, like 100 8, and I count tonnage, records and estimated max myself. The coach sees your history, builds a program split into days and reviews your form from video. It's free.
seo.faq.free.a_html: It's free. There are no paid plans. The AI coach has a daily cap — {questions, plural, one{# question} other{# questions}} and {videos, plural, one{# video review} other{# video reviews}} a day. Logging workouts, taking programs and using the calculators have no limits.
seo.faq.alt_hevy.q: Is there a free alternative to Hevy?
seo.faq.alt_hevy.a_html: Yes: Athlete Diary is free in full, with no Pro tier, and it has an AI coach that reads your diary. You can bring your Hevy history over as a CSV file. A short fact-by-fact comparison is on the Athlete Diary vs Hevy page.
seo.faq.move.q: Can I move my workouts from Hevy or Strong?
seo.faq.move.a_html: Yes. Export a CSV from Hevy or Strong and send it to the bot or upload it in the app — I split it into workouts, match the exercise names and show you the result before anything is saved. Any spreadsheet with date, exercise, weight and reps works too.
seo.faq.video.a_html: Yes. Send the AI coach a clip of one set — up to {seconds, plural, one{# second} other{# seconds}} — and I'll tell you what I see and what to fix first. Free, up to {videos, plural, one{# video review} other{# video reviews}} a day. How to film it so I can see — here.
seo.faq.platforms.q: What does it run on? Is there an Android app?
seo.faq.platforms.a_html: The bot works wherever Telegram does: Android, iPhone and desktop. There's a dedicated app for iPhone. The bot and the app share one diary.
seo.faq.history.q: Does the coach really see my history?
seo.faq.history.a_html: Yes. The coach looks at your workouts, records, estimated max and bodyweight and answers with numbers from your diary. History you imported from another app counts too.
seo.faq.dupes.q: What happens to workouts that are already in my diary?
seo.faq.dupes.a_html: I won't double them: a workout with the same start time or the same exercises on the same day gets skipped. Exercise names I'm not sure about I ask you instead of guessing.
seo.faq.undo.a_html: Yes, for {days, plural, one{# day} other{# days}}. Undo import removes exactly what that file added — the rest of your diary stays as it is.

seo.tools.description: Free strength training calculators: one-rep max, warm-up sets to a working weight with plates per side, RPE chart, Wilks, DOTS and IPF GL, strength standards, daily protein and calories.
seo.tools.lead: They run right in your browser, no sign-up. The strength ones use the same formula my diary does.

seo.tool.warmup.title: Warm-up calculator: sets up to your working weight — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.warmup.description: How many warm-up sets to do before your working weight and with what weight: a ladder from the empty bar with plates per side, in kg and lb.
seo.tool.warmup.lead: Give me your working weight and reps — I'll lay out a warm-up from the empty bar so you reach your work sets warm, not tired.
seo.tool.warmup.light: Your working weight isn't heavier than the bar — warm up with the bar itself.
seo.tool.warmup.how_html:
First set — the empty bar for 10 reps. Then 40%, 60% and 80% of your working weight for 5, 3 and 2 reps. Before a heavy set (5 reps or fewer) I add 90% for a single: the closer you get to your max, the smaller the last step.

Every weight is rounded down to a step you can load with plates: 2.5 kg or 5 lb. A step that ends up no heavier than the one before drops out — light working weights get a shorter ladder. Warm-up reps aren't work: rest a minute between them, no more. I list what goes on each side right next to every warm-up set.
seo.tool.warmup.cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll track working weights and records myself.
seo.tool.rpe.card: RPE, reps and percent of max.
seo.tool.rpe.title: RPE calculator: RPE chart, reps and % of 1RM — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.rpe.description: RPE chart online: what percent of your one-rep max a set of N reps is at RPE 6–10, and what weight to use for your next set.
seo.tool.rpe.lead: Did a set and rated the RPE? I'll work out your estimated max and suggest a weight for the next set with a different rep count.
seo.tool.rpe.chart_note: Row — RPE, column — reps in the set, cell — percent of estimated max. The formula switch above changes it.
seo.tool.rpe.how_html:
RPE rates how hard a set was, up to 10: 10 — not one more rep, 9 — one left in the tank, 8 — two. I add the reps in reserve to the reps you did and work out your estimated max with the same formula the diary uses (Epley or Brzycki, reserve capped at 5 reps).

The chart is that formula run backwards: percent of max = 1 ÷ e1RM of a 1 kg set. It's not someone else's table, it's my arithmetic: real percentages differ by a few points from person to person, so the next-set weight is a starting point, not an order.
seo.tool.rpe.cta: Add RPE next to a set in the diary — I'll adjust your estimated max for the reserve myself.

seo.strength.title: Strength standards: bench press, squat, deadlift by bodyweight — Athlete Diary
seo.strength.description: Strength standards for men and women by bodyweight: bench press, squat and deadlift. Our own DOTS-based scale with an open method, plus a calculator.
seo.strength.lead: What people lift at your bodyweight — and where you are now. The scale is mine, built on DOTS; the method is open below.
seo.strength.cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll show you how you climb from one standard to the next.
seo.strength.tool.top: That's the top of this scale.
seo.strength.table_note: Each cell is the one-rep max where that standard starts. Kilograms are rounded to 2.5, pounds to 5.
seo.strength.lift_lead: {lift}: the one-rep max that matches each standard at your bodyweight. Don't know your max? Enter the weight and reps of a work set and I'll estimate it.
seo.strength.method_html:
This is my scale, not someone else's table. It's built on DOTS: a formula that puts results on a common footing across bodyweight and sex (coefficients as used by OpenPowerlifting). The thresholds are a DOTS equivalent of a powerlifting total: {thresholds}. 450 is roughly the top 5% of men in classic powerlifting meets, 300 is first-meet level.

DOTS is for a total, and this is a single lift. So I make an assumption: your result in one lift is its usual share of a total. The shares are medians from classic powerlifting results in OpenPowerlifting open data (USAPL, about 17 thousand entries): for men squat {m_squat}%, bench {m_bench}%, deadlift {m_dead}%; for women {f_squat}%, {f_bench}% and {f_dead}%.

Your proportions may differ — some people bench strong, others pull strong — and then a single-lift table shifts. Treat it as a guide to where to grow, not a verdict.
