seo.ex.decline_barbell_bench_press.lead: The decline barbell bench press shifts more of the work to your lower chest and loads the shoulders less than a flat bench.
seo.ex.decline_barbell_bench_press.setup: Hook your feet under the pads and lie down with your eyes under the bar. Pull your shoulder blades together and pin them to the bench. Grip a little wider than your shoulders, same as a flat bench. Unrack with a spotter or on your own, arms straight over your lower chest.
seo.ex.decline_barbell_bench_press.mista:
Lowering the bar to your neck or mid-chest — bring it to the bottom edge of your pecs.
Lifting your hips and sliding on the bench — the leg pads hold you, relax into them.
Going heavy without a spotter — your head is below your feet, and getting out from under the bar is hard.
Bouncing the bar off your chest — lower it under control and touch, don't hit.
seo.ex.close_grip_barbell_bench_press.le: The close-grip bench press is a core triceps lift: same bar, but your elbows stay closer to your body and your arms do most of the work.
seo.ex.close_grip_barbell_bench_press.se: Set up like a regular bench: eyes under the bar, shoulder blades pinched, feet on the floor. Grip at shoulder width — no narrower, or your wrists will hurt. Unrack and hold the bar over your mid-chest, elbows pointing down and slightly out.
seo.ex.close_grip_barbell_bench_press.mi:
Grip too narrow, hands almost touching — your wrists bend back; keep your hands shoulder-width.
Elbows flaring out wide — keep them angled toward your body so the triceps work.
Lowering the bar to your neck — touch your lower chest.
Cutting the lockout short — straighten your arms fully, that's where the triceps work hardest.
seo.ex.machine_bench_press.lead: The machine chest press is a press on a fixed path: handy for finishing your chest after the barbell or learning the movement without a spotter.
seo.ex.machine_bench_press.setup: Set the seat so the handles line up with your mid-chest. Sit back firmly, press your back into the pad and pull your shoulder blades together. Feet on the floor or the footrest. Grab the handles with your elbows just below shoulder height.
seo.ex.machine_bench_press.mistakes:
Seat too high or too low — the handles should travel at chest level, not at your neck or belly.
Peeling your back off and pushing with your torso — keep your back on the pad the whole set.
Slamming into a hard lockout — finish the rep smoothly, no snap at the elbows.
Letting the weight drop — lower it slower than you press it.
seo.ex.cable_crossover.lead: The cable crossover is a chest isolation move: the cables keep tension through the whole range, even where your hands meet.
seo.ex.cable_crossover.setup: Set the pulleys just above shoulder height and grab the handles. Step forward, one foot in front, torso leaning slightly. Arms open, elbows slightly bent — keep that angle for the whole set. Chest up, shoulders down.
seo.ex.cable_crossover.mistakes:
Bending and straightening your elbows — that turns it into a press; keep the elbow angle fixed.
Yanking the weight with your torso — stand stable and bring the handles together with your arms only.
Shoulders creeping up to your ears — drop them, or your traps take over.
Opening too far back — stop when you feel the stretch in your chest, not your shoulder.
seo.ex.butterfly.lead: The pec deck fly is simple chest isolation: the machine holds the path, and all you do is squeeze your pecs.
seo.ex.butterfly.setup: Set the seat so the handles or pads sit at chest height. Sit with your back against the pad and shoulder blades pulled together. Elbows slightly bent, hands or forearms on the handles.
seo.ex.butterfly.mistakes:
Seat too low so your arms travel above your shoulders — that stresses the shoulder joint; handles at chest height.
Lifting your back off and leaning in — back against the pad the whole set.
Letting the weight fly back — return it slowly, the stretch should be controlled.
Squeezing with your hands instead of your chest — think of bringing your elbows together.
seo.ex.dumbbell_flyes.lead: The dumbbell fly works the stretch and shape of your chest: a light weight moving in an arc, not a press.
seo.ex.dumbbell_flyes.setup: Lie on a flat bench, dumbbells over your chest, palms facing each other. Bend your elbows slightly and lock that angle. Shoulder blades together, feet on the floor.
seo.ex.dumbbell_flyes.mistakes:
Going heavy and turning it into a press — this is isolation, use less than you'd press.
Lowering the dumbbells too deep — stop with your elbows about level with the bench.
Arms nearly straight — keep a soft bend, it's easier on your shoulders.
Clanking the dumbbells together at the top — stop a bit short, where your chest is still working.
The rope triceps pushdown is a cable pushdown where you can split the rope at the bottom and squeeze the triceps harder.
Clip a rope to the high pulley. Grab the ends, palms facing each other. Stand close to the stack, torso leaning slightly, elbows bent and tucked to your sides.

Elbows drifting forward and back — pin them to your sides, only your forearms move.
Rocking your torso to help — use a weight you can push down standing still.
Not splitting the rope at the bottom — pull the ends apart at the bottom, that's the hardest squeeze.
Letting it snap up — bring the rope back up under control to just short of a right angle.
seo.ex.cable_rope_overhead_triceps_exten: The overhead cable triceps extension trains the triceps in a stretched position, which works the long head harder than pushdowns do.
Clip a rope to a low or mid pulley. Grab the ends, turn your back to the stack and bring your hands behind your head. Step forward, lean slightly, elbows pointing forward and up.

Elbows flaring out — keep them close to your head.
Straightening your torso instead of your arms — your body stays still.
Arching your lower back — brace your abs and tuck your hips a little.
Short range — let the rope go back behind your head until the triceps stretch.
seo.ex.tricep_dumbbell_kickback.lead: The dumbbell kickback is a light triceps isolation move: the hardest point is at the top, with your arm straight.
seo.ex.tricep_dumbbell_kickback.setup: Brace one hand and knee on a bench, back flat and nearly parallel to the floor. Dumbbell in the other hand, upper arm tight to your side and pointing back, elbow bent to a right angle.
seo.ex.tricep_dumbbell_kickback.mistakes:
Upper arm dropping and rising — it stays fixed along your body, only your forearm moves.
Swinging the dumbbell — extend slowly and hold at the top.
Going heavy — holding a straight arm for a second matters more than the weight.
Rounded back — keep it flat and lean on the bench.
seo.ex.bench_dips.lead: Bench dips are a bodyweight triceps exercise you can do anywhere with a stable edge.
seo.ex.bench_dips.setup: Sit on the edge of a bench, hands beside your hips, fingers pointing forward. Slide your hips off the bench and hold yourself up on your arms. Knees bent, feet on the floor; straight legs or feet on a second bench make it harder.
seo.ex.bench_dips.mistakes:
Going too deep — your shoulder gets pulled forward; stop when your upper arm is about parallel to the floor.
Hips drifting away from the bench — keep your back close to the edge.
Pushing with your legs — your arms do the work, your legs just balance.
Elbows flaring out — point them back.
seo.ex.ez_bar_curl.lead: The EZ-bar curl is a barbell curl on an angled bar: easier on your wrists than a straight one.
seo.ex.ez_bar_curl.setup: Grab the EZ-bar on the bends with an underhand grip, hands about shoulder-width. Stand tall, feet hip-width, knees soft. Elbows at your sides, shoulder blades slightly back.
seo.ex.ez_bar_curl.mistakes:
Swinging your torso — if the weight won't move without it, it's too heavy.
Elbows drifting forward at the top — keep them at your sides, or the biceps get a break.
Dropping the bar — lower it under control to nearly straight arms.
Using the narrow bend when the wide one feels better — pick the bend that doesn't strain your wrists.
seo.ex.dumbbell_bicep_curl.lead: The dumbbell curl is the simplest way to load your biceps: each arm works on its own, and a weaker side shows right away.
seo.ex.dumbbell_bicep_curl.setup: Stand tall with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing forward or toward your thighs. Elbows at your sides, shoulders down. Curl both arms together or alternate.
seo.ex.dumbbell_bicep_curl.mistakes:
Lifting with your shoulder — your elbow stays put, your forearm moves.
Swinging your body — stand still with your abs braced.
Not turning your hand — if you start palm-in, rotate it up as you curl.
Half reps — lower to nearly straight arms.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_curl.lead: The incline dumbbell curl trains your biceps in a stretched position: your arms hang behind your body, so the bottom of the curl is the hardest part.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_curl.setup: Set the bench back to 45–60 degrees and lie back on it. Let your arms hang straight down with the dumbbells, palms forward. Shoulders against the pad, head on the bench.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_curl.mistakes:
Bringing your elbows forward as you curl — your upper arms hang straight down, only your forearms move.
Lifting your shoulders off the pad — that kills the stretch this exercise is for.
Using your standing weight — go lighter here.
Jerking out of the bottom — start each rep smoothly.
seo.ex.concentration_curls.lead: The concentration curl is a one-arm curl with your elbow braced on your thigh: no swinging, no help from your shoulder.
seo.ex.concentration_curls.setup: Sit on the edge of a bench, feet wide. Lean forward and brace the working elbow against the inside of your thigh. Dumbbell hanging near the floor, other hand on your knee.
seo.ex.concentration_curls.mistakes:
Elbow sliding off your thigh — it stays braced the whole set, that's the point.
Leaning back to help — your torso stays forward and still.
Heavy dumbbell, short range — lower to nearly straight.
Rushing — pause at the top and lower slowly.
seo.ex.preacher_curl.lead: The preacher curl puts your elbows on an angled pad, so your biceps work with no cheating from the shoulders.
seo.ex.preacher_curl.setup: Set the seat so your armpits rest on the top edge of the pad. Take an EZ-bar or barbell with an underhand grip. Upper arms and elbows on the pad, arms nearly straight.
seo.ex.preacher_curl.mistakes:
Dropping the weight at the bottom — that's how biceps get hurt; lower slowly and don't snap to full extension.
Lifting your elbows off the pad — they stay down the whole set.
Pad under your belly instead of your armpits — raise or lower the seat.
Rolling your shoulders forward to finish — finish with your arms only.
seo.ex.arnold_dumbbell_press.lead: The Arnold press is a seated dumbbell press with a rotation: palms face you at the bottom and away at the top, so your front delts work through a long range.
seo.ex.arnold_dumbbell_press.setup: Sit on a bench with back support, dumbbells in front of your chest at chin height, palms facing you, elbows in front. Back against the pad, feet on the floor.
seo.ex.arnold_dumbbell_press.mistakes:
Rotating only at the very end — the turn happens through the whole press.
Arching your lower back — back on the pad, abs braced.
Dropping low with elbows flared — at the bottom your elbows are in front, like the start.
Using your regular dumbbell press weight — go lighter here.
seo.ex.face_pull.lead: The face pull works your rear delts and upper back: the exercise that balances out all the pressing in a program.
seo.ex.face_pull.setup: Set a rope on a pulley at face height or a bit higher. Grab the ends with an overhand grip and step back until the weight hangs. Stand tall, chest up, arms straight out in front.
seo.ex.face_pull.mistakes:
Pulling to your chest or belly — pull toward your face, ends going to your ears.
Elbows lower than your hands — keep your elbows high, at shoulder level.
Leaning back with your whole body — if the weight won't move without it, drop it.
Not splitting the rope — pull the ends apart at the end, like a double-biceps pose.
seo.ex.reverse_flyes.lead: The bent-over dumbbell fly isolates your rear delts: a small muscle, so the weight is light and technique is everything.
seo.ex.reverse_flyes.setup: Stand with dumbbells, feet hip-width, hinge forward until you're nearly parallel to the floor, back flat, knees soft. Arms hang down, palms facing each other, elbows slightly bent.
seo.ex.reverse_flyes.mistakes:
Squeezing your shoulder blades and pulling with your back — think of reaching wide, not pinching your blades.
Rocking your torso — the hinge stays fixed.
Lifting above your back line — shoulder height is enough.
Rounded back in the hinge — keep it flat, or lie chest-down on an incline bench.
seo.ex.upright_barbell_row.lead: The upright row works your side delts and traps: the bar travels up along your body with your elbows leading.
seo.ex.upright_barbell_row.setup: Grab the bar overhand, hands a little wider than your shoulders. Stand tall with the bar at your thighs. Shoulders down, chest up.
seo.ex.upright_barbell_row.mistakes:
Narrow grip pulled to your chin — that pinches the shoulder; go wider than shoulder-width and pull to your lower chest.
Hands above your elbows — your elbows lead and stay higher than your hands.
Bouncing the bar with your hips — stand still.
Shoulder pinching or clicking — stop lower, or swap in lateral raises.
seo.ex.front_dumbbell_raise.lead: The dumbbell front raise isolates your front delts; they already work hard in presses, so treat this as a finisher, not a base.
seo.ex.front_dumbbell_raise.setup: Stand tall with dumbbells in front of your thighs, palms facing you or down. Elbows slightly bent, shoulders down, abs braced.
seo.ex.front_dumbbell_raise.mistakes:
Raising above eye level — shoulder height is enough.
Swinging and using your torso — stand still, the weight is light.
Shoulders creeping up — drop them before each rep.
Dropping the dumbbells — lower them as slowly as you raise them.
seo.ex.machine_shoulder_military_press.l: The machine shoulder press is an overhead press on a fixed path: you can push close to failure without a spotter or the risk of dropping the weight.
seo.ex.machine_shoulder_military_press.s: Set the seat so the handles sit at shoulder height or a bit below at the bottom. Sit with your back against the pad, feet on the floor. Grab the handles with your elbows under your hands.
seo.ex.machine_shoulder_military_press.m:
Seat too low — the press starts behind your ears, which is rough on the shoulder; handles at shoulder height.
Lifting your hips and arching — back on the pad the whole set.
Slamming into lockout — straighten your arms smoothly.
Short reps at the top — bring the handles down to shoulder level.
seo.ex.chin_up.lead: Chin-ups are pull-ups with your palms facing you: the biceps help more, so many people find them easier than an overhand grip.
seo.ex.chin_up.setup: Grab the bar underhand at shoulder width. Hang with straight arms, shoulders pulled down away from your ears, legs together or crossed. Brace your abs so you don't swing.
seo.ex.chin_up.mistakes:
Kipping and swinging — every rep starts from a dead hang with no leg kick.
Chin not reaching the bar — pull until your chin clears it.
Shoulders at your ears at the bottom — set your shoulder blades down before each rep.
Dropping down — lower yourself under control, that's half the work.
seo.ex.t_bar_row_with_handle.lead: The T-bar row is a bent-over row with one end of the bar anchored: your back works heavy on a steadier path than with a free barbell.
seo.ex.t_bar_row_with_handle.setup: Straddle the bar, feet shoulder-width, bar between your feet. Hinge over with a flat back and bent knees. Grab the handle, set your shoulder blades and lift the bar off the floor to straight arms.
seo.ex.t_bar_row_with_handle.mistakes:
Rounded back — keep your lower back flat and hinge from the hips.
Standing up with each rep — keep the same torso angle.
Yanking the weight to your chest — row to your lower belly.
Not lowering to straight arms — let your back stretch at the bottom of every rep.
seo.ex.sumo_deadlift.lead: The sumo deadlift uses a wide stance with your hands inside your knees: the torso stays more upright, your legs and glutes do more, and the bar travels a shorter path.
seo.ex.sumo_deadlift.setup: Take a wide stance, toes turned out, bar over mid-foot. Drop down with a flat back and grab the bar shoulder-width, inside your legs. Push your knees out over your toes, chest up, pull the slack out of the bar.
seo.ex.sumo_deadlift.mistakes:
Knees caving in — push them out over your toes the whole set.
Hips shooting up first — chest and hips rise together.
A stance so wide you can't get your hips down — find the width where your shins are nearly vertical.
Jerking the bar off the floor — take the slack out first, then push the floor away.
seo.ex.rack_pulls.lead: The rack pull is a partial deadlift: the bar starts above or around your knees, so you can handle more than your normal max.
seo.ex.rack_pulls.setup: Set the safety pins or blocks so the bar sits just below or just above your knees. Step in close, feet hip-width, grip at shoulder width. Back flat, shoulders over the bar.
seo.ex.rack_pulls.mistakes:
Bar set too high — it turns into a shrug; start around your knees.
Rounded back under heavy weight — if your back won't hold, the weight is too heavy.
Leaning back at the top — standing tall and squeezing your glutes is enough.
Dropping the bar onto the pins — lower it under control.
seo.ex.straight_arm_pulldown.lead: The straight-arm pulldown pulls a cable down with straight arms: your lats work without the biceps, a good way to feel your back before rows.
seo.ex.straight_arm_pulldown.setup: Face a high pulley with a straight bar or rope. Grab it overhand at shoulder width, step back and lean forward, arms nearly straight and raised in front.
seo.ex.straight_arm_pulldown.mistakes:
Bending your elbows — that makes it a row; keep your arms nearly straight the whole set.
Rocking your torso — the lean stays fixed.
Shoulders shrugging up — drop them and pull the bar to your thighs.
Letting the bar fly up — return it slowly to a stretch in your back.
seo.ex.trap_bar_deadlift.lead: The trap bar deadlift uses a hexagonal bar you stand inside: the weight sits at your centre, which is easier on your back than a conventional deadlift.
seo.ex.trap_bar_deadlift.setup: Step into the centre of the bar, feet hip-width. Squat down and grab the side handles, back flat, eyes forward. Brace and pull the slack out.
seo.ex.trap_bar_deadlift.mistakes:
Dropping into a full squat and shoving your knees forward — hips sit a bit higher than a squat, shins nearly vertical.
Rounded back at the start — chest up, shoulder blades down.
Standing off-centre — the bar tilts; keep the handles level with your feet.
Lowering by bending only your back — bend your knees and hips together.
seo.ex.inverted_row.lead: The inverted row is a bodyweight horizontal row under a low bar: a step toward pull-ups and a solid back exercise in its own right.
seo.ex.inverted_row.setup: Set a bar in a rack or Smith machine at about waist height. Lie under it, grip a little wider than your shoulders and hang with straight arms. Body in a straight line from heels to head, heels on the floor.
seo.ex.inverted_row.mistakes:
Hips sagging — squeeze your glutes and abs, body like a plank.
Reaching for the bar with your chin — pull your chest to the bar.
Short range — lower all the way to straight arms.
Too easy — set the bar lower or put your feet on a bench.
seo.ex.hack_squat.lead: The hack squat is a machine squat with an angled back pad: your back stays supported, so you can load your quads heavy without a bar on your shoulders.
seo.ex.hack_squat.setup: Step into the machine with your back and shoulders against the pads. Feet on the platform at shoulder width, centred or a little high. Release the safeties with your legs nearly straight.
seo.ex.hack_squat.mistakes:
Heels lifting — keep your whole foot down; if your heels rise, move your feet higher.
Knees caving in — track them over your toes.
Short reps with heavy weight — go at least to thighs parallel with the platform.
Snapping your knees into lockout — finish softly, no knee pop.
seo.ex.leg_extensions.lead: The leg extension isolates your quads: the one exercise where the front of your thigh works alone, without glutes or back.
seo.ex.leg_extensions.setup: Adjust the back pad so your knees line up with the machine's pivot. Roller on your lower shins, just above your feet. Sit back firmly and hold the handles.
seo.ex.leg_extensions.mistakes:
Knees off the pivot — it's rough on the knee; move the back pad.
Kicking your legs up — extend smoothly and pause at the top.
Hips lifting off the seat — hold the handles and stay seated.
Dropping the weight — lower it slowly.
seo.ex.lying_leg_curls.lead: The lying leg curl isolates your hamstrings: they work apart from the glutes, which deadlift variations don't give you.
seo.ex.lying_leg_curls.setup: Lie face down with your knees just past the bench edge, lined up with the pivot. Roller above your heels. Hold the handles and keep your hips on the bench.
seo.ex.lying_leg_curls.mistakes:
Hips lifting — press them into the bench, or your lower back takes over.
Swinging your legs — curl smoothly and pause at the top.
Partial range — curl until the roller nearly touches your glutes.
Dropping the weight — lower slowly, it's half the work.
seo.ex.seated_leg_curl.lead: The seated leg curl isolates your hamstrings in a stretched position, so they work harder than when lying down.
seo.ex.seated_leg_curl.setup: Sit with your knees on the pivot. Lower roller above your heels, upper pad tight on your thighs just above the knees. Back against the pad, hold the handles.
seo.ex.seated_leg_curl.mistakes:
Thigh pad not holding you down — your legs lift off the seat; lower it tighter.
Knees off the pivot — move the back pad.
Yanking the curl — pull smoothly and pause at the bottom.
Letting the weight snap back — straighten your legs slowly.
seo.ex.barbell_hip_thrust.lead: The barbell hip thrust is the main glute exercise: your hips rise against the load, and your glutes work in full contraction.
seo.ex.barbell_hip_thrust.setup: Sit on the floor with your back to a bench, bottom of your shoulder blades on its edge. Roll the bar into the crease of your hips with a pad under it. Feet hip-width, knees bent so your shins are vertical at the top.
seo.ex.barbell_hip_thrust.mistakes:
Arching your lower back at the top — tuck your hips and look forward, not at the ceiling.
Feet too far or too close — your shins should be vertical at the top.
Pushing through your toes — drive through your heels and mid-foot.
Stopping short of full hip extension — at the top, knees to shoulders make a straight line.
seo.ex.dumbbell_step_ups.lead: Dumbbell step-ups train your legs and glutes one side at a time: differences between sides show up and even out.
seo.ex.dumbbell_step_ups.setup: Set a sturdy bench or box in front of you, knee height or a bit lower. Dumbbells hanging at your sides. Put one whole foot on the platform.
seo.ex.dumbbell_step_ups.mistakes:
Pushing off the bottom leg — rise with the leg on the box; the bottom one only helps you start.
Working knee caving in — track it over your toes.
Box too high — your knee above your hip at the start makes good form hard.
Jumping down — lower yourself slowly, controlling with the working leg.
seo.ex.barbell_lunge.lead: Barbell lunges put the weight on your back: legs and glutes work under a squat-like load, but each leg on its own.
seo.ex.barbell_lunge.setup: Set the bar on your upper back as for a squat and walk it out. Stand tall, feet hip-width. Abs braced, eyes forward.
seo.ex.barbell_lunge.mistakes:
Stepping onto one line like a tightrope — keep your feet hip-width or you'll lose balance.
Back knee slamming the floor — come close, but touch softly.
Torso folding forward — keep your chest up.
Short step with the knee far past your toes — step so your front shin is nearly vertical at the bottom.
seo.ex.stiff_legged_barbell_deadlift.lea: The stiff-legged deadlift keeps your knees almost straight: your hamstrings stretch more than in a Romanian deadlift.
seo.ex.stiff_legged_barbell_deadlift.set: Stand holding the bar, shoulder-width grip, feet hip-width. Knees slightly bent and locked at that angle for the whole set. Shoulder blades back, back flat.
seo.ex.stiff_legged_barbell_deadlift.mis:
Rounding your back to reach lower — go only as low as your back stays flat; depth comes with flexibility.
Bending your knees on the way down — keep the knee angle fixed.
Rocking onto your toes — weight on your heels and mid-foot.
Bar drifting away from your legs — keep it close to your thighs and shins.
seo.ex.crunches.lead: Crunches are the basic move for your rectus abdominis: a short movement where your ribs pull toward your hips.
seo.ex.crunches.setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet on the floor. Hands behind your ears or crossed on your chest. Lower back pressed down, chin slightly tucked.
seo.ex.crunches.mistakes:
Pulling your head with your hands — they only support it, your abs do the work.
Sitting all the way up — lifting your shoulder blades is enough; this isn't a sit-up.
Rushing with momentum — curl slowly and breathe out.
Lower back lifting off the floor — press it down, or your hip flexors take over.
seo.ex.cable_crunch.lead: The cable crunch is a kneeling crunch with a rope: your abs work against a load you can add to like any other exercise.
seo.ex.cable_crunch.setup: Clip a rope to the high pulley and kneel facing it. Hold the ends beside your head. Hips over your knees, thighs still.
seo.ex.cable_crunch.mistakes:
Sitting back onto your heels by bending at the hips — your thighs stay put, only your spine curls.
Pulling with your arms — the rope stays by your head, your abs pull.
Going too heavy — if you can't round your back, your arms and bodyweight are doing it.
Letting the weight yank you up — come back slowly.
seo.ex.ab_roller.lead: The ab wheel rollout has you roll out forward with a wheel: your abs hold your torso against the stretch, one of the hardest core exercises.
seo.ex.ab_roller.setup: Kneel and grab the wheel handles under your shoulders. Tuck your hips, brace your abs and glutes. Back slightly rounded, not arched.
seo.ex.ab_roller.mistakes:
Lower back sagging at the far point — roll out only as far as your back stays flat.
Hips staying back while only your arms roll — your body moves as one line.
Coming back by folding at the hips — pull the wheel back with your abs.
Starting with full rollouts — beginners do fine with a quarter range or rolling into a wall.
seo.ex.side_bridge.lead: The side plank is a static hold for your obliques and the side of your core: it teaches you to keep your body straight when the load comes from the side.
seo.ex.side_bridge.setup: Lie on your side, elbow under your shoulder, forearm on the floor. Legs straight, feet stacked or one in front of the other. Lift your hips until your body is a straight line.
seo.ex.side_bridge.mistakes:
Hips sagging toward the floor — lift them, heels to head in one line.
Hips drifting back — keep your hips in line with your torso.
Shoulder creeping up to your ear — elbow right under the shoulder, push the floor away.
Only training one side — hold both sides for the same time.

seo.tool.tonnage.card: How much you lifted in a workout — and how many elephants that is.
seo.tool.tonnage.title: Tonnage calculator: total weight lifted in a workout — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.tonnage.description: Work out your workout tonnage: weight × reps × sets for every line, the total in kg or tonnes, reps, average weight and a real-world comparison — the same one the bot gives after a workout.
seo.tool.tonnage.lead: Enter your sets line by line — weight, reps and how many sets — and I'll add up everything you lifted in the workout.
seo.tool.tonnage.rows: Sets: weight × reps × number of sets
seo.tool.tonnage.how_html:
Tonnage is the sum of weight × reps over all working sets. Three sets of 8 with 80 kg is 80 × 8 × 3 = 1920 kg. Past a tonne I show it in tonnes.

The comparison under the total uses the same list I use in the bot after a workout: a Saint Bernard, a motorcycle, a bear, a grand piano, a horse, a cow, a car, a delivery van, an elephant, an orca and a bus. I pick an object that fits between 2 and 40 times into your tonnage, so the number makes sense. In the diary every workout gets its own object; here you get the lightest one that fits.

Average weight is tonnage divided by all reps: it shows whether you worked heavier than last time even if you did more sets. Tonnage tracks volume, not strength — for strength look at your estimated max. Why volume matters at all is in the guide on sets per muscle per week.
seo.tool.tonnage.cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll count the tonnage of every workout and show you whether it's going up.
seo.tool.rest-timer.card: 60, 90, 120 or 180 seconds between sets — with sound and vibration.
seo.tool.rest-timer.title: Rest timer between sets, online — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.rest-timer.description: A free gym rest timer: 60, 90, 120 and 180 seconds or your own time, sound and vibration at the end, and the screen stays on. Works in your phone's browser.
seo.tool.rest-timer.lead: Pick a time and hit Start after your set. When the rest is up I'll beep and, where your phone allows it, buzz.
seo.tool.rest-timer.log_cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll remember the weight and reps
seo.tool.rest-timer.how_html:
For muscle growth, resting longer than a minute gives a small edge, and past about ninety seconds the difference mostly disappears — that's what the Singer et al. (2024) meta-analysis found. For strength on heavy compound lifts, 2–3 minutes: in Schoenfeld's 2016 study the group resting 3 minutes gained more strength than the one resting 1 minute. The details, with numbers and links, are in the guide on how long to rest between sets.

  • 60 s — isolation work, abs, light sets.
  • 90 s — most hypertrophy work.
  • 120 s — heavy sets in moderate reps.
  • 180 s — squats, deadlifts, bench for 3–6 reps.

The countdown runs off the phone's clock, so switching tabs doesn't slow it down. Sound kicks in after your first tap on Start — that's how browsers allow it. Vibration works on Android; iPhone browsers don't vibrate. Keep the screen on holds the display awake during the rest, where the browser supports it.
seo.tool.rest-timer.cta: Rested? Log the set. The diary keeps the weight and reps, and I'll work out the target for next time.
seo.tool.goal.card: A forecast for when you'll hit your target on bench, squat or deadlift.
seo.tool.goal.title: When will I bench 100 kg? Strength goal forecast for bench, squat and deadlift — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.goal.description: A forecast of how many months it'll take to hit your target weight, from your best set or 1RM, training age and how often you train the lift. A date range, milestones by week and an image for stories.
seo.tool.goal.lead: Tell me what you lift now and what you're after — I'll estimate the month you get there if you keep training steadily.
seo.tool.goal.freq: Workouts with this lift per week
seo.tool.goal.now: Your estimated max right now is {max}.
seo.tool.goal.too_long: Longer than three years — set a closer milestone first.
seo.tool.goal.honest: This is a forecast, not a promise: illness, holidays, sleep and food move the dates both ways.
seo.tool.goal.log_cta: Let the diary walk you to it
seo.tool.goal.how_html:
I start from your estimated max (e1RM): from your best set with the Epley formula — the same one the diary uses — or your 1RM as is. Sets longer than {max_reps} reps don't count; the formulas fall apart there.

Then comes the weekly growth rate, as a share of your current max, with a fast and a slow end. Under six months of training — 0.8% to 1.5% a week, under two years — 0.3% to 0.6%, beyond that — 0.1% to 0.25%. The rate fades: after a year it's half of where it started, after two years a third, because every next kilo costs more. Frequency is a multiplier: one session a week with the lift grows slower (×0.8), three a bit faster than two (×1.1). These are our assumptions, not a law of nature: frequency matters more for strength than for size (the Pelland et al. meta-analysis), but nobody knows your exact rates.

There's a ceiling on top — how my diary actually moves weight: double progression adds at most one rep per workout, and a rep is about 1/30 of the weight. The forecast never gets near that ceiling, but it keeps me from promising you the impossible.

So the answer is a range of months, not a date. The table shows where you'll be every four weeks at the slow and at the fast rate. How to stay on the fast end is in the guide on progressive overload; what to do if you stall is in the one on plateaus.
seo.tool.goal.cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll check your progress against the forecast and tell you when it's time to change the plan.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.card: Your squat, bench, deadlift and total against competitive powerlifters in your class.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.title: Strength level calculator: how strong am I? — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.strength-percentile.description: Compare your squat, bench press, deadlift and total with raw powerlifting meet results from the open OpenPowerlifting data: your percentile in your IPF weight class.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.h1: Strength level calculator: how strong am I?
seo.tool.strength-percentile.lead: Enter your best lifts and I'll show what share of competitive powerlifters in your weight class you're stronger than, lift by lift. They're a strong, self-selected crowd, so even a third is serious.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.raw: Raw: a belt and wrist wraps are fine, suits and knee wraps aren't.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.context: These are people who prepared for a meet. Among regular gym-goers the same lift ranks a lot higher.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.cooper: For reference: in a Cooper Center study of 7,627 ordinary adults (mostly men), the average bench press was 0.82× bodyweight. Yours is {r}×.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.cls: Class up to {cls} kg, {n} lifters in the table.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.empty: Enter your bodyweight and at least one lift.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.how_html:
With people who step on the platform. This is the open OpenPowerlifting data (public domain) — results from {meets} USAPL meets. Only completed raw full-power performances go into the table; every lifter counts once, with their best result in the class.

Keep in mind: these are people who prepared for a meet. Among everyone who goes to the gym, the same lift ranks a lot higher. Stronger than 30% on the platform is already serious strength.

There are no open tables for regular gym-goers, so for the bench I add one reference point from ordinary people: in a Cooper Center study of 7,627 adults (mostly men), the average bench press was 0.82× bodyweight. There's no open figure like that for the squat or deadlift, so I don't make one up.

The classes are IPF weight classes: for men up to 59, 66, 74, 83, 93, 105, 120 kg and 120+, for women up to 47, 52, 57, 63, 69, 76, 84 kg and 84+. Between the table points I interpolate linearly. A script builds the table from the open meet results; it was built on {built}.

For a level that accounts for bodyweight, see the strength standards and DOTS and Wilks.
seo.tool.strength-percentile.cta: Log your sets in the diary — I'll recalculate your estimated max after every workout.
seo.template.workout-log.title: Workout log template for Excel and Google Sheets (xlsx, csv) — Athlete Diary
seo.template.workout-log.description: A free workout log template: xlsx and csv with date, workout, exercise, set, weight, reps, RPE and notes. Fill it in and upload it to the bot — your history imports without manual fixes.
seo.template.workout-log.lead: A spreadsheet for people who live in Excel or Google Sheets. Its columns are exactly what my importer reads, and the exercise names come from my catalog — fill it in and upload your history without a single question.
seo.template.workout-log.files_note: The xlsx has three sheets: an empty Log, an Example with two workouts and Exercises — the whole catalog by muscle group. You can upload the example csv to the bot right away to see how the import lands (and undo it right after).
seo.template.workout-log.upload_cta: Upload your filled-in template — I'll sort out the history.
seo.template.workout-log.upload_html:
1. Save the Log sheet as CSV — how to do it in Excel and Google Sheets is below.
  2. In the bot open {settings} → {import_btn} and send the file as a document. In the iPhone app — Settings → Import CSV.
  3. I'll show what I read: workouts, sets, exercises. Tap {upload} and I log it. Until then nothing shows up in your diary.
seo.template.workout-log.columns_note_ht: Four are required: date, exercise, weight and reps. The rest can stay empty. Don't rename the headers — that's how I recognise the columns. More on what I do with the file is on the CSV import page.
seo.template.colhelp.date: The workout day. YYYY-MM-DD works best, like 2026-10-14.
seo.template.colhelp.workout: The workout name, like Upper or Day A. Two workouts on one day with different names stay two.
seo.template.colhelp.exercise: The exercise name. Take it from the Exercises sheet so I match it to the catalog exactly. Your own name works too.
seo.template.colhelp.set: The set number: 1, 2, 3. A W (warm-up) gets skipped.
seo.template.colhelp.weight: Weight in kilograms. For pull-ups or push-ups without extra weight, leave it empty.
seo.template.colhelp.rpe: How hard it was, 6 to 10. Optional.

seo.template.workout-log.example.h: What a filled-in one looks like
seo.template.workout-log.excel_html:
1. Open the Log sheet and fill it in — one row per set.
  2. File → Save As → file type CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited). Excel saves only the open sheet — which is what you want.
  3. If Excel warns that some features will be lost, say yes: a CSV keeps only the values.

The date column is already formatted as YYYY-MM-DD, so dates go into the CSV unambiguously, however your computer is set up.
seo.template.workout-log.sheets_html:
I can't hand you a ready Google Sheet — the site has no Drive of its own. But the xlsx opens in Sheets as is:

  1. Create a blank spreadsheet, choose File → Import → Upload and drop in the workout-log.xlsx you downloaded.
  2. In the import dialog pick Replace spreadsheet — all three sheets and the exercise drop-down come along.
  3. Fill in Log. To upload, open that sheet and choose File → Download → Comma-separated values (.csv). Sheets downloads only the current sheet.

Even quicker: open the xlsx in Google Drive and choose Open with Google Sheets.
seo.template.workout-log.why_html:
This isn't just another spreadsheet. The headers are the exact words my importer uses to recognise columns, so there's no "which column is the weight?". Weight (kg) tells me the unit: if you train in pounds, rename it to Weight (lb) and I'll convert to your diary's units.

The names on the third sheet are my catalog in English. A catalog name gets matched exactly: the exercise gets its images and technique notes and lands in the right muscle group. The set number and workout name keep two workouts on one day from merging into one.

You can keep logging in the spreadsheet — but in Telegram it's one line, 100 8, and I work out tonnage, records and your estimated max myself. How to keep a log that actually helps you grow is in the workout log guide.
seo.template.workout-log.cta: Rather log as you train? Log each set straight into the diary — on iPhone or in Telegram, no spreadsheet.
seo.template.example.note_squat: Last set was hard, depth was fine
seo.template.example.note_press: Fifth rep of the last set with a lean back
seo.faq.tpl_why_csv.q: Why upload a CSV and not the xlsx itself?
seo.faq.tpl_why_csv.a_html: The bot and the app read CSV — every spreadsheet and every tracker exports it, from Hevy to Strong. Saving a sheet as CSV takes two seconds; the steps are above. The xlsx is there for convenience: the exercise drop-down, the date format and an example on the next sheet.
seo.faq.tpl_lb.q: I train in pounds. What do I do?
seo.faq.tpl_lb.a_html: Rename the Weight (kg) header to Weight (lb). I read the unit from the header and convert the weights to your diary's units. Without a unit in the header I assume the weights are in the units from your settings.
seo.faq.tpl_names.q: What if my exercise isn't on the list?
seo.faq.tpl_names.a_html: Type your own name — the list suggests, it doesn't forbid. If you already have a similar exercise, I'll ask where to put it. If not, I'll create a new one under your name.
seo.faq.tg_install.q: Do I need to install anything?
seo.faq.tg_install.a_html: No. The bot lives in Telegram: open it from the link and log your first set. The iPhone app is optional, and it shares the same diary with the bot.
seo.faq.tg_voice.a_html: Yes. Send a voice message like "a hundred for eight" — I'll pick out the weight and reps and log the set just like the line 100 8.
seo.telegram.s7.p_html: Hands busy or in gloves? Say "a hundred for eight" in a voice message. I pick out the weight and reps and log the set as if you'd typed 100 8.
seo.telegram.s8.p_html: Training with a coach? Invite them — they'll see your diary, comment on a workout and assign you a program. You read their notes right where you log your sets.
seo.telegram.s9.p_html: The bot runs in Telegram on Android, iPhone and desktop — open the link and start logging. Want a separate iPhone app? Same diary, signed in through Telegram.

seo.ai-coach.ex.note: These are examples: the numbers are made up, but the questions and answers are the kind the coach gives from a real diary.
seo.ai-coach.ex.history.q: Why isn't my bench going up?
seo.ai-coach.ex.history.a_html:
Over the last 8 weeks your estimated bench max has been sitting at 92–93 kg. You do 3×5 with 80 kg every time, and your reps haven't moved in three weeks.

Try double progression: 3 sets of 6–10 with 72.5 kg. Add a rep until you hit 3×10, then +2.5 kg and back to 6.
seo.ai-coach.ex.program.q: I train three times a week and have a barbell, a rack and a pull-up bar. I want to get stronger.
seo.ai-coach.ex.program.a_html:
Here's "Full body — 3 days":

  • Day 1: squat 3×5, bench 3×5, barbell row 3×8
  • Day 2: deadlift 2×5, overhead press 3×6, pull-ups 3×max
  • Day 3: squat 3×6, bench 3×6, barbell row 3×10

Like it? Take it into your programs and I'll show the plan at every workout.
seo.ai-coach.ex.video.q: Video: squat, 100 kg for 5 — what's off?
seo.ai-coach.ex.video.a_html:
From the side I can see it: on the last two reps your hips rise before your chest, your torso tips forward and the load shifts to your lower back. Fix that first — drive up with your chest, not your hips.

Depth is good, below parallel. I can't see your knees from this angle — film slightly from the front if you want me to check them too.
seo.ai-coach.ex.load.q: How many sets for my back should I do a week?
seo.ai-coach.ex.load.a_html:
Right now your diary shows 8 working sets for back a week: barbell rows and pull-ups. For growth the usual range is 10 to 20.

Add 3 sets of lat pulldowns for 10–12 on day two. In a month we'll check whether your rows are moving.
seo.video-review.example.exercise: Deadlift, 140 kg for 3, filmed from the side
seo.video-review.example.body_html:
• At the start your hips sit low and the bar is ahead of mid-foot — it drifts away from your legs in the first few inches.
  • Your lower back stays flat to the knees and rounds slightly on the third rep.
  • Fix the start first: bar over mid-foot, shoulders just ahead of the bar — and pull along your legs.

seo.muscles.count: {n, plural, one{# exercise in the catalog} other{# exercises in the catalog}}
seo.muscles.how.h: How I count volume per group
seo.muscles.how_html:
Every working set counts toward the group its exercise belongs to. For shoulders and legs I also count individual muscles — front, side and rear delts, quads, hamstrings, glutes and calves — otherwise "16 sets for shoulders" hides three sets for the side delts.

The deadlift sits under back, but it's mostly glutes and hamstrings doing the work. So one deadlift set is half a set for back and half for legs (a quarter each for hamstrings and glutes). The diary counts it the same way when it shows weekly volume, and so does the coach when building a program. How many sets a week you need to grow is in the volume guide.

seo.mus.chest.title: Chest exercises: presses, flyes, push-ups — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.chest.description: How to train your chest: bench press, dumbbell press, incline presses, dips, flyes and cable crossovers — technique, volume tips and the programs that give the chest the most sets.
seo.mus.chest.lead: The chest grows from presses and flyes at different angles. The base is a flat press, the upper chest comes from an incline, and the stretch from flyes and cable crossovers.
seo.mus.chest.about_html: The pec major brings your arms together in front of you and pulls the upper arm down — so both presses and flyes load it. Its upper (clavicular) part works harder on a 30–45° incline, the lower part a bit more on dips and decline presses. In almost every press the front delts and triceps work alongside the chest.
seo.mus.chest.tips:
Pull your shoulder blades back and keep them pinned — the chest takes the load and the shoulder stays in a safe position.
Add an incline press to the flat one so the whole chest works, not just the middle.
Don't chase weight on flyes: the work is in the stretch at the bottom, not the last inches at the top.
Mix the tools: a barbell lets you load heavy, dumbbells give range and work each arm on its own.
seo.mus.back.title: Back exercises: pull-ups, rows, deadlifts — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.back.description: How to train your back: pull-ups, lat pulldowns, barbell and dumbbell rows, cable rows and deadlifts — technique, balancing vertical and horizontal pulls, and programs.
seo.mus.back.lead: Two kinds of pulls build a back: vertical — pull-ups and pulldowns — for width, horizontal — rows — for thickness. The deadlift adds the lower back and the whole posterior chain.
seo.mus.back.about_html: The lats pull your arm down and back — pull-ups and pulldowns. The traps and rhomboids squeeze the shoulder blades together — rows to the waist and chest. The spinal erectors keep your spine straight when you're bent over and when you deadlift. The biceps and rear delts help in almost every pull, and your grip often gives out before your back.
seo.mus.back.tips:
Keep it balanced: a vertical and a horizontal pull every week. I'll flag it in your progress review if one's been missing for a while.
Start the pull with your shoulder blade, not your arm: pull it down and back first, then bend the elbow.
Your grip goes before your back — use straps on heavy pulls.
Don't count the deadlift as your main lat exercise: it's about hamstrings, glutes and lower back.
seo.mus.shoulders.title: Shoulder exercises: presses, raises, face pulls — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.shoulders.description: How to train shoulders: standing barbell press, dumbbell and Arnold presses, lateral raises, upright rows, reverse flyes and face pulls — all three delt heads, technique and programs.
seo.mus.shoulders.lead: The delts have three heads and one press isn't enough: presses hit the front, lateral raises the side, rows and reverse flyes the rear. Wide shoulders take all three.
seo.mus.shoulders.about_html: The front delt raises your arm forward and works hard in every press, overhead and flat. The side delt lifts your arm out to the side and gives your shoulders width. The rear delt takes your arm back, stabilises the joint and often lags, because presses barely touch it. The diary counts sets for each head separately — more on the side delt and rear delt pages.
seo.mus.shoulders.tips:
If you bench a lot, your front delts are already busy — separate front raises are often overkill.
Add lateral raises 2–3 times a week: side delts need volume and recover fast.
Train rear delts as much as side delts — for the look and for healthy shoulders.
In the standing press, squeeze your glutes and abs and don't arch your lower back.
seo.mus.side-delts.title: Side delts: exercises for wider shoulders — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.side-delts.description: How to build your side delts: dumbbell lateral raises, cable lateral raises, upright rows and presses — technique, sets per week and the programs that load them.
seo.mus.side-delts.lead: The side delts give your shoulders width, and presses barely load them. Lateral raises build them — light weight, clean range and plenty of volume.
seo.mus.side-delts.about_html: The middle head of the deltoid lifts your arm out to the side up to horizontal. Raises use light weights, so the mistake is almost always the same — swinging the torso and letting the traps steal the work. The shoulder does the job: the elbow leads, the hand stays no higher than the elbow.
seo.mus.side-delts.tips:
Pick a weight you can raise for 12–20 clean reps without jerking your body.
Cable raises keep tension at the bottom of the range — a good partner for dumbbells.
A wide-grip upright row also hits the side delts, but keep your elbows no higher than your shoulders.
Raise more often, not heavier: 2–3 sessions a week, 3–4 sets each.
seo.mus.rear-delts.title: Rear delts: exercises and how not to forget them — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.rear-delts.description: How to train rear delts: face pulls, bent-over reverse flyes, reverse pec deck and chest-height rows — technique, volume and the programs that give rear delts their sets.
seo.mus.rear-delts.lead: The rear delt is the most neglected part of the shoulder: presses barely load it. Face pulls and reverse flyes keep your shoulders balanced and healthy.
seo.mus.rear-delts.about_html: The rear head takes your arm back and rotates the shoulder outward. It works in rows to the waist and chest, but the back drowns it out there. Dedicated work — bent-over reverse flyes, the reverse pec deck and rope face pulls — gives it volume of its own. The rotator cuff works with it, the muscles that hold the joint steady when you press.
seo.mus.rear-delts.tips:
Pull to your face and turn your hands out: at the end, fists by your temples, elbows above your hands.
In reverse flyes don't squeeze your shoulder blades all the way — that shifts the work to the mid back.
Put 2–3 rear delt sets into every upper-body day — they're short and barely tire you.
If presses pull your shoulders forward, your rear delts aren't getting enough work.
seo.mus.biceps.title: Biceps exercises: barbell, dumbbell and hammer curls — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.biceps.description: How to build your biceps: barbell and EZ-bar curls, incline dumbbell curls, hammer curls, preacher and concentration curls — technique, volume and programs.
seo.mus.biceps.lead: The biceps bend the elbow and turn the hand. They grow from full-range curls, and hammer curls add the brachialis — the muscle that makes your arm look thicker.
seo.mus.biceps.about_html: The biceps have two heads. The long head stretches more when your arm is behind you — hence incline curls. The short head works harder with your arms in front — the preacher bench. Underneath sits the brachialis, which takes over with a neutral grip, as in hammer curls. Every back pull loads the biceps too, so your arms need less direct volume than you'd think.
seo.mus.biceps.tips:
Lower the weight to straight arms — the bottom third of the range does more than an extra plate.
Keep your elbows at your sides and don't help with your back: if you swing, it's too heavy.
Mix grips: palms up for the biceps, neutral for the brachialis and brachioradialis.
Count your pulls too: underhand pull-ups are biceps work as well.
seo.mus.triceps.title: Triceps exercises: skull crushers, pushdowns, close-grip bench — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.triceps.description: How to train triceps: cable, rope and overhead extensions, skull crushers, close-grip bench, dips and bench dips — technique, volume and programs.
seo.mus.triceps.lead: The triceps make up two thirds of your arm. Heavy close-grip presses and extensions build them, and overhead work adds the long head.
seo.mus.triceps.about_html: The triceps have three heads and all of them straighten the elbow. The long head starts on the shoulder blade, so it stretches and works more with your arm overhead — overhead extensions and skull crushers. The lateral and medial heads do more in pushdowns and presses. Every chest and shoulder press already loads the triceps.
seo.mus.triceps.tips:
Add one overhead exercise — the long head needs a stretched start.
In pushdowns your elbows stay still and pinned to your sides; only the forearm moves.
The close-grip bench is the strength base for triceps: shoulder-width grip, elbows along your body.
If skull crushers hurt your elbows, swap them for overhead cable extensions.
seo.mus.abs.title: Ab exercises: planks, crunches, leg raises, ab wheel — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.abs.description: How to train abs: crunches and cable crunches, hanging leg raises, planks and side planks, the ab wheel — technique, how much and how often, and programs with ab work.
seo.mus.abs.lead: Abs work in two modes: they bend the torso — crunches and leg raises — and keep it from bending — planks and the ab wheel. You need both, with load, like any other muscle.
seo.mus.abs.about_html: The rectus abdominis bends your spine and pulls your pelvis toward your ribs, the obliques twist and side-bend the torso, and the deep core keeps it rigid under a bar. In squats and deadlifts your abs brace, but to grow they need their own load: weight on cable crunches, a slow ab wheel, hanging leg raises. A visible six-pack only shows at a low body-fat percentage — that's about food, not the number of crunches.
seo.mus.abs.tips:
Progress like any other lift: add weight on the cable or reps on the bar, not minutes to an endless plank.
In crunches bend your spine — ribs to pelvis — instead of pulling on your head.
In leg raises curl your pelvis up, otherwise the hip flexors do most of the work.
The ab wheel is hard: start from your knees with a short range.
seo.mus.quads.title: Quad exercises: squats, leg press, lunges — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.quads.description: How to train your quads: back and front squats, goblet and hack squats, leg press, lunges, Bulgarian split squats, step-ups and leg extensions — technique and programs.
seo.mus.quads.lead: The quads — the front of your thigh — grow from deep knee bending under load: squats, leg press, lunges. Leg extensions add work without loading your back.
seo.mus.quads.about_html: The quadriceps straighten the knee, and the rectus femoris also flexes the hip. The further your knee travels forward and the deeper you squat, the more work they get: front squats and hack squats hit them harder than a back squat. Single-leg work — lunges and split squats — evens out your legs and needs less weight.
seo.mus.quads.tips:
Squat as deep as you can with a flat back — for the quads, deeper is better.
Knees track over your toes and can travel past them — that's fine.
Add a single-leg exercise: lunges or split squats show which leg is lagging.
The leg press is a good way to add volume when your back is tired from squats.
seo.mus.hamstrings.title: Hamstring exercises: Romanian deadlifts, leg curls — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.hamstrings.description: How to train hamstrings: Romanian and stiff-leg deadlifts, good mornings, lying and seated leg curls — two ways they work, technique and programs.
seo.mus.hamstrings.lead: Hamstrings work two ways: they extend the hip when you hinge — Romanian deadlifts — and bend the knee — leg curls. You need both for full development.
seo.mus.hamstrings.about_html: The hamstrings run from your pelvis to your shin and cross two joints. In flat-back hinges — Romanian deadlifts, stiff-leg deadlifts, good mornings — they stretch and hold the weight at the hips. In leg curls they bend the knee; seated, the muscle is more stretched than lying. Squats barely work them, so squats alone aren't enough.
seo.mus.hamstrings.tips:
Push your hips back rather than folding your back down: the bar slides along your legs, knees slightly bent.
Go down until you feel the stretch in your hamstrings, not to the floor at any cost.
Add leg curls to your hinges: hinging and bending the knee are different jobs.
Hamstrings recover slowly from heavy hinges — don't put them on back-to-back days.
seo.mus.glutes.title: Glute exercises: glute bridges, hip thrusts, lunges — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.glutes.description: How to build your glutes: hip thrusts and glute bridges, squats, deadlifts and Romanian deadlifts, lunges and step-ups — technique, volume and the Glutes and legs 3-day program.
seo.mus.glutes.lead: The glutes are the largest muscle in your body. Squats, hinges and lunges all load them, and hip thrusts and bridges add load right at the fully contracted top.
seo.mus.glutes.about_html: The gluteus maximus extends the hip: it straightens your pelvis coming out of a squat, in a deadlift and at the top of a bridge. The medius and minimus move your thigh out to the side and keep your pelvis level when you stand on one leg — which is why lunges and step-ups are glute work too. In the diary a deadlift set gives the glutes a quarter of a set — that's how I count their weekly volume.
seo.mus.glutes.tips:
In the hip thrust, hold the top for a second and don't arch your lower back — your glutes finish the movement, not your spine.
Add single-leg work: reverse lunges and step-ups load the standing leg's glute harder.
Squat deep — at the bottom the glutes are stretched and work more.
There's a dedicated program for glutes — Glutes and legs, 3 days.
seo.mus.calves.title: Calf exercises: standing and seated calf raises — Athlete Diary
seo.mus.calves.description: How to train calves: standing, seated, machine and leg-press calf raises — why you need both straight and bent knees, full range and pauses, and programs.
seo.mus.calves.lead: Calves grow slowly and love full range: drop the heel into a stretch, rise all the way onto your toes — and don't bounce.
seo.mus.calves.about_html: The gastrocnemius crosses the knee and the ankle, so it works best with straight knees — standing calf raises. Underneath sits the soleus, which takes more of the load seated, with bent knees. Calves carry your bodyweight all day and are used to it, so they need weight, volume and a pause at the bottom.
seo.mus.calves.tips:
Pause for a second at the bottom in the stretch — no bouncing.
Do them standing and seated: a straight knee for the gastrocnemius, a bent one for the soleus.
Go for 10–20 reps and as many sets as for any other muscle, not "two at the end of the workout".
You can train calves often: 2–3 times a week.
seo.pair.title: {a} vs {b}: the difference and which to pick — Athlete Diary
seo.pair.cta: Log both in the diary — your estimated max will show which one is growing faster for you.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-dumbbell-bench-p: The barbell gives you load, dumbbells give range and work each arm.
Barbell bench press or dumbbell bench press: which muscles work, which is heavier, which is easier on the shoulders and when to pick each — a table and a breakdown.
Both are the main flat presses for the chest. A barbell lets you lift more and progress easily; dumbbells let you go deeper and even out a weaker arm.

With a barbell your hands are tied by the bar: you press heavier and adding 2.5 kg is easy. Dumbbells are free: each arm works on its own, you can lower below chest level and bring your hands slightly together at the top. Shoulders usually like dumbbells better — the wrist finds its own angle. The price is less weight (a pair of dumbbells usually totals 15–20% less than the bar) and heavy dumbbells are harder to get into position.
Yes, and it's a common setup: the barbell first, for strength in 3–6 reps, dumbbells second, for volume in 8–12. If the barbell bothers your shoulder, dumbbells can replace it entirely.
You want to progress in weight and strength, and you have a spotter or safety pins.
Your shoulder dislikes a straight bar, one arm lags or you want more range.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-leg-press.card: A free squat versus a machine: which one does more for your legs.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-leg-press.descrip: Barbell squat or leg press: which muscles work, load on your back, technique and which to pick for leg strength and size.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-leg-press.lead: Both load the quads and glutes. The squat is a free movement where your whole torso works; the leg press is a machine where you can give your legs a lot of weight with almost no load on your back.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-leg-press.diff_ht: In the squat you carry the bar on your back and balance it yourself: legs, glutes, spinal erectors and abs all work, and the strength carries over to life and other lifts. In the leg press your back rests on a pad and the machine holds the path — you can work closer to failure without worrying about losing form. The weight on the sled is almost always higher than on the bar, and the two numbers can't be compared.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-leg-press.both_ht: Yes. The classic is squats first and heavy, leg press second to add quad volume once your back is tired. If your lower back won't let you squat, the leg press and hack squat keep your legs working.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-leg-press.when_a_: You want strength and a demanding lift, and you're ready to work on technique and film a set.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-leg-press.when_b_: Your back is tired or sore, you're new or you want leg volume with little risk.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-sumo-deadlift.card: Wide stance or narrow: where you pull more and who each one suits.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-sumo-deadlift.descr: Conventional or sumo deadlift: stance, which muscles work, lower-back load and how to pick a style for your build.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-sumo-deadlift.lead: Both are deadlifts: the bar from the floor to lockout. Conventional uses a narrow stance with hands outside the knees, sumo a wide stance with hands between the legs — and that changes who does the work.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-sumo-deadlift.diff_: In conventional the torso leans further over: the lower back and hamstrings work harder and the range is longer. In sumo the torso is more upright, the bar travels less, the quads and adductors work more and the lower back less. Which one feels stronger depends on your arm, leg and torso length and your hip mobility: a long torso with short arms often pulls more sumo, long arms often favour conventional.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-sumo-deadlift.both_: You can: your main style heavy, the other as an accessory, lighter and for reps. Log them as separate exercises in the diary — they have different records and shouldn't share one chart.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-sumo-deadlift.when_: Your back and hamstrings are strong, you have long arms and want strength through the whole posterior chain.
You pull with a cranky lower back, you have good hip mobility or a long torso.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-lat-pulldown.card: Your bodyweight on a bar or a weight stack — which is better for a wider back.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-lat-pulldown.descrip: Pull-ups or lat pulldowns: muscles, difficulty, how to progress and what to do if you can't do a pull-up yet.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-lat-pulldown.lead: It's the same movement — elbows down to your sides. In a pull-up you lift yourself; in a pulldown you pull the stack to you and pick the weight.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-lat-pulldown.diff_ht: Pull-ups are harder: you lift your whole bodyweight, your whole torso works, and progress means more reps, then a belt with a plate. The pulldown lets you start at any weight and add one plate at a time, so it's easier to build volume and refine technique. For the lats they're close; pull-ups also teach you to hold your torso and load your grip more.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-lat-pulldown.both_ht: Yes: pull-ups first, for strength, the pulldown second, for 10–15 reps. If you can't do a single pull-up yet, pulldowns plus slow negatives on the bar will get you to your first clean rep quickly.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-lat-pulldown.when_a_: You can do at least 5 pull-ups and want strength and core work.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-lat-pulldown.when_b_: You can't do pull-ups yet, you want precise loading and volume, or the bar's taken.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-front-squat.card: Bar on your back or on your chest: which loads the quads more.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-front-squat.descr: Back squat or front squat: where the bar sits, which muscles work, how much weight, mobility, and when to pick each.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-front-squat.lead: Same squat, different bar position: behind the neck on your traps or in front on your shoulders. That changes your torso angle and which muscles work harder.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-front-squat.diff_: With the bar on your back the torso leans more and you lift more weight: glutes, hamstrings and lower back pitch in. The front squat keeps your torso nearly upright — the knees travel further forward, the quads work harder, the back is loaded less, and the weight is usually 15–25% lower. The front squat needs wrist and shoulder mobility to hold the bar and a strong upper back.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-front-squat.both_: Yes. Many people make the back squat their main lift and the front squat a second-day or accessory lift. If you can't hold the bar on your chest, try the goblet squat: same upright torso, with a kettlebell.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-front-squat.when_: You want maximum weight and strength through the whole posterior chain.
You want more quads and less load on your lower back.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-romanian-deadlift.c: From the floor or from the top — which works the hamstrings harder.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-romanian-deadlift.d: Deadlift or Romanian deadlift: starting from the floor or the top, knees, muscles, weight and where each fits in a program — a table and a breakdown.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-romanian-deadlift.l: The deadlift starts on the floor and straightens both knees and hips. The Romanian deadlift starts at the top and barely bends the knees — it's a hip hinge that stretches the hamstrings.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-romanian-deadlift.d: In the deadlift every rep starts from the floor, from a dead stop, and almost your whole body works — you'll lift the most here. In the RDL you lower the bar only to mid-shin or until you feel the stretch, knees slightly bent and fixed, and the work goes to the hamstrings and glutes. The RDL is easier on the lower back and suits 8–12 reps; the deadlift suits strength work in 1–5.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-romanian-deadlift.b: Yes, and it's a good pair: deadlifts heavy once a week, RDLs on another day for hamstring volume. Don't put both heavy in one session — your lower back will tire before your legs do.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-romanian-deadlift.w: Your goal is strength, maximum weight, powerlifting.
Your goal is hamstrings and glutes, volume and reps, or you're protecting your lower back.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-seated-cable-row: A free bent-over row or a seated cable row: back thickness without the risk.
Bent-over barbell row or seated cable row: lower-back load, muscles, weight and when to put each in your program.
Both are horizontal pulls for back thickness. In the barbell row you hold the hinge yourself; on the cable you sit braced with your feet, and your back only has to pull.

The bent-over row means holding your torso parallel to the floor — your spinal erectors and hamstrings work too, you can load it heavy, but your lower back tires. On the cable row your torso is upright, tension stays constant through the range, and you can stretch the lats forward and squeeze your shoulder blades at the back without thinking about your lower back. The cable is simpler to learn and suits 10–15 reps.
Yes: the barbell first and heavy, the cable second for volume. If your lower back is already cooked from deadlifts, stick to the cable that day.
You want back and lower-back strength and hold the hinge confidently.
You're protecting your lower back, you're new, or it's after heavy deadlifts.
seo.pair.overhead-press-vs-seated-dumbbe: Standing with a barbell or seated with dumbbells — which is better for shoulders.
Standing barbell press or seated dumbbell press: delts and core, weight, load on the lower back and shoulder, and when to pick each.
Both are vertical presses for the shoulders. Standing with a barbell your whole torso works; seated with dumbbells it's only shoulders and triceps, in a path the joint likes.

The standing press is a strength lift: legs, glutes and abs hold you up, and the bar has to travel around your face. It carries over better to overall strength, but loads the lower back more, and heavy sets need technique. Seated with a back rest your torso is locked in — you can work closer to failure, and dumbbells let each arm take its own path and go a little deeper. A pair of dumbbells usually totals less than the bar.
Yes: the standing press heavy for 3–6 reps, seated dumbbells on another day or second for 8–12. If your shoulder dislikes a straight bar, dumbbells can replace the barbell entirely.
You want strength and core work and have a strong back.
You want delt volume, you're protecting your lower back or one shoulder is weaker.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-incline-bench-pr: Flat bench or a 30–45° incline — where you get more upper chest.
Flat or incline barbell bench press: the best angle, upper chest and front delts, weight and how to combine them in a program.
Same press, but the bench is raised 30–45°. The incline shifts the load toward the upper chest and front delts and lowers your working weight.

On a flat bench you press the most, the whole chest works and the bar touches mid-chest. On an incline the bar comes down to the upper chest, the clavicular head works harder and the front delts take more of the load. The steeper the incline, the more it becomes a shoulder press: above 45° it's nearly an overhead press. Incline weight is usually 15–25% lower.
Yes, that's standard: the flat press as your main lift, the incline second, with a barbell or dumbbells. You can also swap their order week to week if you want to bring up your upper chest.
You want maximum weight on the bench and strength.
Your upper chest lags or your shoulders like an incline better.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-chin-up.card: Overhand or underhand: more back or more biceps.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-chin-up.description: Pull-ups or chin-ups: how the lats and biceps work differently, which is easier and which to pick.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-chin-up.lead: One movement, two grips: palms away is a pull-up, palms toward you is a chin-up. Almost everyone finds the chin-up easier.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-chin-up.diff_html: With an underhand grip the biceps join in more, the elbows travel along your sides, and most people get 1–3 more reps. The overhand grip is a bit wider, puts the biceps in a weaker position and shifts more of the work to the lats and rear delts. Both are good for the back — the lats work in both; if your elbows or wrists complain about one grip, use the other or a neutral grip.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-chin-up.both_html: Yes: alternate grips between sessions or do both on one day. While pull-ups are still hard, chin-ups help you build pull-up volume.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-chin-up.when_a_html: You want more back and rear delts.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-chin-up.when_b_html: You want more biceps or can only do a few reps so far.
seo.pair.hip-thrust-vs-glute-bridge.card: Back on a bench or on the floor — where the glutes work harder.
seo.pair.hip-thrust-vs-glute-bridge.desc: Hip thrust or barbell glute bridge: range of motion, glutes and hamstrings, convenience and which to pick.
seo.pair.hip-thrust-vs-glute-bridge.lead: Both drive your hips up against a load and hit the glutes at the top. In the hip thrust your shoulder blades rest on a bench; in the bridge they're on the floor.
seo.pair.hip-thrust-vs-glute-bridge.diff: The bench gives the hip thrust a longer range: your hips drop lower, the glutes stretch more, and you usually load it heavier. The floor bridge is shorter and easier to set up — no bench, easier to roll the bar over your legs — and works well for high reps or at the end of a workout. Both keep the work at the fully contracted top, where squats and deadlifts barely load the glutes.
seo.pair.hip-thrust-vs-glute-bridge.both: Yes: the hip thrust as your main glute lift, heavy, the bridge as a finisher for 15–20 reps. If the bench is taken, the bridge stands in for the hip thrust without losing the point.
seo.pair.hip-thrust-vs-glute-bridge.when: You want maximum weight and a long range for the glutes.
There's no bench, you want something simple or a high-rep finisher.
seo.pair.lying-leg-curl-vs-seated-leg-cu: Lying or seated: where the hamstrings get more stretch.
Lying or seated leg curl: how hip position changes the hamstring stretch, and when to pick each machine.
Both machines bend the knee against a load and work the hamstrings. The difference is the hip: lying, it's straight; seated, it's bent and the muscle is more stretched.

The hamstrings cross both the knee and the hip. Seated, your hip is flexed, so the muscle starts the movement stretched — and in a study by Maeo et al. (2021) the hamstrings grew noticeably more after seated curls than after lying ones. Lying, the hip is straight and the muscle shorter, but it's easier to feel it working and the calves join in more. In practice both are good; use whichever machine your gym has and use the full range.
Yes: one on leg day, the other on your second day, or both for 2–3 sets. Curls pair well with Romanian deadlifts, which load the same muscle through the hip.
It's the one you have, or you want to feel the muscle better.
You want more hamstring stretch and your gym has the machine.
seo.pair.romanian-deadlift-vs-stiff-leg-: Knees slightly bent or nearly straight — almost the same thing?
Romanian deadlift or stiff-legged deadlift: knee position, depth, lower-back and hamstring load, and which to pick.

Both are barbell hip hinges for the hamstrings. They differ in the knees and the start: the RDL starts at the top with slightly bent knees, the stiff-leg version keeps the knees nearly straight and often starts from the floor.

In the RDL your knees are bent and stay put, your hips go back, the bar slides down your thighs, and you stop where the stretch ends. In the stiff-legged deadlift your knees are nearly locked — the hamstring stretch is bigger, but going deep without rounding your back is harder, and your lower back works more. The working weight is usually lower.
You can, but one is usually enough: pick the one where your back stays flat. Stiff-legged deadlifts are handy off a box or with dumbbells — lighter and no banging the floor.
You want more weight and a flat back, or you're new to hinging.
You have good mobility and want the maximum hamstring stretch.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-dumbbell-curl.c: The barbell gives load; dumbbells free your wrists and work each arm.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-dumbbell-curl.d: Barbell curl or dumbbell curl: weight, arm work, load on the wrists and elbows, and which is better for biceps growth.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-dumbbell-curl.l: Both bend the elbows against a load. A barbell ties your hands together and lets you lift more; dumbbells give each arm its own path and let you turn your wrist.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-dumbbell-curl.d: A barbell is easier to progress in weight and both arms work at once — but a straight bar locks your wrists in one position, and some people get wrist or elbow pain (an EZ bar helps). With dumbbells you can turn your palm up as you lift — that loads the biceps more — and alternate arms, resting one. A weaker arm can't hide behind the stronger one.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-dumbbell-curl.b: Yes: the barbell first for arms, heavier, dumbbells second, alternating or on an incline bench. Biceps need little direct volume — back pulls already load them.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-dumbbell-curl.w: You want heavier, simpler progression and your wrists are fine.
A straight bar bothers your wrists or elbows, or one arm lags.
seo.pair.dumbbell-curl-vs-hammer-curl.ca: Palms up or palms facing — biceps versus a thicker arm.
seo.pair.dumbbell-curl-vs-hammer-curl.de: Dumbbell curl or hammer curl: grip, which muscles work — biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis — and why to do both.
seo.pair.dumbbell-curl-vs-hammer-curl.le: Same dumbbells, different grip: palm up is a classic curl, a neutral grip with palms facing each other is a hammer curl.
seo.pair.dumbbell-curl-vs-hammer-curl.di: With your palm up the biceps are in their best position and do almost all the work. With a neutral grip the load shifts to the brachialis under the biceps and the brachioradialis on the forearm — your arm looks thicker, and you usually lift a little more in the hammer. Hammer curls are kinder to wrists and elbows.
seo.pair.dumbbell-curl-vs-hammer-curl.bo: Yes, and doing both is better: the classic curl for the biceps, the hammer for arm and forearm thickness. 2–3 sets of each is plenty.
seo.pair.dumbbell-curl-vs-hammer-curl.wh: You want to load the biceps themselves.
You want a thicker arm and forearm, or you're protecting your wrists.
seo.pair.triceps-pushdown-vs-skull-crush: Cable or skull crusher: which triceps heads work harder.
Triceps pushdown or skull crusher: which head of the triceps works more, elbow load and how to combine them.
Both straighten the elbow and load the triceps, but the arm position differs: in the pushdown your upper arm is by your side; in the skull crusher it's raised and the long head is stretched.

The pushdown is simple and gentle: constant tension, easy to add a plate at a time, and the lateral and medial heads do more. In a lying skull crusher your arm points up and back, so the long head starts stretched — and works harder. The price is elbow stress: start with a moderate weight and an EZ bar.
Yes: skull crushers first for triceps, pushdowns second for 12–15 reps. If skull crushers hurt your elbows, an overhead cable extension gives the same stretch more gently.
You want easy triceps volume without stressing the elbows.
You want more long head and more arm size.
seo.pair.dips-vs-push-up.card: Bodyweight on the bars or on the floor — which hits chest and triceps harder.
seo.pair.dips-vs-push-up.description: Dips or push-ups: load, chest, triceps and shoulder work, difficulty, progression and which to pick.
seo.pair.dips-vs-push-up.lead: Both are bodyweight presses. On dips you lift nearly your whole bodyweight; in a push-up about two thirds, because your feet hold the rest.
seo.pair.dips-vs-push-up.diff_html: Dips are harder: the lower chest, triceps and front delts work, and you progress with a belt and a plate. No need to go very deep — down to a right angle at the elbows, or it gets hard on the shoulder. Push-ups are more accessible and gentler on the shoulders, easy to make harder — feet up, a pause at the bottom, a backpack — and they train your core like a plank. The diary counts your bodyweight in both: nearly all of it on dips, about two thirds in push-ups.
seo.pair.dips-vs-push-up.both_html: Yes: dips as a strength lift, push-ups as a finisher or the home option. While dips aren't there yet, incline push-ups are a good stepping stone.
seo.pair.dips-vs-push-up.when_a_html: You can already do 20+ push-ups and want something harder, and your shoulders are healthy.
