seo.pair.dips-vs-push-up.when_b_html: You're new, train at home or dips are hard on your shoulders.
seo.pair.cable-crossover-vs-dumbbell-fly: Cable or dumbbells: where chest tension holds through the whole range.
Cable crossover or dumbbell fly: where the load is, chest stretch, convenience and which to pick.
Both isolate the chest: your arms sweep in an arc with a slight bend in the elbows. The difference is where the load pulls from: down with dumbbells, toward the pulley with a cable.

With dumbbells the load peaks at the bottom, in the stretch, and nearly disappears at the top, where your arms hold the weight vertically. On a crossover the cable pulls sideways, so the muscle works in the middle and as your hands come together too. The cable lets you change the angle — high to low, low to high — and target a part of the chest more precisely. Dumbbells are simpler: all you need is a bench.
Yes, both work as a second or third exercise after presses. If you only do one, pick the one where you feel your chest better and don't chase weight.
You want tension through the whole range and different angles.
There's no crossover, or you want a bigger stretch at the bottom.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-trap-bar-deadlift.c: Straight bar or hex bar: easier on the back, same weight.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-trap-bar-deadlift.d: Straight-bar or trap-bar deadlift: where the weight sits, back and leg load, difficulty and which to pick.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-trap-bar-deadlift.l: With a trap bar you stand inside the hexagon and the weight hangs at your sides, not in front of your legs. Your torso stays more upright and the work is shared between legs and back.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-trap-bar-deadlift.d: A straight bar has to clear your knees, so your torso leans more: more load on the lower back and hamstrings, and the technique is harder. With a trap bar the weight is in line with your feet — you sit down more, the quads work harder, the lower back is loaded less, and you can often lift as much or more. For a beginner the trap bar means heavy pulling with little room for mistakes.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-trap-bar-deadlift.b: Yes: a straight bar if you specifically need the deadlift (powerlifting), the trap bar for leg and back strength and size without overloading your lower back. Log them as separate exercises: their records don't compare.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-trap-bar-deadlift.w: Powerlifting, or you need the classic deadlift.
You're new, your lower back hurts or you want a heavy pull for leg strength.
seo.pair.bulgarian-split-squat-vs-dumbbe: Rear foot on a bench or stepping: which single-leg exercise is harder.
Bulgarian split squat or dumbbell lunge: stance, balance, quad and glute work, difficulty and which to pick.
Both are single-leg work. In the Bulgarian split squat your rear foot sits on a bench and barely helps; in a lunge you step and share the weight between legs.

The Bulgarian split squat is harder: the front leg does nearly all the work, the range is bigger, and the position doesn't change — easy to hold technique and load. Lunges are more dynamic: a step forward or back, braking and driving up — they need more balance and tire your whole body faster. Regular lunges are easier to start; Bulgarians give the quads and glutes more load with less weight.
Yes, but one per session is usually enough: Bulgarians as your main single-leg lift, lunges on another day or in your leg warm-up. Start with lunges if your balance still wobbles.
You want to load one leg hard with light weight.
You're new to single-leg work, there's no bench, or you want something dynamic.
seo.glossary.title: Gym glossary: e1RM, RPE, RIR, tonnage, plateau, deload — Athlete Diary
seo.glossary.description: Twelve terms you need to read a program and a training log: e1RM, RPE, RIR, tonnage, double progression, superset, drop set, warm-up and working sets, plateau, deload, hypertrophy.
seo.glossary.lead: Words you'll meet in programs, calculators and my answers. Short, with an example, and with how the diary counts it.
seo.glossary.cta: In the diary I work out all of these numbers myself — you just log the set.
seo.guides.title: Gym guides: progression, volume, plateaus, nutrition and supplements — Athlete Diary
seo.guides.description: Guides in a coach's voice: keeping a workout log, progressive overload, rest, plateaus, volume, programs — and nutrition: protein per day, calories for a bulk, cutting, creatine, caffeine and which supplements work.
seo.guides.lead: What people ask at the gym — straight to the point, with numbers from research and links to it. Plus how to do it in the diary.
seo.guides.glossary_link: Gym glossary: e1RM, RPE, tonnage and other terms
seo.guides.cta: Read it? Now log it. The diary will show whether it works for you.
seo.term.e1rm.name: e1RM (estimated one-rep max)
seo.term.e1rm.h1: e1RM — what an estimated max is
seo.term.e1rm.title: e1RM — estimated one-rep max: what it is and how to work it out — Athlete Diary
seo.term.e1rm.short: The weight a formula says you could lift once, worked out from a set of several reps.
seo.term.e1rm.body_html:
e1RM is your estimated one-rep max. You did 100 kg for 5 — the Epley formula says you could lift about 117 kg once. You don't need to test it with a real max: an estimate is easier to compare from workout to workout, even if you always train for 5–8 reps.

There are several formulas. Epley: weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30). Brzycki: weight × 36 ÷ (37 − reps). They nearly agree on short sets and drift apart on long ones — which is why I leave sets longer than {max_reps} reps out. If you give an RPE, the reps in reserve get added: 100 kg for 5 at RPE 8 counts like 7 reps to failure.

The diary works out e1RM for every set; the best one in a workout goes to the chart and to your records. That's how I see whether you're growing or stuck — and it's the base of the goal forecast.
seo.term.rpe.name: RPE (rating of perceived exertion)
seo.term.rpe.h1: RPE — what it is and how to use the scale
seo.term.rpe.title: RPE in the gym: the 6–10 effort scale for a set — Athlete Diary
seo.term.rpe.short: A rating of how hard a set was on a 6–10 scale, where 10 is not one more rep, 9 is one left, 8 is two.
seo.term.rpe.body_html:
RPE stands for rating of perceived exertion. In strength training the scale is tied to reps in reserve (RIR): RPE 10 is failure, RPE 9 means one more rep was there, RPE 8 two, RPE 7 three. Halves exist too: 8.5 means "maybe two, definitely one". That's how Zourdos and colleagues described it in 2016, and that's how programs use it.

Why bother: the same weight feels different on different days. "3×5 at RPE 8" adapts to the day — on a good one you'll load more, on a bad one less, but the effort stays the same. Beginners rate less accurately; it gets better with experience. An honest question after the set helps: "how many more did I have?"

In the diary you can add an RPE to a set, and I'll factor the reps in reserve into your estimated max. To turn an RPE into a weight for your next set, use the RPE chart.
seo.term.rir.name: RIR (reps in reserve)
seo.term.rir.title: RIR: reps in reserve and how they relate to RPE — Athlete Diary
seo.term.rir.short: How many more reps you could have done when you ended the set. RIR 2 means you stopped two reps short of failure.
seo.term.rir.body_html:
RIR stands for reps in reserve. It's the same scale as RPE, seen from the other side: RIR 0 = RPE 10, RIR 1 = RPE 9, RIR 2 = RPE 8. Many people find reserve easier to think in: "I left two" is clearer than "an eight".

You don't have to go to failure to grow: in the Refalo et al. (2023) meta-analysis, training to failure showed no clear advantage over sets stopped a little short. The working zone for most sets is RIR 1–3: hard enough to grow, without the extra fatigue that eats into your next sets.

The diary handles reserve through RPE: I add it to the reps when I work out your estimated max, but never more than five — beyond that, a guess is too rough.
seo.term.tonnage.name: Tonnage
seo.term.tonnage.h1: Workout tonnage — what it is and why to track it
seo.term.tonnage.title: Workout tonnage: the sum of weight × reps — Athlete Diary
seo.term.tonnage.short: The sum of weight × reps over all working sets: how many kilograms you lifted in a workout.
seo.term.tonnage.body_html:
Three sets of 8 with 80 kg is 1920 kg of tonnage. A workout adds up to anything from a few hundred kilograms to tens of tonnes — it depends on the exercises and your experience.

Tonnage shows how much work you did, not how strong you are. It's handy for comparing similar workouts in one program: if it goes up and your technique holds, you're doing more. Comparing tonnage across exercises makes no sense — a leg press always beats a curl.

In the diary I work out every workout's tonnage and put it in the summary — with a playful comparison like "that's about 3 grand pianos". For bodyweight exercises I count a share of your bodyweight: nearly all of it in pull-ups, about two thirds in push-ups. To work out tonnage without the diary, use the tonnage calculator.
seo.term.double-progression.name: Double progression
seo.term.double-progression.h1: Double progression — add reps, then weight
seo.term.double-progression.title: Double progression: reps first, then weight — Athlete Diary
seo.term.double-progression.short: A way to progress: you work in a rep range, add a rep at a time, and once you hit the top you add weight and start from the bottom again.
seo.term.double-progression.body_html:
Example: 3×8–12 with 50 kg. Today you get 10, 9, 8 — next time you go for 11, 10, 9. Once all three sets reach 12, you add 2.5 kg and start again from eight. Reps grow first, then weight — hence "double".

Why it works: adding 2.5 kg to an 8-rep bench every week won't last long, but adding a rep will. In the Plotkin et al. (2022) study, progressing by reps and progressing by load gave similar muscle growth, with a small edge in strength for load.

My diary suggests your target for a set exactly this way: within 5–12 reps (or whatever range the program's scheme sets) — one more rep, and at the top of the range — one weight step, usually 2.5 kg, 5 kg on heavy lifts. If the weight hasn't moved for three workouts in a row at 12+ reps, I'll remind you it's time to add.
seo.term.superset.name: Superset
seo.term.superset.h1: Superset — two exercises back to back
seo.term.superset.title: Superset: what it is, when to use it and how to log it — Athlete Diary
seo.term.superset.short: Two exercises back to back with no rest in between; you rest after the pair. Saves time and suits opposing muscles.
seo.term.superset.body_html:
The classic is opposing muscles: biceps curls and triceps pushdowns, a press and a row. While one group works the other rests, so you barely lose strength and the workout gets shorter. A superset of two exercises for the same muscle is a way to finish it off, not to save time: you'll need less weight on the second.

Heavy compound lifts — squats, deadlifts, a heavy bench — usually stay out of supersets: they need full rest, or both the weight and the technique suffer. For isolation work and 10–15 rep sets, supersets are great.

In the diary you log a superset with the Superset button — the two exercises' sets go in pairs and the summary counts as usual. How long to rest after the pair — the rest timer will help.
seo.term.drop-set.name: Drop set
seo.term.drop-set.h1: Drop set — a set where you strip the weight
seo.term.drop-set.title: Drop set: how to do a set with a weight drop — Athlete Diary
seo.term.drop-set.short: A set taken to failure, then the weight dropped by 20–30% and continued with no rest — once or several times.
seo.term.drop-set.body_html:
Example: cable pushdowns with 40 kg to failure at 10 reps, straight to 30 kg for 6 more, straight to 20 kg for 5 more. It's one long set with a lot of volume in little time.

Drop sets suit isolation work and machines, where changing the weight is quick. On a barbell squat or bench they're awkward and risky — technique falls apart under fatigue. Make it the last set of an exercise and not every workout: it's very tiring.

In the diary you can log each step as its own set with its weight — that keeps the tonnage honest. When importing from Strong I recognise D (drop set) and F (failure) in the set number and don't choke on them.
seo.term.warm-up-set.name: Warm-up set
seo.term.warm-up-set.h1: Warm-up sets — why and how many
seo.term.warm-up-set.title: Warm-up sets before your working weight: how many and how heavy — Athlete Diary
seo.term.warm-up-set.short: A light set before your working sets: it warms up muscles and joints and rehearses the movement with less weight.
seo.term.warm-up-set.body_html:
Warming up to a working weight is a ladder: the empty bar, then 40%, 60% and 80% of your working weight for 5, 3 and 2 reps, plus 90% for a single before a heavy set. Few reps, short rests: the point is to get ready, not tired.

Warm-up sets don't count toward volume or records. I don't log them in the diary at all — light sets would skew your average weight, tonnage and "last time". When importing from Strong and Hevy I skip warm-ups but say in the report how many there were.

To build the ladder for your working weight, use the warm-up calculator; the what and why are in the guide on warming up for lifting.
seo.term.working-set.name: Working set
seo.term.working-set.h1: Working set — what counts as work
seo.term.working-set.title: Working set: what it is and how to count sets per muscle — Athlete Diary
seo.term.working-set.short: A set at your working weight, hard enough to build strength and muscle — usually with no more than 3–4 reps in reserve.
seo.term.working-set.body_html:
A working set is one you do for the result, not to get ready. Working sets are what people count when they say "10–20 sets per muscle a week", and they're what the diary logs. A set after which you could have done 8 more reps is closer to a warm-up, even if the program calls the weight a working one.

A working set's effort is easiest to describe with RIR or RPE: RIR 1–3 is enough to grow. "3×8" means three working sets of eight; the warm-up comes separately.

The diary counts working sets per muscle group for the week and shows where you're in range and where you're under.
seo.term.plateau.name: Plateau
seo.term.plateau.h1: A plateau in the gym — when the weight stops moving
seo.term.plateau.title: Strength plateau: how to tell you've stalled and what to do — Athlete Diary
seo.term.plateau.short: A stretch of several weeks when your strength or weight on a lift doesn't grow while you train the same way.
seo.term.plateau.body_html:
A plateau isn't one bad workout. Everyone has a couple of bad days. A plateau is when your estimated max sits still for several weeks while you keep training the same way.

I tell two cases apart. One — the weight hasn't moved for three workouts in a row and you're doing 12 or more reps: that's not a stall, it's time to add weight, and I'll remind you. The other — over the last eight weeks your estimated max has grown slower than half a percent a week: that's a real plateau, and the coach breaks it down.

The causes are usually boring: poor sleep, too little food, too little or too much volume, the same scheme for months. What to do about it step by step is in the guide on breaking a plateau.
seo.term.deload.name: Deload
seo.term.deload.h1: A deload week — what it is and whether you need one
seo.term.deload.title: Deload week: how and when to back off — Athlete Diary
seo.term.deload.short: A week of lighter training — less weight, fewer sets or less effort — to shed accumulated fatigue.
seo.term.deload.body_html:
A deload isn't a holiday; it's light training: the same exercises with fewer sets, less weight and more reps in reserve. In a survey of 246 strength and physique athletes (Rogerson et al., 2024), a typical deload lasted about a week and came roughly every 5–6 weeks; stalling lifts and achy joints were the most common triggers.

Dropping the gym entirely for a week is something else. In the Coleman et al. (2024) study, a week off in the middle of a program didn't boost leg strength — it reduced the gains slightly — and made no difference to muscle growth. So back off rather than skip.

A diary program can include a deload every N weeks: in that week the target for a set has no increase, about 90% of the weight, and I remind you to cut sets.
seo.term.hypertrophy.name: Hypertrophy
seo.term.hypertrophy.title: Muscle hypertrophy: what makes muscles grow — Athlete Diary
seo.term.hypertrophy.short: An increase in muscle fibre size, and so in the muscle. In gym talk, putting on size.
seo.term.hypertrophy.body_html:
A muscle grows when it gets enough load, then food and sleep to recover. The main levers in the gym are volume (how many working sets per muscle a week), proximity to failure and progression: doing more over time.

On volume — more weekly sets give more growth on average, but with diminishing returns: that's what the Schoenfeld et al. (2017) meta-analysis found, and the newer Pelland et al. analysis too. Frequency on its own barely matters when the volume is the same: twice a week for 5 sets is about the same as once for 10. The rep range is wide: both 6 and 15 reps build muscle if the sets are close to failure.

The details, with numbers, are in the guide on sets per muscle per week, and exercises by group are in the muscles section.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.titl: How to keep a workout log that actually helps you grow — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.desc: What to write in a workout log, how not to quit after a week and how to read your entries: progression, estimated max, tonnage and volume per muscle. A coach's guide.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.h1: How to keep a workout log
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.card: What to write down, how not to quit, and how to read it so you grow.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.lead: A log isn't there for reporting. It's there for one question before every set: what did I do last time, and what am I doing today? Without an answer, progress turns into a lottery.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.cta: Start your log right now — on iPhone or in Telegram your first set takes a minute.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.take:
Log every working set: exercise, weight, reps. RPE and a note are optional.
Look at the log before the set, not after the workout: today's goal is to beat last time.
Log the bad days too — otherwise the log lies to you about progress.
Once a week, look at the trend in your estimated max, not single workouts.
The easier logging is, the longer you'll keep doing it.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s1.h: Why write it down at all
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s1_h:
Muscle and strength grow when the load goes up over time. That can be weight, reps or sets — but "more" only means something relative to what came before. Without a record you remember last workout roughly, and "roughly" in the gym means taking the same weight and the same reps for weeks because it feels familiar.

A log removes the guessing. Before you bench you see: last time 80 kg for 8, 8 and 7. So today the goal is 8, 8 and 8, and once every set reaches the top of the range, +2.5 kg. That's progressive overload, and in the Plotkin et al. (2022) study adding reps and adding weight produced similar muscle growth — both work, as long as there is some.

The second thing a log gives you is honesty. Feeling stuck or feeling strong often doesn't match the numbers. Your entries show what actually happened over a month, not over your last bad workout.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s2_h:
The minimum without which an entry is useless — four things:

  • Date — to see frequency and gaps.
  • Exercise — by the same name every time. "Bench" and "barbell bench" in two entries are two different exercises for any spreadsheet and for you in six months.
  • Weight — in one unit. Switching from kilograms to pounds? Convert the whole history, not half of it.
  • Reps in every set separately: 8, 8, 7 tells you more than "3×8".

Useful, but optional:

  • RPE or reps in reserve — how hard it was. 80 kg for 8 at RPE 7 and at RPE 10 are different days. The RPE scale tied to reps in reserve is the one Zourdos et al. (2016) described: 10 is failure, 9 means one rep left, 8 means two.
  • A note — one line on what matters: "shoulder ached", "new shoes", "slept 5 hours". A month later it's the notes that explain the dips on the chart.

No need to log warm-up sets — they skew your average weight and tonnage and say nothing about progress. I don't put them in the diary at all.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s3.h: How not to quit after a week
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s3_h:
Most logs don't die from laziness — they die from friction. If logging a set means opening an app, finding the exercise, filling three fields and confirming, by week three you'll be thinking "I'll log it later" — and you won't.

So there's one rule: logging a set should take seconds. In a paper notebook it's a line, "80 × 8". In my bot it's a line too: type 80 8 and the set is logged; I'll sort out the weight and reps. Hands busy? Say "eighty for eight" in a voice message.

Two more tricks:

  • Log right after the set, while you rest, not at the end of the workout. By the end you won't remember whether the second set was 8 or 7.
  • Train on a program. When the day's exercises are known in advance, the log tells you what's next and logging is easier. Ready-made programs are in the programs section.

If you're used to a spreadsheet, keep it — but with columns you can move later: that's what the workout log template is for.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s4_h:
A single workout says little: today you slept badly, last week you were flying. Look at trends — and at the right numbers.

  • Estimated max (e1RM) — the main measure of strength on a lift. It turns sets of different reps into one number: 100 kg for 5 and 90 kg for 8 give almost the same e1RM. If it grows month after month, you're stronger. What it is and how it's calculated is in the glossary.
  • Workout tonnage — how much work you did. Useful for comparing identical program days, useless across different exercises.
  • Sets per muscle per week — how much work each muscle gets. If your chest gets 18 sets and your back 6, the imbalance is obvious.

Spend five minutes once a week: which lifts went up, which are stuck, how many workouts you did. That's enough to spot a plateau in time, not three months later.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s5_h:
• Logging only the good days. A log with no dips shows growth that isn't there. A bad workout is data too.
  • Changing names. "Squat", "barbell squats", "back squat classic" — three charts instead of one. Pick a name once and stick to it; in my diary the catalog name stays attached to the exercise.
  • Changing technique silently. Switched your grip or depth? Note it, or the jump in numbers won't make sense.
  • Chasing a number on every set. A log isn't a reason to add weight at any cost. If your form fell apart for one extra rep, that rep doesn't count.
  • Never looking at the entries. The most common one: logging carefully and never opening the history before a set.
seo.guide.how-to-keep-a-workout-log.s6_h:
I'm built around exactly these rules. A set is one line, 100 8, or a voice message. Before a set you see last time and today's target: within your rep range I suggest one more rep, and at the top of it, one weight step. I work out estimated max, tonnage and records after every workout, and show weekly volume per muscle group on the main screen.

When the weight on a lift hasn't moved for three workouts in a row at 12+ reps, I remind you it's time to add. When your estimated max has barely grown in eight weeks, the coach breaks down why. And history from Hevy, Strong or a spreadsheet can be moved in as a file — it becomes part of the same diary.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.title: Progressive overload: how to add weight, reps and sets — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.progressive-overload.descripti: What progressive overload is and how to do it: weight, reps, sets, double progression, how much to add, when to add and when to stop. With research and examples.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.card: How and when to add weight, reps and sets — without guessing.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.lead: Your body adapts to the load. If the load doesn't grow, there's nothing left to adapt to and you stall. Progression is a plan for doing a little more over time without wrecking your technique.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.cta: Log your sets — I'll work out the target for next time myself, using double progression.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.takeaways:
You can progress with weight, reps or sets — all three work.
The simplest is double progression: add reps within a range, then weight at the top.
Keep weight jumps small: 2.5 kg on a barbell, 5 kg on very heavy lifts, the next pair on dumbbells.
No need to train to failure: 1–3 reps in reserve is enough to grow.
Stuck for 3–4 weeks? Change the plan instead of waiting.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.s1_html:
Progressive overload doesn't mean "heavier every workout". It means gradually increasing the work a muscle does: more weight, more reps with the same weight, more sets, sometimes more range or less rest. What matters is that a month from now you're doing more than today — and can show it in numbers.

At the start, progression almost happens on its own: a beginner adds weight to the squat every week. After six months to a year the steps get smaller and rarer — and that's when, without a plan, you stall. A plan's job is to find where you can still add when adding weight every week no longer works.

One more thing: progress only counts on the same exercise with the same technique. If you started squatting higher and the weight went up, that's not progress — it's a different exercise.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.s2_html:
The most common levers are weight and reps. Which is better? In the Plotkin et al. (2022) study, trained people progressed for eight weeks in different ways: some added weight at constant reps, others added reps at a constant weight. Both groups grew the same amount of muscle, and the weight group had a small edge in squat strength — barely meaningful in practice.

The takeaway is simple: both work, so pick what's convenient. For strength work in 3–6 reps, adding weight makes more sense. For isolation and exercises where weight jumps in big steps (dumbbells in 2 kg steps, a machine in 5 kg plates) — reps. Best of all is combining them.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.s3_html:
Double progression combines both levers. An exercise has a rep range, say 8–12. You work with one weight and add reps until every working set reaches the top of the range. Then you add weight and start again from the bottom.

An example on the seated dumbbell press, 3×8–12:

  • Week 1: 20 kg — 10, 9, 8.
  • Week 2: 20 kg — 11, 10, 9.
  • Week 3: 20 kg — 12, 11, 10.
  • Week 4: 20 kg — 12, 12, 12. Top of the range.
  • Week 5: 22 kg — 9, 8, 8. Back to the bottom.

That way progress shows every week, even when the weight goes up once a month. My diary suggests your target for a set exactly like this: a 5–12 rep range or whatever the program's scheme says, one more rep, and at the top, one weight step. More in the glossary: double progression.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.s4_html:
Less than you'd like. A 10 kg jump breaks your reps and technique and then sets you back. Working steps:

  • Barbell compounds — 2.5 kg (1.25 a side). On very heavy weights, from 200 kg, 5 kg makes more sense: 2.5 there is under a percent, which is noise.
  • Dumbbells — the next pair on the rack. If 2 kg a hand is too big a jump, build reps first.
  • Machines — one plate, and if that's too heavy, reps.
  • Overhead press and isolation grow slower than everything else and often need small plates of 0.5–1.25 kg.

No small plates at your gym? Add reps and sets, and add weight once you've built a buffer. Your estimated max will show you're growing even if the number on the bar is the same for now: the 1RM calculator works it out, and so does my diary after every workout.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.s5_html:
Progression doesn't mean taking every set to failure. In the Refalo et al. (2023) meta-analysis, training to failure showed no clear muscle-growth advantage over sets stopped a little short. Failure brings a lot of fatigue — both your next set and your next workout get worse.

The working zone is 1–3 reps in reserve (RPE 7–9). That's hard enough to grow and leaves something for next time's progression. If you're not sure how many you had left, take the last set of an isolation exercise to failure every few weeks — it calibrates the feeling. More on the scales: RPE and RIR.

Sets are a lever too: if you do 2 working sets per muscle per workout and you've stalled, a third will do more than another 2.5 kg. How many sets a week make sense is in the volume guide.
seo.guide.progressive-overload.s6_html:
One or two flat workouts aren't a reason to change anything: sleep, food and nerves make numbers wobble. The reason is three or four weeks in a row with neither weight nor reps moving and a flat estimated max. Then, in order:

  1. Check sleep, food and frequency — that's where it usually is.
  2. Drop the weight by 10% and climb the double-progression ladder again.
  3. Change the rep range: from 8–12 to 5–8 or the other way round.
  4. Add one or two weekly sets for the lagging muscle.
  5. If you're tired overall — a lighter week.

The details, with research, are in the guide on breaking a plateau. My diary doesn't wait for you to notice: if the weight sits still for three workouts at 12+ reps, I remind you to add; if there's no growth for eight weeks, the coach breaks down why.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.title: How long to rest between sets: for strength and for size — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.description: How long to rest between sets: what research says about 1 versus 3 minutes, rest for strength and for muscle growth, compounds and isolation, supersets and how not to rest too little.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.h1: How long to rest between sets
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.card: One minute, ninety seconds or three — what research says and what to do in the gym.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.lead: Rest is part of the workout too. Too short and your next set comes up a couple of reps short; too long and the workout drags on for two hours. The good news: the right range is fairly wide.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.cta: Start the timer and log your sets in the diary — the weight and reps stay.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.takeaways:
For muscle growth rest at least a minute; for most exercises, ninety seconds to two minutes.
Heavy compounds for 3–6 reps — 2–3 minutes, sometimes more.
Past 90 seconds, extra rest adds little for growth — but it doesn't hurt either.
Short rest eats reps — and reps are the work.
Supersets save time if the pair are opposing muscles.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.s1_html:
After a hard set a muscle needs time to restore its energy and clear the fatigue that built up. Start the next set too soon and you'll get fewer reps with the same weight, or need less weight. And what drives growth is the work itself — how many hard reps you got in over the workout.

So short rest isn't "more intense". It's just less work for the same fatigue. A burn and sweat aren't signs of a good workout; the sign is weight and reps going up over time.

Fatigue comes in two kinds. Local — in the muscle itself — clears in a minute or two. General — breathing, heart rate, focus — lasts longer after a heavy squat, and that's what decides rest on big lifts. That's why the same minute is plenty for a curl and too little for a deadlift.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.s2_html:
In the Schoenfeld et al. (2016) study, trained men followed the same program for eight weeks with one difference: one group rested a minute, the other three. The three-minute group gained more squat and bench strength, and their front thighs grew more. Short rest offered no advantage at all.

A newer meta-analysis, Singer et al. (2024), pooled studies where only rest changed. The finding: resting longer than 60 seconds gives a small edge for muscle growth — probably because it preserves reps. Past 90 seconds there's no noticeable difference: the recovery that affects how much work you do has mostly happened by then.

Note that the effects are small and the studies vary. This doesn't mean 70 seconds is a mistake and 100 is ideal. It means that under a minute you're probably losing work, and past two minutes for size you're just spending time — if you don't mind spending it.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.s3_html:
If the goal is lifting more for one to five reps, rest longer. A heavy set of squats for 3–5 taxes not just your legs but your back, nervous system and breathing. A minute later you're not ready to repeat it at the same quality.

  • Squat, deadlift, bench and overhead press for 1–6 reps — 2–3 minutes, up to 4–5 on the heaviest sets.
  • Compound accessories for 6–10 — 2 minutes.
  • If a lift is technically demanding, rest long enough that the next set is clean — even if the timer says go.

A good guide is your breathing and heart rate: once your breathing is steady and you're ready to focus, go.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.s4_html:
• Compound exercises for 8–12 — dumbbell press, pulldown, leg press — 90 seconds to 2 minutes.
  • Isolation — raises, curls, extensions — 60–90 seconds. The muscle is small and recovers fast, and overall fatigue barely builds.
  • Abs and calves — about a minute.

In a hurry? Don't cut rest on compounds — drop a set of isolation instead. Five minutes saved by short rest on squats will cost you a couple of reps on every set.

Rest doesn't have to be the same throughout a workout: rest longer early on, on the heavy compounds, and shorter toward the end, on isolation. What matters is keeping it roughly the same week to week for a given exercise, or comparing reps in your log won't be fair.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.s5.h: How to save time without losing work
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.s5_html:
The honest way is supersets of opposing muscles. Do a set of presses, then straight into a row, then rest. While your back works, your chest rests, and vice versa: within the pair you rest almost as long as you would alone, and the workout is shorter. Biceps with triceps, presses with rows, leg extensions with leg curls all pair well.

Don't superset two heavy compounds — say, squats and deadlifts: both load your back and the second will suffer. And don't confuse a superset with a drop set — that's something else.

Another way is to cut dead time rather than rest: set up plates and the bench in advance, don't drift off on your phone longer than the timer, and order exercises so you're not walking across the whole gym. That usually saves more than trimmed rest seconds, and costs nothing.

Cutting rest on purpose is a form of progression too — density: the same volume in less time. But it's weaker for growth and strength than weight and reps, and fits isolation and conditioning blocks better than compound lifts.
seo.guide.rest-between-sets.s6_html:
Rest without a timer is almost always shorter than it feels — or much longer if your phone is in your hand. Set the time before the set and stop thinking about it: that's what the rest timer is for, with presets for 60, 90, 120 and 180 seconds, sound and vibration.

And the log shows how rest affects your work. If reps drop hard on the second and third sets — 10, 7, 5 — your rest is short or the weight's too heavy. If they hold — 10, 10, 9 — you're fine. Log sets, not feelings, and in a couple of weeks you'll see your own picture. If you want to know how this ties in with growth, read the guide on sets per muscle per week.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.title: How to break a plateau in the gym: what to do when the weight won't move — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.description: Strength plateaus: how to tell you've stalled and what to do step by step — sleep and food, technique, volume, rep ranges, a deload week. With research.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.card: Weight not moving for a month? A step-by-step check, from sleep to deloads.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.lead: Everyone who trains longer than six months hits a plateau. It's not a verdict and not a reason to change everything at once. It's a signal: something that used to work isn't enough any more — and most often that something is boring.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.cta: Log your workouts — I'll spot a stall before you do and tell you where to start.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.takeaways:
A plateau is weeks without growth in your estimated max, not one bad workout.
Sleep, food and consistency first — then the program.
Film a set: the weight often stalls because of technique, not strength.
Change one thing at a time: volume, rep range or the exercise.
Tired? A lighter week, not a week out of the gym.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s1.h: Are you really on a plateau?
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s1_html:
One bad workout isn't a plateau. Neither are two. The weight on the bar swings with sleep, stress, food, even the time of day you train. A plateau is when your estimated max on a lift sits still for several weeks while you train as usual.

Here's how I look at it: I take your best estimated max for each workout over the last eight weeks and work out the slope. If it's growing slower than half a percent a week — under half a kilo a week on a hundred-kilo lift — that's flat, a stall. Fewer than four sessions with the lift in that time is too few to judge: two or three points can make any slope.

There's also the opposite case people mistake for a plateau: the weight hasn't moved in three workouts and you're doing 12 or more reps. That's not a stall. You've simply outgrown that weight and it's time to add — I remind you about that.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s2_html:
Before changing the program, answer three questions honestly:

  • Sleep. Under seven hours for weeks — strength doesn't grow, however you change your sets.
  • Food. Eating in a calorie deficit to lose fat slows strength gains, and for advanced lifters can stop them. That's normal: holding your numbers while cutting is already good. Protein — around 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight a day: past that, according to the Morton et al. (2018) meta-analysis, the extra benefit nearly flattens out.
  • Consistency. Open your log: how many workouts were there last month? A "plateau" is often two workouts a week instead of three and a skipped one every third week.

If any answer is bad, start there. It's boring, but that's where most stalls live.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s3_html:
The weight often stalls not because you lack strength but because your technique stopped transferring it. On the bench your shoulder blades slip, in the squat your hips rise too early, in the deadlift the bar drifts away from your legs. You don't feel it on your own lifts — on video it's obvious.

Film a working set from the side — how to do it right is in the guide on filming your set — and send it to me for a review. I'll say what I see and what to fix first. Sometimes one fix — bar position, depth, grip — unlocks a few kilos within a couple of weeks.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s4_html:
If sleep, food and technique are fine, it's time to change the load — one thing at a time, so you know what worked.

  • Volume. Doing fewer than 10 working sets per muscle a week? Add 2–3. More sets give more growth on average, but with diminishing returns: that's what the large Pelland et al. analysis shows. If you're already at 20+, volume probably isn't the problem — fatigue might be.
  • Rep range. Six months in 8–12? Switch to 4–6 with more weight for 4–6 weeks, then come back. The reverse works too: a lifter living at 3–5 reps benefits from a block of 8–10.
  • Progression. Stopped adding weight every week? Move to double progression: reps, then weight. Small plates of 0.5–1.25 kg help too.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s5_html:
Sometimes a lift stalls while the muscles are still ready to grow. A similar movement for 4–8 weeks helps then: instead of the bench, a paused bench or an incline; instead of the back squat, a front squat; instead of the conventional deadlift, a block pull or a Romanian deadlift. A variation loads the weak point of the main lift and gives a fresh stimulus.

When you go back to the main lift, start 5–10% below your record and climb the ladder again — a couple of weeks later you're usually above where you were. Comparisons of similar exercises are in the comparisons section.

You don't need to grind sets to failure to break through: in the Refalo et al. (2023) meta-analysis, failure showed no clear muscle-growth advantage, and it brings more fatigue.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s6_html:
If you've been training hard for a long time, your joints ache, motivation is gone and your numbers aren't just flat but dropping, fatigue has built up. The answer is a deload week: the same exercises, about half the sets and 85–90% of your usual weight, with plenty of reps in reserve.

How experienced athletes do it: in a survey of 246 strength and physique athletes (Rogerson et al., 2024), a deload lasted about a week on average and came roughly every 5–6 weeks, most often triggered by stalling lifts and joint pain. They usually kept training frequency and exercises, and cut volume and effort.

Don't confuse a deload with time off. In the Coleman et al. (2024) study, a week with no training at all in the middle of a nine-week program didn't help: that group's leg strength gains were even slightly smaller, and the break made no difference to muscle growth. Back off rather than skip. More in the glossary: deload.
seo.guide.break-a-plateau.s7_html:
A stall shows best in numbers, not feelings. I work out the estimated max for every lift after every workout and see where it's been flat for eight weeks. If the weight hasn't moved for three workouts at 12+ reps, I'll remind you to add. If you've really stalled, ask the coach "why isn't my bench going up?" and you'll get an answer from your diary: what's going on with frequency, volume and reps, and what to change first.

A diary program can include a deload every N weeks — in that week the target for a set has no increase, about 90% of the weight, and I remind you to cut sets.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.title: How many sets per week to build muscle: what the research says — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.descr: How many working sets per muscle a week you need to grow: meta-analyses on volume and frequency, where to start, how to count sets on compound lifts and how to know it's time to add.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.h1: How many sets per week to build muscle
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.card: 10 to 20 working sets — where the numbers come from and how to use them.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.lead: Volume — how many working sets a muscle gets in a week — is one of the main levers for growth. More is better on average, but not forever, and that's exactly where people go wrong in both directions.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.cta: Log your workouts — I'll show how many sets each muscle group gets per week myself.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.takea:
Count working sets — those with 0–3 reps in reserve, no warm-ups.
The range for growth is 10–20 sets per muscle per week; beginners need less.
More sets mean more growth, but with diminishing returns.
Compound lifts count toward helper muscles too, just not in full.
Split the volume over 2 sessions a week — it's easier to keep quality up.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s1_ht:
Only working sets: at a working weight and close to failure — with roughly 0–3 reps in reserve. Warm-ups don't count, and neither, really, does a set after which you could have done eight more. The weight and reps within it — anywhere from 5 to 30 — matter less for muscle growth than proximity to failure: both 6 and 15 reps build muscle if the set is hard.

Sets are counted per muscle, not per exercise. The bench press is a chest set, but it does something for the triceps and front delts too. How to count that is below.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s2_ht:
The Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (2017) meta-analysis pooled 15 studies and found a dose-response relationship: each extra weekly set gave a little more growth on average — about 0.37% more increase in muscle size. Groups doing 10 or more sets a week per muscle grew more on average than those doing fewer than five — though in that comparison the difference fell just short of statistical significance.

A newer and larger analysis by Pelland et al. (67 studies, over 2,000 people) refined the picture. Muscle size and strength both grow with volume, but returns diminish: the first sets give a lot, each next one less. For strength the drop-off is steeper — frequency and heavy work matter more than endless volume. And one important detail: the data fit best when a set on a "helper" exercise counted as half — more on that below.

Both are averages across groups of people. Your own optimum may be higher or lower, and the only way to find it is your log.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s3_ht:
• Beginner (under six months) — 6–10 working sets per muscle a week. You grow from almost any sensible volume, and extra sets only get in the way of recovery and learning technique.
  • Intermediate — 10–15 sets. That's where most people grow.
  • Advanced — 15–20 or more for lagging muscles, if you recover in time. More than 20 on everything at once is rarely a good idea.

Legs are a special case: several large muscles, and the quads, hamstrings and glutes each need their own volume, not "12 for legs" in general. Shoulders are the same: the front delt gets plenty from presses, but the side and rear delts need their own work. I've counted the volume each ready-made program gives every group in the muscles section.

An example from my programs: one pass through "Full body — 3 days" gives the chest 9 working sets, the back 13 and the quads 6. That's a good start for a beginner; at an intermediate level, top up your legs with leg presses or lunges, say. The two-day "Upper / Lower" gives the chest 4 sets per pass — it's meant to run twice a week, which makes 8.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s4.h: How to count sets on compound lifts
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s4_ht:
Count every bench set as a full triceps set and your triceps look overtrained on paper. Don't count it at all and they look neglected. The Pelland et al. analysis found the middle works best: a set where a muscle helps counts as half.

In practice:

  • presses — a full set for chest or shoulders, half for triceps;
  • rows and pulls — full for back, half for biceps and rear delts;
  • squats and leg presses — full for quads and glutes.

I count the deadlift separately: it sits under back, but it's mostly glutes and hamstrings doing the work. So a deadlift set is half a set for back and half for legs, a quarter each for hamstrings and glutes. That's how the diary counts weekly volume, and how the coach builds a program.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s5_ht:
Frequency — how many times a week a muscle gets loaded — barely matters for growth on its own when total volume is the same. But an earlier study by Schoenfeld et al. (2016) found that training a muscle twice a week gave more growth than once, largely because it's easier to get the volume in without losing quality. In the Pelland et al. analysis, frequency clearly mattered only for strength.

A practical rule: if a muscle gets more than 8–10 sets, split them over two workouts. Twenty chest sets in one day means the last ten on a tired chest with less weight. Two workouts of ten each means twenty good sets.
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s6.h: How to know it's time to add
seo.guide.sets-per-muscle-per-week.s6_ht:
Look at your log every 4–6 weeks. If the estimated max on your main lifts for a muscle is growing and reps are going up, the volume is fine — change nothing. If it's flat and you're recovering well, add 2–3 sets a week. If it's flat or dropping, your joints ache and you don't feel like training, the volume is too high, and you need a deload first.

Add a little at a time and to one or two muscles at once, or you won't know what worked. And to skip the manual counting, just log your sets: I count the working sets for every group each week and show them on the main screen, and the coach sees the imbalances and tells you where you're short.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.title: How to find your 1RM safely: estimating and testing your one-rep max — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.descriptio: How to find your one-rep max without the risk: estimating 1RM from a set (Epley, Brzycki), which sets work for an estimate, RPE, and if you test it live — warm-up, spotting and mistakes.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.card: Estimates from a set, RPE and live testing — without unnecessary risk.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.lead: Your one-rep max (1RM) is useful for working out program percentages and seeing your strength. But you don't have to find it by grinding out a single every time — and most people don't need to.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.cta: Log your sets — I'll work out the estimated max for every exercise myself.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.takeaways:
An estimated max from a set of 3–8 reps is almost as useful as a real one, and safer.
Sets longer than 10–12 reps give a poor estimate — don't use them.
RPE makes the estimate more accurate: account for the reps you had left.
Testing live? A warm-up ladder, a spotter and no more than 3–4 attempts.
For your log, the trend of your estimated max matters more than one number.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s1_html:
A one-rep max does two jobs. One — working out weights in a program: "5×5 at 80%", "triples at 85%". Two — seeing whether you're getting stronger. Both work without a real max: percentages and progress both run fine off an estimate.

A real 1RM test is for powerlifters before a meet and people who just want to know the number. For everyone else it's risk without much payoff: an all-out attempt loads your joints and technique harder than any working set, and you recover from testing more slowly.

There's a subtlety too: a real max depends on the day. Slept well, ate, got fired up — a few percent more; drained from work — less. One number every six months says less than an estimated max worked out from every workout: a trend of twenty points is more honest than one.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s2.h: How an estimated max is calculated
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s2_html:
The formulas take the weight and the reps of a set done close to failure and estimate what you could lift once. The most common:

  • Epley: weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30). 100 kg for 5 → about 117 kg.
  • Brzycki: weight × 36 ÷ (37 − reps). 100 kg for 5 → about 113 kg.

At 2–6 reps the formulas nearly agree; beyond that they drift apart. Neither knows you personally: some people have more endurance and get lots of reps off their max, some fewer. So an estimate carries an error of a few percent — but use one formula on similar sets and the trend stays honest. To work it out from your numbers, use the 1RM calculator, which also has a percentage table.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s3_html:
• 3–8 reps — the best window: heavy enough for an accurate estimate, light enough not to take risks.
  • Close to failure. If you left 4 reps in reserve, the formula will underestimate — unless you account for RPE (below).
  • No longer than 10–12 reps. On long sets endurance decides and the formulas fall apart. In my diary, sets longer than {max_reps} reps don't go into the estimated max at all.
  • Clean technique. A set with cheating gives an estimate you don't have.
  • One formula for good. Switch from Epley to Brzycki and the whole chart shifts. In my diary you pick the formula in settings, and I recalculate the whole history with it so you never compare apples and oranges.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s4.h: RPE makes the estimate more accurate
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s4_html:
Working sets rarely go to failure. If you did 100 kg for 5 and felt you had two more, that's RPE 8 — strength-wise, like 7 reps to failure. An estimate that counts the reserve gives about 123 kg instead of 117 — closer to the truth. The RPE scale where each point is one rep in reserve was described by Zourdos et al. (2016); experienced lifters rate more accurately, beginners more roughly.

My diary counts it the same way: give an RPE for a set and I'll add the reserve to the reps, but never more than five. To work out "what to load for a triple at RPE 9", use the RPE chart.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s5_html:
Decided to find your real max? Do it on a good day, fresh, without a heavy session the day before.

  1. A warm-up ladder. The empty bar, then roughly 40%, 60%, 75%, 85% and 90% of your expected max for 5, 3, 2, 1 and 1 reps. Get ready, don't get tired. The warm-up calculator will build the ladder for your weight.
  2. Attempts. The first around 95% of expected, the second for the record, a third if the second moved easily. More than 3–4 attempts after the warm-up is no longer a test, just fatigue. Jump 2.5–5 kg between attempts on the bench and 5–10 kg on the squat and deadlift — no just-in-case leaps.
  3. Rest 3–5 minutes between attempts.
  4. A spotter is a must. Bench with a spotter or in a rack with safety pins; squat in a power rack with pins set just below your bottom position. A deadlift you can drop if it goes wrong.
  5. The standard is a clean rep. If the bar went up but your technique fell apart, count the previous attempt.
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s6.h: An alternative: a heavy single at RPE 8–9
seo.guide.estimate-1rm-safely.s6_html:
The middle ground between estimating and testing is warming up to a heavy single that feels like RPE 8–9: "one or two more were there". That gives you almost the same information as a max, without the risk of missing. Do a single like that at the start of a workout every few weeks and watch its weight go up.

Want to check yourself with no risk at all? Do a set of 3–5 reps with one or two in reserve and log it with an RPE. It's a working set you'd do anyway, and the estimated max from it will be accurate.

For your log you need neither: I work out the estimated max from every set you log and show its trend on a chart. If it climbs month after month, you're stronger — even if you've never tested a 1RM. Want to know when you'll hit a round number? The goal forecast works from your estimated max.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.title: Warming up for strength training: what to do and how much — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.descrip: How to warm up for lifting: a general warm-up, ramp-up sets to your working weight, how many reps and how much rest, stretching and common mistakes. With research.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.card: Five minutes of general warm-up and a ladder of sets — without extra fatigue.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.lead: A good warm-up isn't twenty minutes on the treadmill or stretching on a mat. It's a short prep after which your first working set goes the way it should, not like your fifth.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.cta: Work out the ladder for your working weight — and log only your working sets in the diary.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.takeawa:
General warm-up — 5–10 minutes of easy cardio or dynamic moves, to a light sweat.
Specific warm-up — a ladder of sets on the same lift, from the empty bar to your working weight.
The heavier the working weight, the more steps and the fewer reps per step.
A warm-up shouldn't tire you: few reps, short rests.
Warm-up sets don't go in the log — they're not work.
If the warm-up feels heavy or something aches, take 5–10% off your working weight today — that's fine.
Don't work out the ladder in your head — the warm-up calculator does it for you.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.s1_html:
A warm muscle contracts faster and harder, joints move more freely, and your nervous system gets a chance to "remember" the movement. In the review and meta-analysis by Fradkin, Zazryn and Smoliga (2010), warming up improved performance in 79% of the measures tested — from jumps to strength.

On injuries, honestly: the evidence that warming up prevents them is weaker than people think, but what there is leans in its favour. And in the gym a warm-up has a simple practical job too: check your technique and how you feel on a light weight before you put your working weight on your back.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.s2_html:
5–10 minutes to raise your body temperature and heart rate: treadmill, bike, rower, a skipping rope at an easy pace. The target is a light sweat and faster but easy breathing. This isn't a cardio session: if it tired you out, it was too much.

Then a couple of minutes of dynamic work for the joints you're about to use: leg swings and lunges before squats, arm circles and band pull-aparts before pressing, hinges and cat-cows before deadlifts. The key word is dynamic: moving through the range, no long holds.

How much general warm-up you need depends on conditions. In a cold gym in winter, early in the morning, after a day at a desk or as you get older — closer to ten minutes. In summer, midday, if you walked to the gym — five is enough. The test is the same: your joints move freely instead of creaking on the first rep.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.s3_html:
The main part is warm-up sets on the lift you're about to do. In the Ribeiro et al. (2021) review, a specific warm-up with a load close to your working weight did the best job of supporting strength and rep performance. The ladder I use:

  1. Empty bar — 10 reps.
  2. 40% of your working weight — 5 reps.
  3. 60% — 3 reps.
  4. 80% — 2 reps.
  5. Before a heavy set (5 reps or fewer) — another 90% for 1 rep.

Example: a working squat of 100 kg for 5. Warm-up — 20 × 10, 40 × 5, 60 × 3, 80 × 2, 90 × 1, then your working sets. Each weight is rounded down to something you can load with plates. The warm-up calculator will build the ladder for your weight, with the plates per side.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.s4.h: How much and how to rest
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.s4_html:
• Reps drop as the weight rises: the last steps are 1–2 reps, to feel the weight, not to tire from it.
  • Rest between light steps — as long as it takes to load the plates, 30–60 seconds. Before the last heavy step and before your first working set — as long as between working sets.
  • Light working weight, short ladder. If your working weight is 40 kg, the bar and one step in between are enough. A step that ends up no heavier than the previous one after rounding simply drops out.
  • A second exercise for the same muscle usually doesn't need the full ladder: one or two sets at 50–70% are enough.

The whole warm-up before your first exercise takes 10–15 minutes — about the same as the extra sets you'd lose by starting cold. Upper day or lower day, the logic is the same: general warm-up, the day's joints, a ladder on the first lift. If the first exercise is isolation for a small muscle, the ladder is shorter: a couple of light sets of 15–20.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.s5_html:
Long static stretching — holding a stretch for a minute — isn't needed before a heavy set: it does a different job. If you can't get into position without it, say into a deep squat, stretch briefly, 15–30 seconds, and go back to dynamic moves. Work on flexibility separately or after training.

Common mistakes:

  • Skipping the warm-up and starting straight at your working weight — the first set comes out worse, and on compound lifts it's a risk too.
  • Getting tired warming up — 10 reps on every step eat into your working sets.
  • Jumping from 60% straight to your working weight on a heavy lift — your nervous system needs a step in between.
  • Warming up on machines instead of the bar. A bike warms your body, but only squatting prepares your squat technique.
  • Not listening to the warm-up. If 60% feels heavier than usual and a knee or shoulder aches, take 5–10% off your working weight today rather than grinding through. The warm-up is the best moment to notice it isn't your day.
seo.guide.warm-up-before-lifting.s6_html:
Don't log your warm-up sets. They aren't work: light sets would skew an exercise's average weight, tonnage and "last time", and records never happen in them. I don't log warm-ups myself, and when importing from Strong and Hevy I skip sets marked as warm-ups and say in the report how many there were.

Log only working sets — then your estimated max and volume per muscle stay honest. More on the difference in the glossary: warm-up set. And if you came here to test your max, the warm-up for it is covered in the guide on finding your 1RM safely.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.tit: How to switch from Hevy or Strong without losing your history — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.des: Moving from Hevy or Strong: how to export a CSV, upload it to the bot or the app, what I do with the file — duplicates, names, warm-ups, units, undoing the import — and what to do after.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.h1: How to switch from Hevy or Strong
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.car: Export, upload, check — and don't lose a single workout.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.lea: The most valuable thing in your old tracker isn't the app — it's your history: years of workouts, records, the weight on the bar. Switching means bringing all of it, so your progress carries on from where it was instead of from zero.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.cta: Export the CSV and send it to me — I'll show you what it'll look like before I log anything.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.tak:
Hevy and Strong export your history as a CSV file — that's what I read; no manual editing needed.
Nothing shows up in your diary until you tap Upload all: you see a preview first.
I skip duplicates, ask about names I'm unsure of, and list warm-ups and cardio in the report.
You can undo the import — exactly what that file added gets removed.
Run both apps for the first week — it's calmer that way.
Program templates don't come over in the file — pick a ready program or ask the coach to build a new one.
After switching, ask the coach about your year of progress — it already sees your whole history.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.s1_:
From Hevy. Profile → Settings → Export & Import Data → Export Data → Export Workouts. Hevy builds a CSV file with all your workouts — save it or share it straight away. Step by step, with the menu names, on the switch from Hevy page.

From Strong. Profile → Settings → Export Workouts. Strong saves the CSV to your phone or offers to share it. Step by step on the switch from Strong page.

From a spreadsheet or notes. Any CSV with date, exercise, weight and reps works — or my template. Logging workouts in your phone's notes? Paste them into the bot as text and I'll sort that out too.

People write notes every which way: "bench 80x8 80x8 77.5x7", "squat 100 for 5, three sets", with dates and without. I read that kind of text, show what I understood — workouts, exercises, sets — and wait for your go-ahead in the same way. Anything I didn't understand I list separately instead of making it up.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.s2_:
• In the bot: {settings} → {import_btn}. While your diary is empty, the {import_history} button sits right on the main menu. Send the CSV as a document, as is.
  • In the iPhone app: Settings → Import CSV, then pick the file. From Hevy there's a shortcut: choose Athlete Diary in the Share sheet.

Then I show a preview: how many workouts and sets I found, which units the file uses, which exercises I recognised and which I didn't. Until you tap {upload}, not a single entry appears in your diary.

Moving from two places at once — say, older workouts in Strong and newer ones in Hevy? Upload the files one after the other. I'll catch duplicates between them the same way as duplicates with your diary: by start minute or by the same exercises on the same day.

I read dates in the usual formats. If a date like 03/04/2025 could mean two things, I look at the other dates in the file, pick the reading with no impossible days, and tell you in the preview how I read it. A date in the future or before 2000 is a bad row, and I'll give you its number.
What I do with the file
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.s3_:
• I split it into workouts by start time and name, not by day: two sessions on one day stay two workouts.
  • I match names. Standard Hevy and Strong names ("Bench Press (Barbell)", "Lat Pulldown (Cable)") I map to the catalog myself. If you already have a similar exercise of your own and I'm not sure, I'll ask where it goes.
  • I convert units. I spot a pounds column by its header and convert it to your diary's units.
  • I skip warm-ups and cardio — but not silently: the report shows how many rows there were, with examples.
  • I don't duplicate. A workout with the same start minute, or the same exercises on the same day, as one already in your diary gets skipped.
  • I carry over notes — for exercises and for workouts.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.s4_:
You can undo an import for {days} days: Undo import removes exactly what that file added — workouts and new exercises — and leaves the rest of your diary alone. Fix the file or make different name choices and upload again.

If two exercises turn out to be the same one — say, "Bench Press" from Strong and your own "Barbell Bench Press" — you can merge them, and unmerge them again: I keep a log.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.s5_:
1. Check the records and charts for two or three main lifts: do they match what you remember?
  2. Set up a program. Hevy and Strong templates don't come over in the file — only workouts. Pick a ready one from programs or ask the AI coach to build one by days — it already sees all your imported history.
  3. Ask the coach "how has my year gone?" — the first question your old app couldn't answer.
  4. Install the app or pin the bot. The bot runs in Telegram on any phone, the app on iPhone, and they share one diary.

I work out estimated max and charts for imported workouts exactly as for the ones logged with me: same formula, same rules. So your progress line doesn't break on the day you switched — history and new workouts run on one chart.
seo.guide.switch-from-hevy-or-strong.s6_:
Worried about losing something along the way? Log your workouts in both for the first week. It's two seconds a set, and peace of mind is worth it. After a week you'll see everything is in place with me, and you can close the old app — keep its export just in case.

Still choosing where to move? Honest comparisons are on the pages vs Hevy and vs Strong — including how we differ on price, the coach and video reviews.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.title: How to choose a workout program: by days, goal and experience — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.choose-a-program.description: How to choose a gym program: how many days a week, full body or split, strength or size, experience and equipment, volume per muscle and how long to stick with one. With ready-made programs.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.card: Days per week, goal and experience — and which ready-made program fits.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.lead: The best program is the one you'll actually run for months. Not the trendiest and not the hardest, but one that fits your week, suits your goal and gives every muscle enough work.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.cta: Pick a program and log by it — I'll show the plan at every workout.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.takeaways:
Start with how many days a week you really get to the gym — not how many you'd like.
2–3 days — full body; 4 — upper and lower; 5–6 — push-pull-legs.
For strength — fewer exercises, more heavy sets; for size — more volume.
Every muscle at least twice a week and 10+ working sets once you're past the beginner stage.
Stick with a program for 8–12 weeks before judging it.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s1.h: Step 1. How many days a week
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s1_html:
This is the main question, and it needs an honest answer. A five-day program you do three times a week is worse than a three-day program you do every time: missed days break the balance, and some muscle goes weeks without work.

  • 2 days — full body twice a week. Not much, but it works, and missing one workout doesn't leave a group untrained for two weeks.
  • 3 days — full body three times, 5×5 for strength or a three-day split.
  • 4 days — upper and lower, twice each.
  • 5–6 days — push-pull-legs: presses, pulls, legs, on rotation.

If your week is unpredictable, pick a program with fewer days — it's easier to keep.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s2_html:
Most programs build both, but with different emphasis.

  • Strength. Fewer exercises, heavy compounds for 3–6 reps, long rests and adding weight every workout for as long as it keeps working. The classic is 5×5: three big lifts per workout.
  • Size. More volume — sets per muscle per week — a 6–15 rep range, and isolation on top of the compounds. How many sets you need is in the volume guide.
  • Glutes and legs first — a program where the lower body gets more work and the upper body maintenance.

If the goal is just "getting in shape", go full body: it builds both strength and size and forgives missed days.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s3_html:
A beginner (under six months) doesn't need a complicated split. You grow from almost any sensible load, and the main job is learning the compound lifts and getting used to going to the gym. Full body 2–3 times a week or 5×5 is the best start: every movement repeats often, so technique comes faster.

Intermediates (six months to two years) need more volume and variety: upper-lower, a three-day split, push-pull-legs. Now it matters that every muscle gets 10+ working sets a week.

Advanced lifters often outgrow generic programs: they need their own volume balance, priorities for lagging muscles and periodisation. That's a good reason to build a program with a coach rather than take a ready one.

On equipment: almost any program works in an ordinary gym with a barbell, a rack, dumbbells and cables. Training at home with dumbbells and a pull-up bar? Go full body and swap the barbell for dumbbells; the coach will pick substitutes for what you have.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s4.h: Step 4. Frequency and volume per muscle
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s4_html:
Check a program against two numbers. The first — how many times a week each muscle gets trained. In the Schoenfeld et al. (2016) meta-analysis, twice a week gave more growth than once; in the newer Pelland et al. analysis, frequency on its own mattered more for strength, while for size total volume decided. In practice: twice a week is a good norm for nearly everyone.

The second — how many working sets per muscle add up over a week. In the Schoenfeld et al. (2017) meta-analysis, more sets gave more growth, with diminishing returns. For each of my programs I've counted the sets every group gets — see the tables on the muscles pages. For example, "Full body — 3 days" gives the back 13 sets per pass and the quads 6: fine for a beginner, but at an intermediate level your legs need topping up.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s5_html:
• Full body — 2 days — for beginners with two evenings a week for the gym.
  • Full body — 3 days — the classic starter: three similar full-body workouts.
  • Strength 5×5 — for beginners chasing strength: three big lifts, alternating days A and B.
  • Upper / Lower — intermediate, 2–4 workouts a week.
  • 3-day split — intermediate, when you want more work for every group.
  • Push / Pull / Legs — intermediate and up, 3–6 workouts a week.
  • Glutes and legs — 3 days — when the lower body comes first.

Each has exercises by day and set schemes. Take a program into your diary and during the workout I show what's next on the plan.
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s6.h: How long to stick with one program
seo.guide.choose-a-program.s6_html:
Longer than you'd like: 8–12 weeks at least. The first two weeks go into finding working weights and getting used to the exercises — it's too early to judge before that. Changing programs every month means starting over every month and never getting to the progression.

Change when your estimated max on the main lifts hasn't grown for several weeks while sleep, food and consistency are fine (what to do then is in the guide on plateaus), or when life changed: less time, a new gym, a new goal.

If none of the ready ones fits, tell the AI coach how many days you train, what your gym has, your experience and goal. It'll build a program by days with exercises and set schemes, count the volume for every group and let you take it into your diary.
seo.guide.film-your-set.title: How to film a set for a form check: angle, light, length — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.film-your-set.description: How to film a set on your phone so the video can be used for a technique review: angles for squats, presses and deadlifts, camera height, framing, light, clip length and what can and can't be seen.
seo.guide.film-your-set.h1: How to film your set for a form check
seo.guide.film-your-set.card: Angle, height, framing and clip length — so there's something to review.
seo.guide.film-your-set.lead: A video of your set is the best technique coach there is — if it's filmed right. A bad angle hides exactly what needs to be seen, so filming has its own rules: simple, but not optional.
seo.guide.film-your-set.cta: Film a set by these rules and send it to me — I'll review it and tell you what to fix first.
seo.guide.film-your-set.takeaways:
Film from the side, at hip height, from 2–3 metres — the main angle for nearly every exercise.
Your whole body and the whole bar in frame, from the first rep to the last.
The phone stays still: a stand, a tripod or a bench, not a friend's hands.
One set, one video, up to {seconds} seconds.
Film your working weight: technique on a warm-up is different.
Light from the front or side, clothes that show your knees and back.
Compare clips filmed from the same spot — that's how you see technique change.
seo.guide.film-your-set.s1.h: The main angle is from the side
seo.guide.film-your-set.s1_html:
For squats, deadlifts, bench and overhead presses and bent-over rows, almost everything that matters shows from the side: the bar path, torso angle, depth, hip and back position, where the bar sits relative to your foot. Place the phone perpendicular to the bar, in line with mid-foot.

Why so strict: lifting technique is mostly geometry. Where the bar sits relative to mid-foot, how your torso angle changes, whether your hips rise before your chest — all of it happens in the plane you see from the side. A camera at an angle distorts that plane, so a straight bar path looks crooked and a crooked one straight.

From behind you see less than you'd think: your back hides your hips and the bar, and depth is invisible. From the front you see knees and symmetry well, but not the bar path or your back. So your main video is from the side, and other angles are extras when you want to check something specific.
seo.guide.film-your-set.s2_html:
• Height — hips or mid-thigh. From below a squat looks deeper, from above shallower. At hip height depth shows honestly.
  • Distance — 2–3 metres. Closer and your body leaves the frame at the bottom or top; further and small details vanish.
  • Your whole body and the whole bar in frame, from your feet to the bar at the top, with room to spare above and below. Cropped feet or head means lost information.
  • Portrait or landscape — doesn't matter, as long as everything fits. Portrait usually suits deadlifts and squats, landscape the bench.
  • The phone stays still. Prop it on a bench, a plate, a stand or a tripod. Handheld video shakes and drifts, and camera movement gets mistaken for bar movement.
seo.guide.film-your-set.s3_html:
• Squat — from the side at hip height. Want to check your knees? One more video from the front at 30–45°.
  • Deadlift and Romanian deadlift — strictly from the side: the bar path along your legs and your back are what matter. Plates shouldn't hide your foot — move the camera slightly forward.
  • Bench press — from the side at bench height or a bit higher, from the foot end at 45°, to see both the bar path and your shoulder blades.
  • Overhead press — from the side: you see whether the bar clears your face and whether your torso leans back.
  • Pull-ups — from the side or from behind at 45°, to see range and swinging.
  • Lunges and split squats — from the side of the front leg, and from the front for the knees.

Exercise technique — setup, steps and common mistakes — is in the technique section, with start and finish frames.
seo.guide.film-your-set.s4_html:
• Light in front of you or to the side, not behind: against a window or a lamp you turn into a silhouette.
  • Clothes that show your joints. A baggy hoodie hides your back and hips; shorts and a fitted top show knees and spine.
  • The whole set — from unracking to the last rep. Mistakes most often appear on the last heavy reps, and a cut video loses them.
  • Length. For a review I need a clip of one set up to {seconds} seconds — enough for 5–8 reps. Film a long set in full and send the last part.
  • No sound needed — I only look at the picture.
seo.guide.film-your-set.s5_html:
A working set, not a warm-up. On a light weight almost everyone's technique looks fine — it breaks on heavy reps. The best is the last working set of an exercise, when you're already tired: that's where you see what happens under load.

Don't film a max attempt for a review: a set like that is a risk on its own, and judging technique on it is harder. And don't change your technique for the camera — film it the way you always do it.

Want to see your technique improve? Film the same exercise every few weeks from the same spot and height. Then two clips can sit side by side for an honest comparison: depth, torso angle, bar path.

Common filming mistakes:

  • the phone on the floor — the squat looks deeper than it is;
  • the camera almost head-on at a small angle — the bar path disappears;
  • someone walks between the camera and you and hides half the set;
  • zooming instead of stepping back — a worse picture and a tighter frame;
  • the video starts on the second rep — the first is often the most telling.
seo.guide.film-your-set.s6_html:
Open the AI coach, tap {video_btn} and send the clip. I'll ask which exercise it is and look at it: what's visible from this angle, what's going well and what to fix first — not a score out of ten, but one or two things that pay off most. Anything the angle doesn't show, I'll say so and suggest where to film from instead — I won't make it up.

Then ask how to fix it — the conversation carries on from there, and I'll know your sets from the diary. Up to {videos} reviews a day, free, in the bot and the iPhone app. More on the video form check page.
