seo.llms.ff.history: The AI coach answers from the athlete's history: estimated max, tonnage, frequency, bodyweight, weekly volume per muscle group; it builds a program by days and reviews a video of a set.
seo.llms.ff.limits: AI coach daily limits: {questions} questions and {videos} video reviews a day; clips up to {seconds} seconds.
seo.llms.ff.privacy: The site uses no cookies or third-party trackers; the server counts visits without IP addresses. The account can be deleted entirely from settings.
seo.llms.ff.units: Kilograms or pounds are switched in settings and the history is recalculated; the e1RM formula is Epley.
seo.llms.ff.export: Full history export to CSV; CSV import from Hevy, Strong and any spreadsheet, plus workouts pasted as text from notes; an import can be undone for {days} days.
seo.llms.ff.developer: Developer: Aleksandr Vilman (as listed on the App Store). Contact via the support page.
seo.tool.tonnage.log_cta: Log the workout — I'll add up the tonnage
seo.program.fullbody2.title: 2-day full body workout program for beginners — Athlete Diary
seo.program.fullbody3.title: 3-day full body workout: a beginner program — Athlete Diary
seo.program.strength5x5.title: 5×5 workout program for beginners: 3 days a week — Athlete Diary
seo.program.upperlower.title: Upper/lower split program: 2 or 4 days a week — Athlete Diary
seo.program.ppl.title: Push Pull Legs (PPL) program: 3 or 6 day split — Athlete Diary
seo.program.split3.title: 3-day split workout: a bro split for muscle gain — Athlete Diary
seo.program.glutes3.title: Glute and leg workout program: 3 days a week — Athlete Diary
seo.program.fullbody2.who_html: For anyone with two evenings a week for the gym: work, kids, shifts. Each workout covers the whole body, so even a week with one session doesn't leave a muscle with nothing. Two days are enough for a beginner's first months; once a third evening frees up, move to full body three days.
seo.program.fullbody3.who_html: For beginners in their first six to twelve months and for anyone coming back after a break. Three similar workouts mean three rounds of the same movements every week: technique settles faster than in a split where you see a lift once a week. It also works for experienced lifters who can only make it three times.
seo.program.strength5x5.who_html: For beginners who want strength: the squat, bench and row grow fastest when you do them often and add a little weight each time. The program is short — three lifts per workout — but heavy. If you also want arm and shoulder work, this isn't it: there's no isolation on purpose; look at full body three days.
seo.program.upperlower.who_html: For anyone who's outgrown full body and wants more sets per muscle without five or six workouts. Four days — upper, lower, rest, upper, lower — give every muscle two sessions a week. Two days work too: then it's one upper and one lower workout, closer to a beginner program in volume.
seo.program.ppl.who_html: For lifters with a year or more behind them who want a flexible schedule. Three days hit each muscle once a week with plenty of volume per session. Six days run the same cycle twice — a routine that needs sleep, food and free evenings. In between, you can just run the cycle back to back without tying it to weekdays.
seo.program.split3.who_html: For anyone who likes a "chest day" and a "back day": each workout is two muscle groups with lots of exercises for them and a week to recover. Good for intermediates with three evenings. The downside: each muscle is trained once a week, so missing one workout leaves that group untouched for two weeks.
seo.program.glutes3.who_html: For anyone putting glutes and legs first — often women, but the program is about the goal, not gender. The lower body gets three days and the upper body the minimum so it doesn't fall behind. It works for beginners too if you add weight gradually; upper-body work can come later as a separate session.
seo.split.col.days_n: {n, plural, one{# day} other{# days}} a week
seo.split.volume_note_html: I count working sets from the program's schemes with the same rule the diary uses: a set goes in full to the exercise's muscle, and a deadlift set is split half to the back and half to the hamstrings and glutes. Muscles that only assist (triceps in a press) aren't counted. Volume targets are in the sets-per-week guide, and you can check your own plan with the volume calculator.
seo.split.progress_html:
Any program works as long as the load keeps going up. The simplest way is double progression: in a "3×8–12" scheme, push the reps to 12 on every set, then add weight and start again at 8. Heavy compounds for 3–6 reps grow by weight: 2.5 kg at a time on presses and 5 kg on squats and pulls, while it keeps working.

When the weight stalls for 2–3 weeks, don't scrap the program — check sleep, food and technique first, then take a deload. More in the progressive overload guide. If you log your sets, I suggest a target for each one from your last workout.
seo.split.cta_html: Take a program into your diary and start with day one — in the bot it's under {programs} → {ready}. Templates aren't in the ready-made list: build one in your programs or ask the coach — {ai} will put it together for your days.
seo.splits.title: Workout splits: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 day gym programs — Athlete Diary
seo.splits.h1: Workout splits: how to lay out your week
seo.splits.description: How to lay out your training week: options for 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 days, upper/lower, push/pull/legs, PHUL and the bro split — each with a schedule and sets per muscle per week.
seo.splits.lead: A split is how you divide your muscles across the days. Don't start with a name — start with how many evenings you really have for the gym, and the choice gets short.
seo.splits.card: 2–6 days a week: schedule and volume per muscle.
seo.splits.workouts.h: Two muscle groups in one workout
seo.splits.how_html:
Every option shows the week day by day and the sets per muscle per week, counted from the program's own schemes. That's more honest than names: "upper/lower" and "push/pull/legs" can give the same chest 8 sets or 16, depending on how the days are built.

What matters most for muscle growth is volume — hard sets per muscle per week — and whether the load keeps rising week to week. Frequency on its own decides very little: at equal volume, twice and three times a week grow muscle about the same, as covered in the frequency guide. So the best split is the one you won't skip.
seo.split.2-day.title: 2 day workout split: full body or upper/lower — Athlete Diary
seo.split.2-day.description: Training twice a week: a full body program and an upper/lower split — schedule, exercises and how many sets each muscle gets per week.
seo.split.2-day.lead: Two days a week isn't a compromise, it's a normal start. What matters is that every muscle gets work and the weight slowly goes up.
seo.split.2-day.card: Full body twice, or upper and lower once each.
seo.split.2-day.who_html: For beginners, people with a packed schedule and anyone coming back after a break. Two sessions with two or three days between them are enough to grow in the first months, and easy to recover from. If you've trained for years, two days will hold your shape, but there's too little volume for steady progress.
seo.split.2-day.choose_html:
If you're a beginner, take full body for two days: every muscle works twice a week, and missing a day doesn't wipe out the week. "Upper / Lower" once each gives more sets per workout, but each muscle works once a week — an option for people who like splits and will move to four days soon.

Either way, space the days two or three days apart: Monday and Thursday, Tuesday and Friday. Two days in a row followed by five days off works worse.
seo.split.3-day.title: 3 day workout split: five ways to train three times a week — Athlete Diary
seo.split.3-day.description: Training three times a week: full body, 5×5, a bro split, push/pull/legs and a glute focus — the day-by-day schedule and weekly sets per muscle for each.
seo.split.3-day.lead: Three days is the most common choice and the most convenient: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, with a rest day between sessions. There are five options, and their volume differs a lot.
seo.split.3-day.card: Full body, 5×5, bro split, PPL or glutes.
seo.split.3-day.who_html: Almost everyone: beginners, intermediates and anyone without time for four or five workouts. Three days give you both frequency and rest: a day off between sessions and enough sets over the week to grow. The key is picking the option that fits your goal, not the name.
seo.split.3-day.choose_html:
• Beginner who wants a bit of everything — full body three days: every muscle three times a week, the fastest way to learn technique.
  • Beginner who wants strength — 5×5: three big lifts and weight that goes up every session.
  • Intermediate who likes a day per muscle — the 3-day split: two groups per workout with plenty of sets.
  • Want push, pull and legs — push/pull/legs, one round a week.
  • Glutes and legs come first — glutes and legs three days.

Look at the volume tables: 5×5 has almost no direct arm or delt work, the split has lots of chest and back but all of it once a week. That's neither good nor bad — they're different tools.
seo.split.4-day.title: 4 day workout split: upper/lower and PHUL — Athlete Diary
seo.split.4-day.description: Training four times a week: upper/lower twice and PHUL — the day-by-day schedule, exercises and how many sets each muscle gets per week.
seo.split.4-day.lead: Four days is the point where every muscle works twice a week without workouts stretching to ninety minutes. The classic here is upper and lower.
seo.split.4-day.card: Upper/lower twice or PHUL: strength and size.
seo.split.4-day.who_html: For intermediates — anyone with six months or more behind them who has outgrown the volume of full body. Four workouts mean four evenings and time to recover: two days on, a day off, two more and the weekend.
seo.split.4-day.choose_html:
"Upper / Lower" repeats the same two days twice: easier to run and to progress. PHUL has four different days: two strength days for 3–5 reps and two volume days for 8–15. It fits if you want both strength in the big lifts and volume for growth; it's also harder — the squat and deadlift strength day comes right after the upper one.

If in doubt, start with "Upper / Lower": it's the same program that lives in the bot, one tap to take it.
seo.split.5-day.title: 5 day workout split: bro split and upper/lower + PPL — Athlete Diary
seo.split.5-day.description: Training five times a week: the classic bro split (chest, back, legs, shoulders, arms) and upper/lower + push/pull/legs — the schedule and weekly sets per muscle.
seo.split.5-day.lead: Five days is a routine. You can give each day its own muscle group, bodybuilding-magazine style, or stack upper/lower with push/pull/legs and train everything twice.
seo.split.5-day.card: A bro split by body part or upper/lower + PPL.
seo.split.5-day.who_html: For lifters past their first year who enjoy the gym and can train five times a week without giving up sleep. Beginners don't need five days: three-day programs drive progress in the first months, and five sessions are harder to recover from and easier to quit.
seo.split.5-day.choose_html:
The bro split (chest, back, legs, shoulders, arms) gives each group its own workout and lots of exercises, but each muscle once a week. That suits you if you like long sessions on one group and rarely skip: missing chest day means two weeks without chest.

Upper/lower + PPL runs days from two of the bot's programs back to back: upper, lower, rest, push, pull, legs. Every muscle works twice, with more weekly volume than four days. If you're choosing between them for growth, the second gives more frequency for the same time; if you love an "arm day", take the first — it works too.
seo.split.6-day.title: 6 day workout split: push pull legs twice a week — Athlete Diary
seo.split.6-day.description: Training six times a week: two rounds of push/pull/legs — the day-by-day schedule, exercises and how many sets each muscle gets per week.
seo.split.6-day.lead: Six days means push/pull/legs twice over with one day off. High volume, each muscle twice a week — and a price: your sleep and food have to keep up.
seo.split.6-day.who_html: For advanced lifters and people whose main hobby is the gym. Six workouts of 60–75 minutes is a lot: if you sleep six hours and skip meals, recovery won't keep up and progress will stall sooner than on three days.
seo.split.6-day.choose_html: Six days is the bot's push/pull/legs run in a loop with no gaps. If the week gets tough, drop to three days — same program, one round, nothing to rebuild. Not sure you can handle six? Look at four or five days: less volume, almost the same frequency.
seo.split.phul.title: PHUL workout: power hypertrophy upper lower, 4 days — Athlete Diary
seo.split.phul.description: PHUL is four days: power upper and lower for 3–5 reps and hypertrophy days for 8–15. A day-by-day template, the schedule and weekly sets per muscle.
seo.split.phul.lead: PHUL stands for Power Hypertrophy Upper Lower: upper and lower twice a week, once heavy for low reps and once lighter for more. Strength and size in the same week.
seo.split.phul.who_html: For intermediates who want more than plain upper/lower and want to build strength in the big lifts without dropping size work. The power days need solid squat, deadlift and press technique: if those still wobble, start with plain "Upper / Lower".
seo.split.phul.choose_html: This PHUL is my template built from catalog exercises, not a program in the bot: copy the days into your own programs or ask the coach to build it for you. On power days rest 2–3 minutes and add weight once you hit the top of the range; on hypertrophy days rest 60–90 seconds and use double progression. The difference from other four-day options is the power days: if strength isn't a priority, the volume upper/lower twice is simpler.
seo.split.full-body-vs-split.title: Full body vs split: full body, upper/lower, PPL and bro split compared — Athlete Diary
seo.split.full-body-vs-split.h1: Full body vs split: which to choose
seo.split.full-body-vs-split.description: Full body vs split: full body, upper/lower, push/pull/legs and a bro split side by side — workouts a week, sets per session, frequency and volume per muscle.
seo.split.full-body-vs-split.lead: The full body vs split argument is usually about taste. I put four of the bot's programs side by side and counted what each gives your muscles per week — the numbers show the difference.
seo.split.full-body-vs-split.card: Full body, upper/lower, PPL and a bro split in numbers.
seo.split.full-body-vs-split.who_html: Full body suits beginners and anyone with three evenings or fewer: frequent work for every muscle, similar workouts, fast technique learning. Upper/lower is the next step: four days and two sessions per muscle. Push/pull/legs over six days has the most volume, for those ready for the routine. A bro split gives lots of work per group in one go, but each muscle once a week.
seo.split.full-body-vs-split.choose_html:
Research says that at equal volume, frequency barely affects muscle growth — so volume decides, and whether you can keep the schedule. Look at "sets per workout" and "workouts a week": full body is fewer sets at a time but more often; a split is the opposite. If workouts longer than an hour don't fit your day, pick programs with fewer sets per session, even if there are more sessions a week.

More on frequency in the frequency guide, and on how many sets you need in the volume guide. Options by number of days are in splits.
seo.tpl.bro5.name: 5-day bro split
seo.tpl.bro5.about_html: One group a day: chest, back, legs, shoulders, arms. My template from catalog exercises: it's not among the bot's ready-made programs — build it in your programs or ask the coach.
seo.tpl.phul.name: PHUL, 4 days
seo.tpl.phul.about_html: Power upper and lower for 3–5 reps, then hypertrophy upper and lower for 8–15. My template from catalog exercises — it's not among the bot's ready-made programs.
seo.tpl.ulppl.name: Upper/lower + push/pull/legs
seo.tpl.ulppl.about_html: Two days from "Upper / Lower" and three from push/pull/legs — both programs are in the bot, and running them together over five days is my template: take both and alternate the days.

seo.wkt.chest-and-triceps.title: Chest and triceps workout: exercises, sets and reps — Athlete Diary
seo.wkt.chest-and-triceps.description: A chest and triceps workout: five exercises with sets and reps from one of the bot's programs, how many sets each muscle gets and how to fit it into your week.
seo.wkt.chest-and-triceps.lead: The chest and triceps work in the same presses, so they share a day: heavy presses first while the triceps are fresh, then isolation for them.
seo.wkt.chest-and-triceps.card: Presses, flyes and triceps in one day.
seo.wkt.chest-and-triceps.why_html:
In every press — flat, incline, dips — the triceps straighten the elbow while the chest brings the arms together. Train them on different days and the triceps get tired twice: on chest day and on their own day. On the same day they get the rest of the week off — or until the next upper workout.

Order matters: start with the bench press while your triceps are fresh — otherwise they give out before your chest. Triceps isolation goes last: by then they've already worked in the presses, so two exercises are enough.
seo.wkt.chest-and-triceps.tips:
Warm up with two or three light sets of the press — the warm-up calculator gives you the weights.
Rest 2–3 minutes between bench sets and 60–90 seconds on isolation.
If your triceps give out before your chest by the second exercise, swap the barbell for dumbbells or cut a set.
In flyes keep the elbow angle fixed: it's a chest stretch, not a press.
Log every set: next time I'll tell you where to add a rep or some weight.
seo.wkt.chest-and-triceps.week_html: In the 3-day split this day comes first, followed by back and biceps and then legs and shoulders. If you train five days, chest and triceps can each get their own day — that's the bro split. Leave at least a day between this one and shoulder day: the front delts work in presses too.
seo.wkt.back-and-biceps.title: Back and biceps workout: exercises, sets and reps — Athlete Diary
seo.wkt.back-and-biceps.description: A back and biceps workout: pull-ups, rows and curls with sets and reps from one of the bot's programs, volume per muscle and where it fits in your week.
seo.wkt.back-and-biceps.lead: The biceps bend your elbow in every row and pull-up, so they go on back day: heavy pulls first, then a couple of exercises for the biceps themselves.
seo.wkt.back-and-biceps.card: Pull-ups, rows and biceps in one day.
seo.wkt.back-and-biceps.why_html:
A row is drawing your shoulder blades together and bending your elbow. The lats and mid back pull, the biceps help, and by the end of the rows they're already loaded. Training them separately the next day doesn't let them recover; on back day they rest with your back.

Start with pull-ups or another vertical pull, then a horizontal one — the barbell row. Biceps go last: barbell curls and hammer curls for the brachialis.
seo.wkt.back-and-biceps.tips:
Start every pull with your shoulder blades, not your arms — otherwise it's biceps work, not back.
If you can do fewer than five pull-ups, swap some sets for lat pulldowns or band-assisted pull-ups.
In the bent-over row hold the torso angle: a torso that rises every rep means the weight is too heavy.
In curls keep your elbows at your sides; swinging means the weight is too much.
Log your sets — I'll show whether your estimated max is rising in pull-ups and rows.
seo.wkt.back-and-biceps.week_html: In the 3-day split it's the second day, between chest and triceps and legs and shoulders. Don't add heavy deadlifts here: in that split they sit with legs, and on back day your lower back is already holding the bent-over row. In the 5-day bro split back and arms get separate days.
seo.wkt.shoulders-and-arms.title: Shoulders and arms workout: delts, biceps and triceps in one day — Athlete Diary
seo.wkt.shoulders-and-arms.description: A shoulders and arms workout: press, raises, face pulls, biceps and triceps — a template with sets and reps, volume per muscle and where it fits in the week.
seo.wkt.shoulders-and-arms.lead: Shoulders and arms are small muscles, and on chest and back days they only assist. A day of their own gives them real work: all three delt heads, biceps and triceps.
seo.wkt.shoulders-and-arms.card: Delts, biceps and triceps in one day.
seo.wkt.shoulders-and-arms.why_html:
Presses load the front delts, but the side and rear delts barely work in them — they need lateral raises and face pulls. On back and chest days the biceps and triceps assist without getting a full load. A shoulders-and-arms day brings it all into one hour-long workout.

Order: the overhead press first while your shoulders are fresh, then side and rear delts, then arms — alternate biceps and triceps so one rests while the other works.
seo.wkt.shoulders-and-arms.tips:
Do raises and face pulls light, for 12–15 reps: delts care more about range than kilos.
Alternate biceps and triceps as a superset — the workout gets shorter and each muscle still gets its rest.
If your shoulder doesn't like the overhead barbell or dumbbell press, try the machine press or a neutral grip.
Don't put this day right after chest: the front delts and triceps worked in the presses.
Log your sets — progress on raises is slow, and without a log you won't see it.
seo.wkt.shoulders-and-arms.week_html: This day belongs to a 5-day bro split, where shoulders and arms get separate days, or works as a fifth day on top of "Upper / Lower" if your arms lag. Put it a day after chest and back: shoulders and arms need time to recover from the presses and rows.

seo.me.lead: {n, plural, one{# exercise} other{# exercises}} from the diary's catalog, all with photos. Below are the list and a sample {muscle} workout: compounds first, then isolation.
seo.me.session.name: {muscle} workout
seo.me.session.note_html: Four exercises from the list: compounds first, then isolation. It's a template for one day; how many sets a muscle needs per week is in the volume guide, and how to progress is in the progressive overload guide.
seo.me.dumbbell.why_html:
Dumbbells give each arm its own path and its own weight: your strong side can't carry the weak one, and any difference shows right away. The range is usually bigger than with a barbell, and a pair of dumbbells and a bench is enough to start — so these {muscle} exercises work at home too.

The downside is the weight ceiling: heavy dumbbells are hard to get into position, and jumps are 2 kg per hand rather than 1 kg on the bar. When the weight climbs slowly, add reps instead — double progression is made for dumbbells.
seo.me.barbell.why_html:
A barbell lets you lift the most and add the smallest steps — from 1 kg with 0.5 kg plates. That's why the heaviest {muscle} exercises with the clearest progress are barbell ones: the weight in your log climbs right in front of you.

The price is technique and safety. Do heavy sets in a rack with safeties or with a spotter, start light and film a set if you're unsure of your form. The warm-up calculator will lay out the sets up to your working weight.
seo.me.machine.why_html:
A machine sets the path, and a cable keeps tension where a dumbbell goes slack — at the bottom of a raise or the top of a fly. There's nothing to stabilise, so you can safely take sets close to failure without a spotter, and changing the weight is moving a pin. For a beginner, machine {muscle} exercises are the easiest way in.

The downsides: a machine is built for an average person — adjust the seat and handles to fit you — and machines that look identical weigh differently from gym to gym. Only compare your numbers on the same machine.
seo.me.bodyweight.why_html:
Bodyweight {muscle} exercises need a floor and sometimes a bar or a bench — no gym required, so you can do the workout at home. The load is your own weight, so progress comes from reps and harder variations rather than kilos; that's how the diary sets targets for these exercises.

Once you're past 15–20 reps and the set no longer feels hard, move to a tougher variation (feet elevated, slow tempo, a pause at the bottom) or add weight — a backpack, a belt, a dumbbell. Sets far from failure grow muscle less well; more on that in the junk volume guide.

seo.tool.531.card: Training max and weights for the four-week cycle.
seo.tool.531.title: 5/3/1 calculator: training max and weights for the 4-week cycle — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.531.description: Work out a 5/3/1 cycle: a training max of 90% of your one-rep max, three work weeks and a deload with weights, the warm-up and the bump for the next cycle — in kg or lb.
seo.tool.531.lead: Enter a work set or your one-rep max — I'll work out the training max and every weight for the four-week cycle, rounded to loadable plates.
seo.tool.531.cta: Log the cycle's sets in your diary — I'll keep the reps from each "+" set, and they show whether your max is going up.
seo.tool.531.how_html:
5/3/1 is Jim Wendler's scheme for one main lift a day: squat, bench, deadlift or overhead press. Every weight is based not on your one-rep max but on a training max — 90% of it. That leaves room even on a hard day, so the cycle doesn't hit failure in week two.

  • Week 1 — 65%, 75% and 85% of the training max for 5, 5 and 5+.
  • Week 2 — 70%, 80% and 90% for 3, 3 and 3+.
  • Week 3 — 75%, 85% and 95% for 5, 3 and 1+.
  • Week 4 — deload: 40%, 50% and 60% for 5.

The "+" is an as-many-reps-as-possible set, but with good form, not a grind to the last rep. Before the work sets, warm up with 40%, 50% and 60% for 5, 5 and 3. I round the weights down to a loadable step — 2.5 kg or 5 lb — like the warm-up calculator.

After the cycle the training max goes up by 2.5 kg on presses and 5 kg on squats and deadlifts (5 and 10 lb). I estimate the one-rep max from a set with the Epley formula, the same as the 1RM calculator and the diary. The scheme and percentages follow public write-ups of the author's program, such as the 5/3/1 Primer.

seo.tool.weekly-volume.cta: Log your workouts — I'll count the weekly sets per muscle from what you actually did, not the plan.
seo.tool.weekly-volume.how_html:
Each set goes in full to the exercise's muscle: bench press to chest, pulldown to back, lateral raise to side delts. The deadlift sits in back, but the glutes and hamstrings do most of the work, so I split its sets: half to back and a quarter each to hamstrings and glutes. Muscles that only assist — triceps in a press, biceps in a row — aren't counted: that's how the diary counts weekly volume, and how the coach builds a program.

The notes follow the same method the coach uses to build a program: side delts, quads and hamstrings from 6 sets a week, glutes from 4, biceps and triceps from 4 if they're in the plan; over 16 on one muscle is a lot. These are guidelines for growth, not a rule: beginners need less — details in the sets-per-week guide.

I look up names in the diary's catalog in the page language, ignoring case. Ready-made programs with volume already counted are in splits.
seo.pair.hack-squat-vs-back-squat.card: Machine or barbell: quads or the whole body.
seo.pair.hack-squat-vs-back-squat.descri: Hack squat vs back squat: what each one loads, which is harder to learn, which is safer near failure and which to pick for your goal.
seo.pair.hack-squat-vs-back-squat.lead: Both are squats, but the hack squat guides you on rails with your back supported, while the barbell makes you hold everything yourself. That's the whole difference.
seo.pair.hack-squat-vs-back-squat.diff_h:
In the hack squat your back and shoulders rest on pads, the path is fixed, and you can place your feet higher or lower on the platform. Your torso doesn't have to balance, so almost all the work goes to the quads and glutes with minimal lower-back load. Taking a set close to failure is safe: if you can't stand up, drop the safeties.

The back squat loads everything at once: legs, back and the abs holding your torso. It's harder to learn but carries over better to general strength and doesn't depend on a particular gym's machine. For powerlifting results there's no substitute.
seo.pair.hack-squat-vs-back-squat.both_h: Yes, and it's a common pair: a heavy back squat first for 3–8 reps, then the hack squat for 8–15 when your back is tired but your quads can take more volume.
seo.pair.hack-squat-vs-back-squat.when_a: You want quad work without loading your back, or you're learning to squat deep.
seo.pair.hack-squat-vs-back-squat.when_b: You want whole-body strength or you're preparing for powerlifting.
seo.pair.leg-press-vs-hack-squat.card: Two leg machines: which loads the quads more.
seo.pair.leg-press-vs-hack-squat.descrip: Leg press vs hack squat: both machines, but a different torso position — which loads the quads more, which is easier for beginners and which to choose.
seo.pair.leg-press-vs-hack-squat.lead: Both machines take balance out of the picture. In the leg press you sit and push a platform; in the hack squat you stand and squat yourself.
seo.pair.leg-press-vs-hack-squat.diff_ht:
The leg press is the easiest way in: your back is on the pad, the range is easy to limit, and big weights need little technique. Foot position shifts the emphasis: higher on the platform means more glutes and hamstrings, lower means more quads. The weak spot is the lower back at the bottom: if your hips lift off the pad, the range is too deep.

The hack squat is closer to a real squat: you stand, your torso is nearly upright, your knees travel well forward and the quads stretch more. The loads are noticeably lower than on the leg press — you can't compare kilos between machines.
seo.pair.leg-press-vs-hack-squat.both_ht: Yes: the hack squat first while your legs are fresh, then the leg press for reps. Or alternate them between workouts if both don't fit in one.
seo.pair.leg-press-vs-hack-squat.when_a_: You're a beginner, your back complains in squats, or you want leg volume without extra fatigue.
seo.pair.leg-press-vs-hack-squat.when_b_: You want more quads and a movement that feels like a squat.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-t-bar-row.card: Barbell or T-bar: grip and lower-back load.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-t-bar-row.descri: Barbell row vs T-bar row: how the grip, the path and the lower-back load differ, which is harder and which to pick for your back.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-t-bar-row.lead: Both are bent-over horizontal rows. The T-bar is anchored at one end, so the weight travels in an arc and the grip can be narrow and neutral.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-t-bar-row.diff_h:
The barbell row is the classic: an overhand shoulder-width grip, the bar pulled to your waist, and the whole thing held up by your lower back and hamstrings. It's easy to get wrong: your torso rises and the row turns into a bent-over shrug.

On a T-bar one end is anchored, so the path is steadier, and the handle gives a narrow neutral grip — your elbows travel along your sides and the mid back gets more of the work. Your lower back still holds the hinge, but the angle is easier to keep. With a chest pad the back load disappears almost entirely.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-t-bar-row.both_h: Yes: the barbell row heavy first for 6–10, the T-bar second for 8–12. Or alternate them by week if you want grip variety.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-t-bar-row.when_a: You only have a barbell, or you want a strong lower back and posterior chain.
seo.pair.barbell-row-vs-t-bar-row.when_b: You want a steadier path and more mid back.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-rack-pull.card: From the floor or the pins: the full pull or its top half.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-rack-pull.descripti: Deadlift vs rack pull: how the range differs, what each one loads, how much weight you can take and when the rack pull is more useful than the full lift.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-rack-pull.lead: The rack pull is the top part of a deadlift: the bar starts from pins around knee height or just below, so the hardest part — breaking it off the floor — is gone.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-rack-pull.diff_html:
The deadlift from the floor is the full movement: the quads help break the weight off, then the glutes and hamstrings finish the pull while your back holds it all straight. It's one of the hardest lifts, both for your body and your recovery.

From the pins the range is shorter, the quads barely work, and you can lift more than from the floor. The load moves to the glutes, the spinal erectors and the traps holding a heavy bar at the top. Rack pulls are useful when the lockout is your weak point, or when you want to train your back and grip without the full cost of deadlifts.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-rack-pull.both_html: Yes, but not both heavy on the same day: rack pulls usually go in as an accessory on another day of the week, not after heavy deadlifts.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-rack-pull.when_a_ht: You want strength in the full movement or you're preparing for powerlifting.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-rack-pull.when_b_ht: Your lockout is weak, or you want back and grip work without full deadlifts.
seo.pair.front-squat-vs-leg-press.card: Free bar on your chest or a sled with a backrest: two routes to the quads.
seo.pair.front-squat-vs-leg-press.descri: Front squat vs leg press: how the quads work, what holds your torso, how much technique each needs and which to pick for your goal.
seo.pair.front-squat-vs-leg-press.lead: Both are quad-first lifts. In the front squat you hold the bar and your torso yourself; on the leg press your back rests on a pad and the sled sets the path.
seo.pair.front-squat-vs-leg-press.diff_h:
The front squat is a free weight: the bar sits on your front delts, your torso stays nearly upright, and your upper back and abs keep it from tipping forward. It takes wrist and ankle mobility and a couple of weeks of practice, but you train your legs together with everything that holds the bar.

The leg press takes balance out of it: your back is pinned to the pad, so you can load your legs heavy and close to failure without thinking about your torso. Your pelvis sets the depth — lower the sled until your lower back starts to peel off the pad. Don't compare leg press numbers with squat numbers: machine angles and friction vary from gym to gym.
seo.pair.front-squat-vs-leg-press.both_h: Yes, and it's a common pairing: front squats first for 4–6 reps while you're fresh, leg press second for 10–15 to add quad volume without loading your back.
seo.pair.front-squat-vs-leg-press.when_a: You want strong legs together with your core and upper back, and you're ready to learn the technique.
seo.pair.front-squat-vs-leg-press.when_b: You need quad volume without back load, or you're just starting out.
seo.pair.overhead-press-vs-seated-barbel: Standing or seated: your whole torso in it, or just the shoulders.
Standing vs seated barbell overhead press: what the bench changes, how the delts, triceps and core work, where you lift more and which to pick.
Same bar, same path — from your collarbones to overhead. The difference is support: standing, you hold your torso yourself; seated, the bench takes half of that job away.

Standing, the press is a whole-body lift: glutes and abs stay tight so your lower back doesn't arch and the bar stays over mid-foot. You train your shoulders and learn to brace under weight overhead at the same time. What usually limits you isn't the delts, it's how solid you stand.

Seated with a backrest there's almost nothing to balance, so the delts and triceps get all the work. There's one trap: a lot of people lean back and turn it into an incline press. Keep your shoulder blades on the pad and your ribs down — then the weight is honest.

Yes: standing as the main lift for 3–6 reps, seated on another day or as a second exercise for 8–12. If your lower back is tired after squats or deadlifts, the seated press is a sensible swap that day.
You want overhead strength along with your core, or the press is one of your main lifts.
You want to load your shoulders without the core work, or your lower back is already tired.
A barbell overhead or dumbbells with a twist: load against range.
Overhead press vs Arnold press: how the path differs, which delts work harder, where you lift more and which to pick.
The standing barbell press is a heavy compound lift with one bar for both arms. The Arnold press uses dumbbells that start palms facing you and rotate as you press.

The barbell is the easiest way to add weight in small steps, and it builds the most overhead strength. The bar has to travel around your face, so your head moves back and your torso holds the whole thing together.

In the Arnold press the dumbbells start in front of your face, palms toward you, and turn to face forward on the way up. The front delts get a bigger stretch at the bottom, the range is longer, and each arm works on its own. You'll use noticeably less weight than in a regular dumbbell press — the rotation eats strength, and that's fine: this lift is about time under load, not records.

Yes: the barbell first and heavy, the Arnold press second for 8–12 reps, slow and without yanking through the turn. Two heavy overhead presses in one session will fry your triceps, so keep the second one moderate.
You want overhead strength and simple progression by weight.
You want more front delt and a long range with dumbbells.
seo.pair.seated-dumbbell-press-vs-machin: Dumbbells or a machine: a free path against a safe failure.
Seated dumbbell press vs machine shoulder press: stabilisation, bar path, safe failure, progression and which to pick.
Both are seated overhead presses, and the same muscles do the work. The difference is who guides the weight: you with dumbbells, the lever on a machine.

With dumbbells each arm holds its own weight, so a weaker side shows up right away. You pick the path: the elbows can come slightly forward, wherever your shoulder feels right. The downside — heavy dumbbells are awkward to get into position, and on the last rep there's a chance one drifts.

The machine holds the path for you: you can push to failure without worrying about dropping anything, and change the weight in a second with the pin — handy for drop sets. But the lever is the same for everyone, and if its arc doesn't suit your shoulders you can't adjust it — then go back to dumbbells.
Yes: dumbbells first for 6–10, the machine at the end for 12–15 or to failure. The machine is a good call when you train without a spotter and want to grind out the last reps.
You want a free path and each arm working on its own.
You want to push safely to failure, or you're just starting.
seo.pair.incline-dumbbell-press-vs-incli: The incline bench: dumbbells go deeper, the barbell goes heavier.
Incline dumbbell press vs incline barbell press: range of motion, load, upper-chest work, spotting and which to pick.
Same bench at around 30 degrees, same muscles — upper chest, front delts and triceps. What changes is the implement, and with it the depth, the load and how you progress.

Dumbbells go lower than a bar: the bar stops on your chest, the dumbbells only stop where your shoulder mobility ends. The chest gets more stretch at the bottom, and your hands can turn slightly into a comfortable angle. Each arm works on its own, so a weak side can't hide behind the strong one.

With a barbell you lift more and progress more easily — in small plate jumps instead of going straight to the next pair of dumbbells. The downside: a heavy incline press without a spotter is riskier, so set the safety arms or get someone to stand behind you.
Yes: the barbell heavy when the goal is strength, dumbbells for 8–12 when the goal is chest size. You can alternate them by week or put dumbbells after your flat barbell bench.
You want a deep range and each arm working on its own.
You want more weight and small steps in progression.
seo.pair.dumbbell-bench-press-vs-machine: Dumbbells or a chest machine: stability against simplicity.
Dumbbell bench press vs machine chest press: stabilisation, range, failure without a spotter, progression and which to pick.
Both are horizontal chest presses with the front delts and triceps helping. With dumbbells you keep your own balance; on the machine the rails do it.

With dumbbells the shoulder works as a stabiliser: you have to hold the weight over your chest, not just push it up. The range is deeper than with a barbell, and you adjust the path to fit you. You also need to learn to kick heavy dumbbells into position with your knees and set them down just as safely.

The machine is simpler: sit down, set the seat so the handles line up with mid-chest, and press. There's almost no technique to learn, failure is safe and the weight changes with a pin. The cost — the machine doesn't teach you to control a load, and its numbers don't carry over to free-weight presses.
Yes: dumbbells first, the machine as a second exercise or a finisher to failure. For a beginner the machine builds the first strength while the dumbbell technique comes together.
You want a deep range and stable shoulders.
You're new, you train without a spotter, or you're finishing your chest to failure.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-smith-machine-be: A free bar or a Smith: your own path or the rails.
Barbell bench press vs Smith machine bench press: bar path, stabilisation, safety, carryover and which to pick.
Same bar, same bench — but in a Smith machine the bar runs on rails straight up and down and hooks on at any point.

In a regular bench the bar doesn't move in a straight line: you lower it to the bottom of your chest and press it slightly back over your shoulders. Your shoulders and shoulder blades hold that arc and keep the bar balanced — which makes the free bench harder and better for strength that carries over to other presses.

In a Smith the rails set the path: there's almost nothing to stabilise, so you can focus on the chest. The hooks are a built-in safety, which makes the Smith good when you press alone. But the numbers don't transfer: some Smith bars are counterweighted, and without stabilisation the load feels different. Compare Smith only with Smith.
Yes: the free bench as your main lift, the Smith as a second exercise for 8–12 or on days with no spotter. Log them as two separate exercises, or your progress in the diary gets mixed up.
You want pressing strength that shows up everywhere and you're learning to control the weight.
You train without a spotter or want to load your chest without the balance work.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-floor-press.card: From the bench or the floor: the full range or a strong lockout.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-floor-press.desc: Bench press vs floor press: range of motion, triceps and chest work, leg drive, safety and which to pick.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-floor-press.lead: The floor press is the same bench press, only you lie on the floor inside a power rack, and your elbows hit the floor before the bar would touch your chest.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-floor-press.diff:
On the bench you get the full range: the bar touches your chest, your feet push into the floor and help through whole-body tension. It's the main option for pressing strength and for the chest, which works hardest at the bottom.

On the floor the bottom of the movement is gone, your legs barely help, and every rep starts from a short pause on the floor. The load shifts to the triceps and the top half of the press, which is why people use it when the lockout is the weak point. Set the rack's safety arms just below where the bar sits at the bottom: on the floor you can't roll the bar off yourself.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-floor-press.both: Yes: the bench as your main lift, the floor press as an accessory on another day for 5–8 reps. When the bottom of the bench doesn't feel right, the shorter range from the floor often lets you keep pressing.
seo.pair.bench-press-vs-floor-press.when: You want the full lift, the most chest and strength in the competition movement.
Your lockout is weak or you want more triceps in your press.
Two heavy triceps presses: a bar on a bench or your bodyweight on the bars.
Close-grip bench press vs dips: how the triceps, chest and shoulders work, progression, difficulty and which to pick.
Both are compound presses where the triceps do most of the work. In the close-grip bench you move a bar; on dips you move yourself.

The close-grip bench is a regular bench with a shoulder-width grip and your elbows tucked along your sides. Don't go narrower: a very narrow grip wrenches the wrists and adds nothing for the triceps. Progression is simple — by plates — and the weight is heavy, which makes it one of the best strength moves for triceps.

On dips you lift nearly your whole bodyweight. Keep your torso upright and the triceps work more; lean forward and the chest takes over. The bottom is the hardest spot for the shoulder, so go down to a right angle at the elbows, not as deep as you can. Add weight with a belt and a plate once bodyweight gets easy.
Yes, but on different days or back to back with moderate weight: both hit the triceps and front delts hard. A good setup is close-grip bench on press day and dips on arm day.
You want heavy triceps work with precise progression by weight.
You want triceps and lower chest without a barbell, and your shoulders are fine on dips.
seo.pair.skull-crusher-vs-overhead-cable: Lying with a bar or overhead on a cable: the long head two ways.
Skull crusher vs overhead cable extension: long-head triceps work, stretch, elbow load and which to pick.
Both load the long head of the triceps because your upper arm is raised. In the skull crusher it's angled up while you lie down; in the cable extension it's overhead while you stand.

In the skull crusher an EZ bar comes down to your forehead or just behind your head, elbows pointing at the ceiling. You can handle real weight, and it's one of the heaviest isolation moves for triceps. The elbows take the most of it too: add weight carefully and don't jerk the bar out of the bottom.

In the overhead extension your arm is raised higher, so the long head gets its biggest stretch. The cable keeps tension through the whole range, and it's usually easier on the elbows than a bar. The weight is lower, so this one is for 10–15 reps, not for records.
Yes: skull crushers first for 8–10, the overhead cable extension second for 12–15. If your elbows push back against the bar, the cable extension can take over the long head on its own.
You want heavy triceps isolation and your elbows handle it.
You want the biggest long-head stretch and an easier ride for your elbows.
seo.pair.rope-pushdown-vs-triceps-pushdo: Rope or bar on the cable: a spread at the bottom or more weight.
Rope pushdown vs bar pushdown: grip, range, load, triceps heads and which to pick.
One cable, one movement — you straighten your elbows from top to bottom with your upper arms pinned to your sides. All that changes is what you hold on to.

With a straight or V-bar the grip is fixed, your hands are locked together, and you can handle more weight. It's a simple lift where progress comes easily and shows up in your diary.

The rope gives a neutral grip, and at the bottom you can pull the ends apart — the elbows straighten fully and the triceps squeeze harder. The weight is lower, but it's kinder to the wrists and you feel the contraction better. In both, the key is the same: elbows stay put, and your body doesn't lean into the weight.
Yes: the bar heavier for 8–12, the rope after it for 12–20 or as a finisher. You can even do both in one set: the bar to failure, then straight to the rope with a lighter weight.
You want more weight and simple progression.
You want a full squeeze at the bottom and a wrist-friendly grip.
seo.pair.hammer-curl-vs-reverse-curl.car: Neutral grip or overhand: the brachialis and the forearms.
seo.pair.hammer-curl-vs-reverse-curl.des: Hammer curl vs reverse curl: brachialis, brachioradialis and forearm work, load and which to pick.
seo.pair.hammer-curl-vs-reverse-curl.lea: Both curls shift part of the work from the biceps to the brachialis and brachioradialis. In a hammer curl your palms face each other; in a reverse curl they face down.
seo.pair.hammer-curl-vs-reverse-curl.dif:
The hammer grip is a strong position for the elbow: the brachialis and brachioradialis work at full power, the biceps helps, and the weight ends up close to a regular curl. It adds thickness to the arm between the biceps and the elbow.

The overhand grip is the weakest position: the biceps is nearly out of it, and the brachioradialis and forearm extensors, which keep your wrist straight, do the main work. The weight is noticeably lower, and that's fine. Reverse curls are the best way to bring up forearms that lag behind.
seo.pair.hammer-curl-vs-reverse-curl.bot: Yes: hammers as the second exercise on arm day for 8–12, reverse curls last for 12–15 with a weight that lets you keep your wrists straight.
seo.pair.hammer-curl-vs-reverse-curl.whe: You want thicker arms and a heavy curl that's easy on the wrists.
You want to bring up your forearms and brachioradialis.
seo.pair.preacher-curl-vs-concentration-: On a preacher bench or seated with one arm: where the bottom is hard, where the top is.
Preacher curl vs concentration curl: where the load peaks, how much cheating is left, weight and which to pick.
Both are strict curls: your body can't help, so the biceps works alone. The difference is where the movement gets hardest.

On a preacher bench your upper arm lies on an angled pad in front of you, and the hardest point is at the bottom, when the arm is nearly straight and the biceps is stretched. It's usually done with an EZ bar, and the weight is decent. Don't drop the weight at the bottom or snap the arm straight — that's exactly where the elbow has it hardest.

In a concentration curl you sit, brace your elbow against your inner thigh and curl a dumbbell with one arm. It's hardest at the top, where the biceps fully contracts. The weight is small, but it's easy to control every rep and even out a weaker arm.
Yes: preachers earlier for 8–12, concentration curls at the end of arm day for 10–15 per arm. Together they cover both the stretched position and the squeeze.
You want heavy strict isolation with the focus on the stretch.
You want to nail the peak contraction and even out your arms one at a time.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-ez-bar-curl.car: A straight bar or a bent one: biceps against wrist comfort.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-ez-bar-curl.des: Barbell curl vs EZ-bar curl: hand position, biceps work, wrist load and which to pick.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-ez-bar-curl.lea: Same movement, different bend in the bar. On a straight bar your palms face fully up; on an EZ bar they turn slightly in.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-ez-bar-curl.dif:
A straight bar fully turns your forearm palm-up, and that's one of the biceps' jobs — so it works at full strength here. But not every wrist and elbow is comfortable in that position, especially under heavy weight.

On an EZ bar your palms turn slightly inward: easier on the wrists, while the biceps still does the main work and the difference in load on it is small. The weight is usually nearly the same. If the straight bar bothers your wrists, take the EZ and don't fight it.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-ez-bar-curl.bot: Yes, but there's little point doing both on one day — they're nearly the same lift. Pick the one that feels better, or swap them every few weeks. Log them separately in the diary: the weight on them doesn't always match.
seo.pair.barbell-curl-vs-ez-bar-curl.whe: Your wrists don't mind and you want the biceps working with the palm fully up.
The straight bar bothers your wrists or elbows.
seo.pair.lateral-raise-vs-cable-lateral-: Dumbbells or a cable: where the side delts work from the very bottom.
Dumbbell lateral raise vs cable lateral raise: where the load peaks, tension at the bottom, convenience and which to pick.
One movement — raising your arms out to shoulder height, with the side delts doing the work. The difference is where the weight pulls from: a dumbbell pulls down, a cable pulls down and across.

With a dumbbell there's almost no load at the bottom: while your arm hangs by your side, there's nothing to hold. It gets hardest at the top, with the arm horizontal. Dumbbells are in every gym, it's easy to raise both arms at once, and it's where almost everyone starts.

On a cable the line runs from the low pulley across your body, so there's tension from the very start — the side delts work through the whole range, including the stretched position. It's done one arm at a time with less weight, but the load is more even. Keep your torso still and don't swing.
Yes: dumbbells for 12–20 with both arms, the cable after for 12–15 per arm. The side delts handle volume well, so both in one session is a normal setup.
You want simple raises anywhere, both arms at once.
You want tension from the very bottom and an even load through the whole range.
seo.pair.rear-delt-fly-vs-face-pull.card: Bent-over flyes or face pulls: the rear delts and the shoulder girdle.
seo.pair.rear-delt-fly-vs-face-pull.desc: Rear delt fly vs face pull: rear delt, rotator cuff and mid-back work, load and which to pick.
seo.pair.rear-delt-fly-vs-face-pull.lead: Both are for the rear delts, which pressing barely touches. The fly isolates them; the face pull adds the rotator cuff and mid back.
seo.pair.rear-delt-fly-vs-face-pull.diff:
In the fly you bend over until you're nearly parallel to the floor and raise the dumbbells out to the sides with slightly bent arms. The rear delts work almost alone, the weight is light, and control is everything: swing your torso and your back steals the work. It's easiest with your chest on an incline bench.

In the face pull you pull a rope from a high pulley toward your face, spreading the ends, and finish by rotating your hands so your fists point up. The rear delts, mid back and the muscles that rotate the shoulder outward all work. The weight is light and the reps high — plenty of people do it in every upper-body session as a warm-up.
seo.pair.rear-delt-fly-vs-face-pull.both: Yes: face pulls at the start of a session as a shoulder warm-up or at the end for 15–20, flyes on shoulder day for 12–20. The rear delts are small and recover fast, so they take frequent work well.
seo.pair.rear-delt-fly-vs-face-pull.when: You want to isolate the rear delts.
You want the rear delts together with the rotator cuff and mid back.
seo.pair.upright-row-vs-lateral-raise.ca: Upright row or lateral raise: two roads to the side delts.
seo.pair.upright-row-vs-lateral-raise.de: Upright row vs lateral raise: side delt and trap work, load, shoulder comfort and which to pick.
seo.pair.upright-row-vs-lateral-raise.le: Both raise your elbows out to the sides and load the side delts. The upright row is a heavier compound lift; the lateral raise is isolation.
seo.pair.upright-row-vs-lateral-raise.di:
In the upright row you pull the bar up along your body with the elbows going up and out. The traps join in, and you can lift far more than in raises. Grip at shoulder width or wider and bring the elbows up to about shoulder height: a narrow grip with the elbows above your head doesn't suit a lot of shoulders. If yours still complains, swap to raises.

Lateral raises isolate the side delts: the traps do less, the weight is light, and the load is easy to control. It's the safest, most straightforward shoulder move, but progress by weight is slow — reps grow more than the load.
seo.pair.upright-row-vs-lateral-raise.bo: Yes: a wide-grip upright row first for 8–12, raises after for 12–20. If you also do shrugs, remember the upright row already loads the traps — count that in your volume.
seo.pair.upright-row-vs-lateral-raise.wh: You want heavy work for the side delts and traps, and your shoulders are fine with it.
You want to isolate the side delts with minimal trap involvement.
seo.pair.barbell-shrug-vs-dumbbell-shrug: Barbell or dumbbell shrugs: load against a natural line.
Barbell shrug vs dumbbell shrug: where the weight sits, range, grip, how much you can lift and which to pick for your traps.
In both you lift your shoulders toward your ears and train the upper traps. The bar hangs in front of your thighs; the dumbbells hang at your sides.

With a barbell you can go very heavy, and progress is easy — by plates. The downside: the bar rubs your thighs and pulls your shoulders slightly forward, and your grip gives out fast — use straps on heavy sets.

Dumbbells hang at your sides, your shoulders rise along their natural line, and the range is usually a little bigger. Each side works on its own. The ceiling comes sooner: heavy dumbbells are hard to hold and pick up off the rack. In both, lift your shoulders straight up and don't roll them — rolling adds nothing.
Yes, but one is usually enough: the traps also work in deadlifts and rows. You can alternate them by week, or go heavy with the bar and do dumbbells for 12–15 on another day.
You want maximum weight and easy progression by plates.
You want a natural line of movement and each side working on its own.
seo.pair.lat-pulldown-vs-close-grip-lat-: Wide bar or close handle: range and elbow path.
Wide-grip vs close-grip lat pulldown: range of motion, elbow path, lat work, load and which to pick.
Same machine, same muscles — lats, biceps and mid back. What changes is the handle: a wide bar with an overhand grip or a narrow V-handle with your palms facing each other.

With a wide bar the elbows travel down and out, the range is shorter, and the upper back and rear delts work a bit more. Don't pull the bar behind your neck — bring it to your upper chest with your torso leaning back slightly.

With a close handle the elbows travel down along your sides, the range is longer, and the lats get a bigger stretch at the top. The neutral grip is easy on the wrists and elbows, and the weight is usually a little higher. Gym lore splits them into "width" and "thickness" — in practice the difference is smaller than it sounds: both load the lats well.

Yes: one grip first, the other as a second exercise, or swap them between sessions. That way your back gets load from different angles, and your elbows don't wear out from the same movement every time.
You want the classic pulldown with more upper back.
You want a long range and a wrist-friendly neutral grip.
seo.pair.lat-pulldown-vs-underhand-lat-p: Overhand or underhand on the cable: back against biceps.
Overhand vs underhand lat pulldown: lat and biceps work, load, elbow path and which to pick.
It's the pull-up versus chin-up story on a cable: overhand means palms away, underhand means palms toward you at shoulder width.

With a wide overhand grip the biceps sits in a weaker position, and more of the load goes to the lats, upper back and rear delts. The weight is usually a little lower than underhand.

Underhand, the elbows travel down along your sides, the biceps joins in more, and you lift more. The lats still work — pulling to your lower chest with a slight lean suits them just fine. It's a good option if you want some extra biceps work, or if the overhand grip doesn't sit well with your shoulders.
Yes: one grip as the main lift, the other as a second exercise or on another day. The underhand grip is also a good lead-in to chin-ups.
You want more back and rear delts.
You want more weight and biceps, or the overhand grip bothers your shoulders.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-assisted-pull-up.car: Full bodyweight or a band: how to get to clean pull-ups.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-assisted-pull-up.des: Pull-up vs band-assisted pull-up: how the band changes the load, how to progress and when to switch to unassisted.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-assisted-pull-up.lea: Same movement, but the band takes part of your weight. It's the ladder to your first clean pull-ups and a way to build volume while bodyweight is still a lot.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-assisted-pull-up.dif:
A clean pull-up is your whole bodyweight, from a dead hang to chin over the bar. It's tough for a beginner, and if you can do 1–2, it's hard to get decent volume.

The band helps most at the bottom, where it's stretched the most, and barely at all at the top — so the top is the hardest part with a band, exactly where people usually get stuck. Progress from a thick band to a thinner one. Add slow negatives without the band — jump to the top and lower yourself over 3–5 seconds — and clean reps come faster.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-assisted-pull-up.bot: Yes: first as many clean pull-ups as you can, then build volume with the band. Once you get 10–12 reps with the thinnest band, switch to clean ones.
seo.pair.pull-up-vs-assisted-pull-up.whe: You can do at least 4–5 clean reps.
You have few or no clean reps yet and want volume in the same movement.
seo.pair.inverted-row-vs-pull-up.card: A horizontal bodyweight row or a vertical pull: mid back and lats.
seo.pair.inverted-row-vs-pull-up.descrip: Inverted row vs pull-up: pulling direction, difficulty, back work, how to adjust the load and which to pick.
seo.pair.inverted-row-vs-pull-up.lead: Both are bodyweight pulls. In an inverted row you hang under a low bar and pull your chest up to it; in a pull-up you lift yourself vertically.
seo.pair.inverted-row-vs-pull-up.diff_ht:
The inverted row is a horizontal pull: the mid back, rear delts, lats and biceps work, much like a bent-over row. You set the load with the angle: the higher the bar and the more upright your body, the easier; feet up on a box makes it harder. That's why almost anyone can do it from day one.

The pull-up is a vertical pull with your full bodyweight: more lats and grip, and one of the hardest bodyweight lifts there is. You can make it easier with a band or a machine. If you can't do pull-ups yet, inverted rows are a good first step toward them.
seo.pair.inverted-row-vs-pull-up.both_ht: Yes, and they complement each other: a vertical and a horizontal pull together give your back the full load. Pull-ups first, inverted rows second for 10–15.
seo.pair.inverted-row-vs-pull-up.when_a_: You're new, you want a horizontal pull without a barbell, or you can't do pull-ups yet.
seo.pair.inverted-row-vs-pull-up.when_b_: You can already do a few pull-ups and want a vertical bodyweight pull.
seo.pair.one-arm-dumbbell-row-vs-barbell: One supported dumbbell or a bent-over barbell: lower back and range.
One-arm dumbbell row vs barbell row: lower-back load, range of motion, weight, back work and which to pick.
Both are horizontal rows for the lats and mid back. With a dumbbell you brace a hand and knee on a bench; with a barbell you hold the hinge yourself.

The one-arm dumbbell row takes almost all the load off your lower back: your torso rests on the bench, so you think only about your back. The range is longer — the elbow goes past your torso, and at the bottom the shoulder blade stretches forward. Each side works on its own, so the weak one shows right away.

The barbell row is a heavy compound pull: you hold the bent-over position, and your lower back and hamstrings work the whole time. You lift more and progress more easily, but it takes more technique — if your torso rises with every rep, the weight is too heavy.
Yes: the barbell first and heavy for 6–10, the dumbbell second for 10–12 per arm. On a day when your lower back is already loaded with deadlifts, keep just the dumbbell.
You want to spare your lower back and work each side on its own.
You want a heavy row for your whole back and a strong posterior chain.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-goblet-squat.card: A bar on your back or a kettlebell at your chest: the heavy squat or squat school.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-goblet-squat.desc: Back squat vs goblet squat: load, depth, torso position, who each suits and when to move to the barbell.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-goblet-squat.lead: Both are squats, and both load the quads and glutes. With a barbell your legs set the limit; with a goblet squat it's how much you can hold in your hands.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-goblet-squat.diff:
The goblet squat puts a kettlebell or dumbbell at your chest. The weight in front keeps your torso upright on its own and helps you sit deep, which makes it the best way to learn to squat. But your legs soon outgrow what you can comfortably hold at your chest: once your arms and upper back tire before your legs, it stops being a hard leg exercise.

The back squat removes that ceiling: only your leg and back strength limit the weight, and you can keep adding it for years. The cost is technique: the bar on your traps, the torso angle, the depth. Don't squat heavy without the safety arms set in the rack.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-goblet-squat.both: Yes: the goblet squat as a warm-up before the barbell, or as your main squat for the first weeks while the technique comes together. Once you get 15 reps with the heaviest kettlebell, it's time for the barbell.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-goblet-squat.when: You want a heavy squat and long-term progression by weight.
You're new, you're learning depth and torso position, or you train at home.
seo.pair.back-squat-vs-smith-machine-squ: A free bar or a Smith: your own balance or the rails.
Back squat vs Smith machine squat: bar path, stabilisation, foot placement, safety, carryover and which to pick.
In both the bar sits on your traps, but in a Smith it runs up and down on rails and hooks on at any point.

In a free squat you keep the bar over mid-foot yourself: your torso, abs and legs are constantly catching balance. That makes it one of the best whole-body strength lifts, and one of the most technique-heavy.

In a Smith the rails keep the balance. You can put your feet slightly in front of your body — then your back stays more upright and the quads take more of the work. The hooks act as a safety, so you can push to failure alone. But the numbers don't transfer: some Smith bars are counterweighted, and without stabilisation the load feels different. Log it as a separate exercise.

Yes: the free squat as your main lift, the Smith as a second exercise for 8–12 or on days with no spotter. For a beginner the Smith is a fine way to load the legs, but the barbell squat is still worth learning.
You want strength that works everywhere and you're ready to learn the technique.
You want to load your quads without the balance work, or you train without a spotter.
seo.pair.romanian-deadlift-vs-good-morni: Bar in your hands or on your back: one hinge, a different lever.
Romanian deadlift vs good morning: where the bar sits, hamstring and back load, weight, technique and which to pick.
Both are near-straight-leg hinges for the hamstrings and glutes. In the RDL the bar is in your hands sliding down your legs; in the good morning it sits on your traps.

In the RDL the bar hangs in your hands close to your legs, so the lever is short and you can go heavy. The hamstrings stretch, the glutes drive the hips through, and your back holds the hinge. The technique is easier to learn, and the grip is often the limit — use straps.

In the good morning the bar is on your back, far from your hips, so the lever is long: the same hinge with much less weight loads your spinal erectors harder. It's for people who already hold a flat back in a hinge with confidence. Start with an empty bar and bend only as far as your back stays flat.
Yes, but not both heavy on one day: they load the same chain. The RDL is the main hamstring accessory; the good morning goes light for 8–12 on another day or after squats.
You want to load your hamstrings and glutes heavily with simple technique.
You already hinge with confidence and want more spinal-erector work.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-back-squat.card: Deadlift or squat: hinge or squat, posterior chain or quads.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-back-squat.descript: Deadlift vs back squat: what each one trains, how much recovery each needs, how to combine them and what to put in your program.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-back-squat.lead: The two big lifts for legs and back, but different movements: in the deadlift you hinge and pull the bar off the floor; in the squat you sit down under the weight.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-back-squat.diff_htm:
The deadlift is a hinge: the knees bend a little, and the glutes, hamstrings and spinal erectors do the main work. The traps and grip hold the bar, and it's usually your heaviest lift. Heavy deadlifts take the longest to recover from, which is why the deadlift usually comes up less often in a week.

The squat is a squat: knees and hips bend together, the quads and glutes work first, and your back and abs hold the torso. The squat builds the front of the thighs better; the deadlift builds the posterior chain. Neither fully replaces the other.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-back-squat.both_htm: Yes, and most strength programs have both. They're usually split across days: squats 2–3 times a week, deadlifts once. If they're in one session, squat first and keep the deadlift moderate.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-back-squat.when_a_h: You want a strong posterior chain, grip and your heaviest weight in one lift.
seo.pair.deadlift-vs-back-squat.when_b_h: You want strong quads and legs overall.
seo.pair.standing-calf-raise-vs-seated-c: Calves standing or seated: a straight knee or a bent one.
Standing vs seated calf raise: how knee position changes the work of the gastrocnemius and soleus, and which to pick.
The ankle movement is the same; the difference is the knee. Standing, the leg is straight; seated, the knee is bent at a right angle — and that changes which calf muscle works harder.

The gastrocnemius attaches above the knee, so it works at full power when the leg is straight — in standing raises. You can go heavy here, and it's the main calf lift.

With the knee bent the gastrocnemius goes slack and barely helps, so the soleus underneath it takes over. That's why seated raises use less weight, and they're for anyone who wants the whole calf to grow. In both, use the full range: drop the heel down into a stretch, hold for a second and don't bounce.
Yes, and that's the best setup for calves: standing for 8–12, seated for 12–20. Calves recover fast, so you can train them 2–3 times a week.
You want to load the gastrocnemius and work with heavy weight.
You want to work the soleus and the whole calf.
seo.pair.hanging-leg-raise-vs-hanging-kn: Straight legs or knees to chest: a long lever or a short one.
Hanging leg raise vs hanging knee raise: lever length, abs and hip-flexor work, difficulty and how to progress.
You hang from a bar in both. With straight legs the lever is long and it's hard; with bent knees it's shorter and easier.

The knee raise is the starting version: knees come up to your chest, the weight of your legs stays close to your hips, and almost anyone can do 8–10 clean reps. The key isn't just lifting your knees — curl your pelvis up at the end, so your abs do the work and not only the hip flexors.

With straight legs the weight of your legs is far from your hips, so the load on your abs and hip flexors jumps, and your grip has to hold on longer. Don't swing: momentum does the work for you. If your legs only come up with a swing, go back to knees until the raise is slow.
Yes: start the set with straight legs, and when they stop coming up, finish with knees. Once you can do 15 clean knee raises, it's time to move to straight legs.
Knee raises are easy and you want to load your abs harder.
You're starting out, or straight legs only come up with a swing.
seo.pair.cable-crossover-vs-pec-deck.car: Cable crossover or pec deck: angle freedom against simplicity.
seo.pair.cable-crossover-vs-pec-deck.des: Cable crossover vs pec deck: angles, stabilisation, load through the range, convenience and which to pick for your chest.
seo.pair.cable-crossover-vs-pec-deck.lea: Both are chest flyes with no triceps involved. On the cable crossover you stand between two pulleys and set the angle yourself; on the pec deck you sit and the machine sets the arc.
seo.pair.cable-crossover-vs-pec-deck.dif:
The crossover lets you pick the angle: pull from high to low for more lower chest, from low to high for more upper chest. You stand without support, so your core and shoulders do some stabilising and the weight is lower. The cables keep tension through the whole range, especially at the end when your hands meet.

On the pec deck your back is pinned to the pad, the handles follow one arc, and there's almost nothing to think about: sit down and squeeze. It's convenient for working to failure and for drop sets. You can barely change the angle — only through seat height. Set the seat so the handles line up with mid-chest.
seo.pair.cable-crossover-vs-pec-deck.bot: Yes, but one fly per session after your presses is usually enough. You can alternate them by week, or do crossovers at different angles and the pec deck as a finisher to failure.
seo.pair.cable-crossover-vs-pec-deck.whe: You want to change the angle and target the upper or lower chest.
You want a simple supported fly and a safe failure.
seo.term.pr.name: PR (personal record)
seo.term.pr.title: PR: what a personal record is in the gym and how to count it — Athlete Diary
seo.term.pr.short: Your best result in an exercise: the heaviest weight, more reps with the same weight, or the highest estimated max.
seo.term.pr.body_html:
PR stands for personal record — a PB in British gyms. One exercise can have several: the heaviest single, more reps with the same weight (100 kg for 6 after 100 kg for 5), and the best estimated max from any set. The last is the handiest: it compares 90 kg for 8 and 100 kg for 5 in one number.

A record doesn't have to be heavy and scary. Beginners set records almost every week, and that's a normal sign that progressive overload is working. When records dry up for a month, that's a signal to look at your log, not a reason to test your max every day.

I spot records myself when you log a set: a new estimated max gets a flame, and the 1RM calculator works out the one-rep max from any set.
seo.term.1rm.name: 1RM (one-rep max)
seo.term.1rm.title: 1RM: what a one-rep max is and how to find it without testing — Athlete Diary
seo.term.1rm.short: The heaviest weight you can lift once in an exercise with proper form.
seo.term.1rm.body_html:
1RM is your one-repetition maximum. It's how powerlifting measures strength, and programs like 5×5 and 5/3/1 base their percentages on it. But testing it for real is expensive: a max attempt is draining and needs a warm-up, spotting and experience.

So it's usually estimated from a set: 100 kg for 5 is about 117 kg by the Epley formula. That's an estimated max, and it's more accurate the fewer reps the set has. The 1RM calculator works it out from any set, and the guide on estimating safely covers how to test a real max without the risk.

The strength standards show where your max sits among competitive lifters at your bodyweight.
seo.term.amrap.name: AMRAP (as many reps as possible)
seo.term.amrap.h1: AMRAP — as many reps as possible
seo.term.amrap.title: AMRAP: what an as-many-reps-as-possible set means — Athlete Diary
seo.term.amrap.short: A set where you do as many reps as you can with good form. Programs write it with a "+": "3+", "5+".
seo.term.amrap.body_html:
AMRAP means as many reps as possible. It's usually the last set: in 5/3/1 the last work set of each week is "5+", "3+" or "1+". The point is to see from the rep count whether your strength is growing, and to get more work in on a good day.

"As many as possible" means with good form, not grinding to the last inch. Stop when the next rep would break your technique — closer to RPE 9 than to true failure.

A "+" set is handy for estimating your max: 90 kg for 8 is an estimated max of about 114 kg. The 5/3/1 calculator lays out a cycle with these sets.
seo.term.training-to-failure.name: Training to failure
seo.term.training-to-failure.title: Training to failure: do you need to take sets all the way? — Athlete Diary
seo.term.training-to-failure.short: Failure is the point where you can't complete another rep with proper form. A set to failure is a set taken to that point.
seo.term.training-to-failure.body_html:
Failure is RIR 0 and RPE 10: you can't get another rep. What matters for muscle growth is proximity to failure: a set where you could have done eight more grows muscle much worse than a hard one. But you don't have to go all the way to the edge.

In Grgic et al.'s 2022 meta-analysis of 15 studies, training to failure and not to failure produced similar gains in strength and muscle. In Refalo et al. (2023), muscle growth was close whether sets went to failure or stopped a few reps short — and failure added more fatigue.

A practical rule: keep most of your work 1–3 reps from failure and take only the last isolation set to failure, where it's safe. In a heavy squat or deadlift, failure is risk with no payoff. More on sets that do almost nothing in the junk volume guide.
seo.term.volume.name: Training volume
seo.term.volume.title: Training volume: sets per muscle per week and tonnage — Athlete Diary
seo.term.volume.short: How much work you do: usually working sets per muscle per week, sometimes tonnage — the sum of weight × reps.
seo.term.volume.body_html:
Volume is measured two ways. For muscle growth the handiest is working sets — hard ones, close to failure — per muscle per week. For a general picture of a workout there's tonnage: the sum of weight × reps, but it depends heavily on exercise choice — squats give tonnes, lateral raises almost nothing.

Muscle growth follows volume dose-response: more sets, more growth, but each extra set gives less than the last. Targets run from 6–10 sets per muscle per week for beginners to 15–20 for advanced lifters; details in the sets-per-week guide.

You can split your plan by muscle with the volume calculator, and if you log your workouts, I count the weekly sets per group myself.
seo.term.frequency.name: Training frequency
seo.term.frequency.title: Training frequency: how many times a week to train a muscle — Athlete Diary
seo.term.frequency.short: How many times a week a muscle or lift gets trained. Not the same as the number of workouts: a split can have many, while a muscle works once.
seo.term.frequency.body_html:
Frequency is about the muscle, not the gym. A three-day full body program trains the chest three times a week; a five-day bro split trains it once, even though you're in the gym more often.

For muscle growth, frequency barely matters at equal volume: twice and three times a week grow a muscle the same if the set count matches. For strength it matters more: a movement you practise more often gets better. Details with research links are in the frequency guide.

What frequency looks like in real programs is in the full body vs split comparison, where I counted how many times a week each muscle works.
seo.term.training-max.name: Training max
seo.term.training-max.title: Training max: what it is and why it's 90% of your 1RM — Athlete Diary
seo.term.training-max.short: The working number a program bases its percentages on — usually 90% of your one-rep max. Lower than the real thing, so you keep something in reserve.
seo.term.training-max.body_html:
The training max (TM) exists so a program's percentages don't depend on your best day. If you base the weights on your true 1RM, the heavy weeks become a grind and on a bad day they don't happen at all. At 90% the weights are lower, the technique stays clean and progress lasts longer.
