The best-known program with a TM is 5/3/1: every weight in the cycle comes from it, and after a cycle it goes up by 2.5 kg on presses and 5 kg on squats and deadlifts. The 5/3/1 calculator lays out the four weeks, and the 1RM calculator estimates the max itself from a set.

If the TM is set too high, the "+" sets show it: the reps keep shrinking. Don't force it — drop the TM and run the cycle again.
seo.term.linear-progression.name: Linear progression
seo.term.linear-progression.title: Linear progression: adding weight every workout — Athlete Diary
seo.term.linear-progression.short: Adding the same small amount of weight every workout or every week, for as long as it works. It works best for beginners.
seo.term.linear-progression.body_html:
Linear progression is the simplest scheme: hit all your sets and reps, and next time add 2.5 kg on presses and 5 kg on squats and deadlifts. That's how the 5×5 program works: three workouts a week and weight that goes up every time.

It works while you're a beginner and your muscles and nervous system adapt quickly. Sooner or later the reps stop coming — first on the bench, then on the squat. That's not failure, it's the end of a phase: next comes double progression or weekly cycles where the weight rises less often.

How long beginner gains last and what they depend on is in the beginner gains guide.
seo.term.compound-exercise.name: Compound exercise
seo.term.compound-exercise.title: Compound exercise: what it is and how it differs from isolation — Athlete Diary
seo.term.compound-exercise.short: A multi-joint exercise where several joints and big muscles work at once: squat, press, row, pull-up.
seo.term.compound-exercise.body_html:
In a compound exercise two or more joints move: hips, knees and ankles in a squat, shoulders and elbows in a bench press. That's why the loads are big and one set works lots of muscle. In an isolation exercise one joint moves: a curl, a leg extension, a lateral raise.

On the site and in the diary I count as compound the exercises with a movement pattern: squat, hinge (the deadlift family), and presses and rows — horizontal and vertical. Those six movements are what any program is built on.

Compounds are the base of strength and save time, but isolation grows muscle too and covers what compounds don't load much: side delts, hamstrings in knee flexion. More in the compound vs isolation guide.
seo.ex.dumbbell_shrug.lead: Dumbbell shrugs train the upper traps directly: shoulders up toward your ears and back down, arms hanging like hooks.
seo.ex.dumbbell_shrug.setup: Stand tall with the dumbbells at your sides, palms facing in. Feet hip-width, abs braced, eyes forward. Keep your arms straight — they only hold the weight, your shoulders do the work.
seo.ex.dumbbell_shrug.mistakes:
Rolling your shoulders in circles — go straight up and down; the circle adds nothing but stress on the shoulder joint.
Bending your arms and curling the dumbbells up — keep your elbows straight the whole time.
Short range with heavy weight — bring your shoulders to your ears and pause for a second at the top.
Poking your head forward — keep your neck neutral, don't jut your chin.
seo.exf.dumbbell-shrug.muscles: upper traps; forearms hold the grip
seo.ex.barbell_shrug.lead: Barbell shrugs are the heaviest shrug: the bar in front of your thighs, shoulders up to your ears, arms straight.
seo.ex.barbell_shrug.setup: Take the bar from the rack at mid-thigh height with a grip just wider than your hips. Stand tall, shoulder blades slightly set, abs braced. If your grip gives out before your traps do, use straps.
seo.ex.barbell_shrug.mistakes:
Using your legs and torso — that's a jerk; your shoulders lift on their own, no knee bounce.
So heavy your shoulders barely move — drop the weight and use the full range.
Dropping the bar onto loose arms — lower under control and pause at the top.
Leaning back — stay upright, let the bar slide along your thighs.
seo.exf.barbell-shrug.muscles: upper traps; forearms hold the grip
seo.ex.knee_hip_raise_on_parallel_bars.l: The hanging knee raise is the step before straight-leg raises: knees to chest, pelvis curls up, no swinging.
seo.ex.knee_hip_raise_on_parallel_bars.s: Hang from a bar with a shoulder-width grip or set up on a captain's chair. Pull your shoulders down away from your ears, legs together, torso still. Start the movement with your abs, not a leg kick.
seo.ex.knee_hip_raise_on_parallel_bars.m:
Swinging and using momentum — come to a dead stop at the bottom and start each rep from still.
Knees rise but the pelvis doesn't — curl your pelvis toward your chest at the top, or it's all hip flexors.
Dropping your legs — lower them slower than you raise them.
Hanging on loose shoulders — keep your shoulder blades pulled down; it's easier and safer.
seo.ex.seated_palm_up_barbell_wrist_curl: The barbell wrist curl isolates the forearm flexors: forearms rest on your thighs and only the wrist moves.

Sit on the end of a bench, forearms on your thighs palms up, wrists hanging past your knees. Grip at shoulder width. Lower the bar and let it roll toward your fingers, then grip and curl your wrists up.

Lifting your forearms off your thighs and helping with your biceps — forearms stay down, only the wrist moves.
Too heavy and too short — the wrist has a small range, use all of it.
Jerking the bar — keep the tempo even with a one-second squeeze at the top.
Going so heavy your wrists ache — this one grows with reps, keep the weight light.
seo.ex.seated_palms_down_barbell_wrist_c: The reverse wrist curl is the wrist curl done palms down: it works the back of the forearm.
Sit with your forearms on your thighs palms down, wrists past your knees. Use a narrow grip, about shoulder width. Go noticeably lighter than in the wrist curl: the extensors are weaker.

Loading it like a wrist curl — the extensors are weaker, start with an empty or EZ bar.
Helping with your shoulder and lifting your elbows — forearms stay down, the wrist does the work.
Dropping the bar — lower slowly; the extensors work on the way down too.
White-knuckling the bar — hold it firmly, without extra tension in your fingers.
seo.ex.standing_low_pulley_deltoid_raise: The cable lateral raise is a one-arm side raise from a low pulley: the cable keeps tension even at the bottom, where a dumbbell goes slack.
Stand side-on to a low pulley and take the handle in the far hand, cable running across your body. Hold the frame with your free hand. Slight bend in the elbow, shoulder down.

Raising above shoulder height and shrugging — shoulder height is enough; higher, the traps take over.
Swinging your torso — stand still and hold the frame.
Leading with the hand above the elbow — the elbow leads, the hand stays slightly lower.
Rushing down — with a cable the lowering is work too, don't let it snap back.
seo.exf.cable-lateral-raise.muscles: side delts; traps assist at the top
seo.ex.standing_biceps_cable_curl.lead: The cable curl is a biceps curl with a straight bar on a low pulley: constant tension through the whole range.
seo.ex.standing_biceps_cable_curl.setup: Face a low pulley and take a straight bar with an underhand, shoulder-width grip. Step back half a pace so the cable runs at a slight angle. Elbows pinned to your sides, torso upright.
seo.ex.standing_biceps_cable_curl.mistak:
Elbows drift forward and up — they stay put, only your forearms move.
Rocking your back — if it won't go without a swing, the weight is too much.
Not straightening your arms at the bottom — full range grows the biceps better than half.
Curling your wrists at the top — keep the hand in line with the forearm.
seo.ex.dips_triceps_version.lead: Triceps dips keep the torso upright and elbows back, which shifts the load from the chest to the triceps.
seo.ex.dips_triceps_version.setup: Get into a support on the bars, arms straight, shoulders down. Keep your torso upright, legs under you or slightly forward. Lower yourself with your elbows travelling back along your sides.
seo.ex.dips_triceps_version.mistakes:
Leaning forward and flaring your elbows — that's the chest version; stay upright, elbows back.
Going so deep your shoulders roll forward — upper arm parallel to the floor is enough.
Shoulders creep up to your ears — keep them down the whole set.
Bouncing at the bottom — lower under control, no rebound.
seo.exf.triceps-dips.muscles: triceps; chest and front delts assist
seo.ex.standing_dumbbell_triceps_extensi: The overhead dumbbell extension trains the triceps in a stretched position: one dumbbell in both hands, elbows pointing up.
Sit on a bench with back support or stand. Cup the top plate of a dumbbell with both palms and press it overhead. Point your elbows forward and up, brace your abs, don't arch your lower back.

Elbows flare out — keep them close and pointing forward.
Arching your lower back to press the weight — brace your abs or sit against a backrest.
Only lowering halfway — the stretch at the bottom is the point of the exercise.
Moving your upper arms — the upper arm stays put, only the elbow bends.
seo.ex.reverse_crunch.lead: The reverse crunch flips the crunch: your shoulders stay down and your pelvis lifts off the floor and curls toward your chest.
seo.ex.reverse_crunch.setup: Lie on your back, arms by your sides or holding a bench behind your head. Bend your legs, knees over your hips, shins parallel to the floor. Keep your lower back on the floor.
seo.ex.reverse_crunch.mistakes:
Flinging your legs up — the pelvis lifts with your abs, slowly.
Only moving your legs while the pelvis stays down — the point is to lift your tailbone off the floor.
Lowering your legs so far your lower back lifts — stay in the range where it's pressed down.
Pushing with your hands — they're only there for balance.
seo.exf.reverse-crunch.muscles: abs (more of the lower part), hip flexors
seo.ex.reverse_machine_flyes.lead: The reverse pec deck is the pec deck backwards: you sit facing the pad and sweep your arms back to work the rear delts.
seo.ex.reverse_machine_flyes.setup: Sit facing the pad with your chest against it and the handles at shoulder height. Take them with a neutral or overhand grip, arms nearly straight. Set the seat so your arms travel parallel to the floor.
seo.ex.reverse_machine_flyes.mistakes:
Squeezing your shoulder blades as hard as you can — that turns it into a row; sweep with your arms, blades mostly still.
Lifting your chest off the pad — keep it there the whole set.
Bending your elbows more and more — the elbow angle stays fixed.
Jerking out and letting it slam back — even tempo both ways.
seo.ex.lying_dumbbell_tricep_extension.l: The dumbbell skull crusher is a lying triceps extension with a dumbbell in each hand — easier on the elbows than a straight bar.
seo.ex.lying_dumbbell_tricep_extension.s: Lie on a bench with the dumbbells over your chest, palms facing each other. Tilt your arms slightly back toward your head. Lower the dumbbells beside your ears by bending only at the elbows.
seo.ex.lying_dumbbell_tricep_extension.m:
Flaring your elbows — keep them pointing at the ceiling, shoulder-width apart.
Moving your upper arms and turning it into a press — the upper arm stays still, only the elbow bends.
Dropping the dumbbells toward your head — lower slowly, past your ears.
Going heavier than you can control at the bottom — this exercise doesn't forgive jerks.
seo.ex.air_bike.lead: The bicycle crunch is a crunch with a twist: elbow toward the opposite knee while your legs pedal.
seo.ex.air_bike.setup: Lie on your back with your hands behind your head and your shoulder blades slightly off the floor. Lift your legs with your knees bent. Keep your lower back pressed down the whole set.
seo.ex.air_bike.mistakes:
Pulling your head with your hands — they only support it; your torso does the turning.
Fast, short reps — a slow twist with a pause beats speed.
Moving the elbow while the shoulder stays down — lift and turn the shoulder toward the knee.
Legs so low your lower back lifts — raise them higher.
seo.ex.close_grip_front_lat_pulldown.lea: The close-grip lat pulldown is the same pull to the chest with your hands closer: a longer elbow path and more biceps work.
seo.ex.close_grip_front_lat_pulldown.set: Sit with your knees under the pads. Take the bar overhand slightly narrower than your shoulders, or use a narrow handle. Lean back just a little, chest up.
seo.ex.close_grip_front_lat_pulldown.mis:
Pulling with your arms while your shoulder blades stay put — start by drawing them down.
Leaning back so far it becomes a row — keep the lean small and steady.
Flaring your elbows — with a narrow grip they travel down and slightly forward.
Letting the bar fly up — let the lats stretch at the top under control.
seo.ex.cable_hammer_curls_rope_attachmen: The cable rope hammer curl is a hammer curl on a pulley: palms face each other and the tension never drops.
Face a low pulley with a rope attachment. Take the rope ends with a neutral grip, elbows tucked to your sides. Step back half a pace.

Elbows drift forward — the upper arms stay still, only the elbow bends.
Spreading the rope at the top and turning your wrists — keep your palms facing each other.
Short range — straight arms at the bottom, hands near your shoulders at the top.
Rocking your torso — stand still and lighten the stack.
seo.ex.russian_twist.lead: The Russian twist is a seated torso rotation while leaning back: it works the obliques, with a plate or ball for load.
seo.ex.russian_twist.setup: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and heels down or slightly raised. Lean back about 45 degrees with a straight back. Hold the weight in front of your chest with both hands.
seo.ex.russian_twist.mistakes:
Only moving your arms — turn your shoulders and chest, your arms ride along.
Rounding your back — keep it straight and lean back from the hips.
Twisting for speed — stop at each side.
Lifting your feet before you can hold the position — start with heels down.
seo.ex.machine_bicep_curl.lead: The machine biceps curl braces your upper arms against a pad: there's nothing to cheat with, the biceps does all the lifting.
seo.ex.machine_bicep_curl.setup: Set the seat so your elbows rest on the pad in line with the machine's pivot. Take the handles underhand, back straight, chest against the pad.
seo.ex.machine_bicep_curl.mistakes:
The machine's pivot doesn't line up with your elbow — adjust the seat, or it pulls on the joint.
Lifting your elbows off the pad — they stay down the whole set.
Not straightening your arms at the bottom — lower almost all the way.
Dropping the weight — lower slower than you lift.
seo.ex.smith_machine_bench_press.lead: The Smith machine bench press is a bench on rails: the bar can't drift, you barely need a spotter, but your stabilisers do less.
seo.ex.smith_machine_bench_press.setup: Position the bench so the bar comes down to your lower chest, not your neck. Pull your shoulder blades back and down, feet planted. Grip just wider than your shoulders, unhook the bar with a twist of the wrists and set the safeties just below chest height.
seo.ex.smith_machine_bench_press.mistake:
The bench is in the wrong spot and the bar tracks to your neck or belly — check with an empty bar where it lands.
Elbows flared to 90 degrees — keep them at 45–70 degrees to your torso.
Bouncing the bar off your chest — touch and pause, no rebound.
Forgetting the safeties — set them before your first work set.
seo.ex.leverage_high_row.lead: The Hammer Strength row is a chest-supported row with independent arms: your back works without loading your lower back.
seo.ex.leverage_high_row.setup: Set the seat so the handles are at or just below shoulder height and your chest rests on the pad. Grab them, sit tall and drop your shoulders. Each arm pulls its own lever.
seo.ex.leverage_high_row.mistakes:
Lifting your chest off the pad and leaning back — chest stays down, your back does the pulling.
Pulling with your arms while your blades stay put — squeeze your shoulder blades first, then bend your elbows.
Shoulders creep up on the last reps — drop the weight.
Short range — let your shoulder blades spread at the front.
seo.exf.machine-row.muscles: lats, mid back, rear delts, biceps
seo.ex.reverse_barbell_curl.lead: The reverse curl is a barbell curl with your palms down: the biceps is at a disadvantage, so the forearms and brachialis take over.
seo.ex.reverse_barbell_curl.setup: Take a barbell or EZ bar overhand at shoulder width. Stand tall, elbows at your sides. Use noticeably less than in a regular curl.
seo.ex.reverse_barbell_curl.mistakes:
Loading it like a normal curl — the reverse grip is weaker and your wrists collapse.
Wrists bending down — keep your hands in line with your forearms.
Elbows drifting forward — keep them at your sides.
Swinging the bar up — slow on the way up and down.
seo.ex.flat_bench_lying_leg_raise.lead: The lying leg raise brings your legs from the floor or bench up to vertical: easier than hanging, and it teaches you to keep your lower back down.
seo.ex.flat_bench_lying_leg_raise.setup: Lie on a bench or the floor and hold the edge of the bench behind your head. Legs straight or slightly bent. Keep your lower back down — slide your hands under your hips if it lifts.
seo.ex.flat_bench_lying_leg_raise.mistak:
Your lower back lifts when your legs are low — don't lower them further than you can keep it down.
Dropping your legs — lower them slowly.
Kicking your legs up — no swing, start from still.
Legs stop at the top but the pelvis doesn't move — finish by curling your pelvis slightly.
seo.ex.leverage_chest_press.lead: The Hammer Strength chest press is a lever press with independent arms: the path is set and each arm pushes on its own.
seo.ex.leverage_chest_press.setup: Set the seat so the handles line up with your mid chest. Pull your shoulder blades together against the backrest, feet planted. Grip slightly wider than your shoulders, elbows angled to your torso.
seo.ex.leverage_chest_press.mistakes:
Seat too low or too high — handles at mid-chest level, or your shoulders take over.
Shoulders rolling forward at the end — keep your shoulder blades against the pad.
Snapping your elbows straight — press to nearly straight without a lockout jolt.
One arm lagging — the levers are separate, make sure both go all the way.
seo.ex.smith_machine_squat.lead: The Smith machine squat runs on rails: the bar moves straight up and down, and you can put your feet forward to load the quads more.
seo.ex.smith_machine_squat.setup: Step under the bar, rest it on your upper traps, feet slightly in front of you and shoulder-width. Unhook it with a twist of the wrists and set the safeties at your bottom position. Brace before you move.
seo.ex.smith_machine_squat.mistakes:
Feet directly under the bar — in a Smith you set them a little forward, or your knees and lower back sit at an awkward angle.
Knees caving in — push them out along your toes.
Cutting depth — squat as deep as you would freely, if your mobility allows.
Heels lifting — keep your weight on the whole foot.
seo.ex.standing_dumbbell_press.lead: The standing dumbbell press is an overhead press with no support: each arm carries its own weight and your core has to keep you balanced.
seo.ex.standing_dumbbell_press.setup: Stand with your feet hip-width and the dumbbells at your shoulders, palms forward or facing each other. Squeeze your glutes and abs, ribs down. Press up and slightly in until your arms are straight overhead.
seo.ex.standing_dumbbell_press.mistakes:
Arching your lower back to finish — ribs down, abs and glutes tight.
Dipping with your legs — that's a push press; knees stay still.
Only lowering to your ears — bring them down to shoulder level.
Dumbbells drifting wide at the top — keep them over your shoulders.
seo.exf.standing-dumbbell-press.muscles: front and side delts, triceps; abs hold the torso
seo.ex.ab_crunch_machine.lead: The ab crunch machine is a crunch against the weight stack: the abs grow like any other muscle, and the machine lets you add load.
seo.ex.ab_crunch_machine.setup: Set the seat so the machine's pivot is level with your midsection. Hold the handles or brace against the pads, feet under the rollers. Start by curling your ribcage toward your pelvis.
seo.ex.ab_crunch_machine.mistakes:
Pulling with your arms and shoulders — your hands only hold on, your torso curls.
Hinging at the hips — the point is rounding your spine, not bending forward.
So heavy you have to yank it — drop the weight and go slow.
Not uncurling at the top — let the abs stretch between reps.
seo.ex.decline_crunch.lead: The decline crunch is a regular crunch done head-down: the angle adds load without any weight.
seo.ex.decline_crunch.setup: Lie on a decline bench with your feet hooked under the rollers. Cross your arms on your chest or hold your hands by your temples. Your lower back is on the bench at the start of each rep.
seo.ex.decline_crunch.mistakes:
Sitting all the way up — that's a sit-up; only lift your shoulder blades and chest.
Pulling your head with your hands — cross your arms if you feel like pulling.
Starting with a steep angle — begin with a mild one.
Flopping back down — lower slowly.
seo.ex.decline_dumbbell_bench_press.lead: The decline dumbbell press is a bench press on a decline: more lower chest and a shorter path for the dumbbells.
seo.ex.decline_dumbbell_bench_press.setu: Hook your feet under the rollers of a decline bench with the dumbbells on your thighs. Lie back while bringing them to your chest, shoulder blades pinched. Press over your lower chest.
seo.ex.decline_dumbbell_bench_press.mist:
Lying back clumsily and jerking your shoulders — go down slowly with the dumbbells pinned to your chest.
Elbows flared wide — keep them angled to your torso.
Short range — lower until your chest stretches.
Too steep an angle — a mild decline works just as well and is easier on your head.
seo.exf.decline-dumbbell-press.muscles: chest (more of the lower part), triceps
seo.ex.underhand_cable_pulldowns.lead: The underhand lat pulldown is a pulldown with your palms facing you: the elbows travel along your sides and the biceps helps more.
seo.ex.underhand_cable_pulldowns.setup: Sit with your knees under the pads. Take the bar underhand at shoulder width. Chest up, slight lean back.
seo.ex.underhand_cable_pulldowns.mistake:
Grip too wide — underhand works best at shoulder width; wider strains the wrists.
Pulling to your neck — bring the bar to your upper chest.
Rocking your whole torso — small lean, your back and arms do the pulling.
Not straightening your arms at the top — use the full range.
seo.ex.seated_barbell_military_press.lea: The seated barbell press is a military press with back support: the torso is easier to hold, so the shoulders and triceps get all the work.
seo.ex.seated_barbell_military_press.set: Set an upright bench in a rack with the bar at chin height. Sit with your back against the pad and your feet planted. Grip just wider than your shoulders with vertical forearms.
seo.ex.seated_barbell_military_press.mis:
Arching until it becomes an incline press — lower back on the pad, ribs down.
Pressing the bar forward — it travels straight up; move your head back, then under the bar.
Lowering halfway — bring the bar to your chin or upper chest.
Elbows drifting back — keep them under the bar and slightly forward.
seo.ex.push_ups_close_triceps_position.l: Close-grip push-ups put your hands under your shoulders and your elbows along your sides: more triceps work than regular push-ups.
seo.ex.push_ups_close_triceps_position.s: Get into a plank with your hands under your shoulders or a bit narrower. Body straight from heels to head, glutes and abs tight. Lower yourself with your elbows brushing your sides.
seo.ex.push_ups_close_triceps_position.m:
Putting your hands together in a diamond — it's hard on the wrists; shoulder width is enough.
Elbows flaring — keep them close.
Hips sagging — glutes and abs tight the whole set.
Not going all the way down — chest nearly touches the floor.
seo.ex.pallof_press.lead: The Pallof press is an anti-rotation exercise: the cable pulls you sideways while you press the handle out and refuse to turn.
seo.ex.pallof_press.setup: Stand side-on to a cable with the handle at chest height, both hands on it. Step out until the cable is taut, feet shoulder-width, knees soft. Press the handle out and hold.
seo.ex.pallof_press.mistakes:
Your torso turns toward the stack — that's exactly what you're there to stop.
Standing too close — the cable should pull noticeably.
Holding your breath the whole set — breathe steadily and still hold the position.
Rushing — pause with your arms out for two or three seconds.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_flyes.lead: The incline dumbbell fly isolates the upper chest: your arms open in an arc with a slight bend in the elbows.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_flyes.setup: Set the bench to 30–45 degrees, lie back and hold the dumbbells over your chest, palms facing. Bend your elbows slightly and lock that angle. Open your arms until your chest stretches.
seo.ex.incline_dumbbell_flyes.mistakes:
Bending your elbows more and pressing — keep the elbow angle fixed or it becomes a press.
Lowering past what your shoulders allow — stop at a clear stretch.
Going heavy — the stretch does the work here, keep it moderate.
Clanging the dumbbells together at the top — stop just short.
seo.exf.incline-dumbbell-fly.muscles: chest (more of the upper part), front delts
seo.ex.reverse_grip_bent_over_rows.lead: The reverse-grip barbell row is a bent-over row with your palms facing forward: elbows travel closer to your body, with more lower lats and biceps.
seo.ex.reverse_grip_bent_over_rows.setup: Grip the bar underhand at shoulder width. Hinge to 30–45 degrees from the floor, back straight, knees soft. Row the bar to your lower belly.
seo.ex.reverse_grip_bent_over_rows.mista:
Your torso rises with every rep — hold the angle.
Rowing to your chest — with an underhand grip the bar goes to your belly.
Rounding your back — keep it flat or lighten the bar.
Wrists and biceps tire before your back — don't overload it.
seo.ex.seated_calf_raise.lead: The seated calf raise lifts your heels with your knees bent: the gastrocnemius switches off and the soleus underneath does the work.
seo.ex.seated_calf_raise.setup: Sit in the machine with the pads on your lower thighs and the balls of your feet on the platform edge. Drop your heels as low as you can, then rise all the way up. Pause at the bottom and the top.
seo.ex.seated_calf_raise.mistakes:
Bouncing at the bottom — hold the stretch for a second.
Short range — heels all the way down and all the way up.
Pushing the pad with your hands — hands rest, calves work.
Only low reps with heavy weight — calves like 15–20 reps too.
seo.ex.close_grip_dumbbell_press.lead: The close-grip dumbbell press is a bench press with the dumbbells pressed together: elbows tucked, the work goes to the triceps.
seo.ex.close_grip_dumbbell_press.setup: Lie on a bench with the dumbbells over your chest, palms facing and the dumbbells touching. Shoulder blades pinched. Lower them to your chest with your elbows at your sides.
seo.ex.close_grip_dumbbell_press.mistake:
The dumbbells drift apart — keep them together the whole way.
Elbows flaring — they track along your sides.
Lowering to your neck — touch your mid chest.
Jerking to lockout — keep an even tempo.
seo.ex.standing_cable_wood_chop.lead: The cable wood chop is a diagonal torso rotation with a cable: high to low across your body, working the obliques and the whole core.
seo.ex.standing_cable_wood_chop.setup: Set the pulley high, stand side-on and take the handle with both hands above your far shoulder. Feet wider than your shoulders, knees soft. Pull diagonally toward your opposite hip, turning your torso.
seo.ex.standing_cable_wood_chop.mistakes:
Pulling with your arms — they stay nearly straight while your torso turns.
Rounding your back — it's a rotation, not a crunch.
Feet glued to the floor while your knee twists — let your back foot pivot.
Letting the cable snap back — return slowly.
seo.ex.dumbbell_incline_row.lead: The chest-supported dumbbell row is a row with your chest on an incline bench: your lower back holds nothing and there's no way to swing.
seo.ex.dumbbell_incline_row.setup: Set a bench to 30–45 degrees and lie chest-down, dumbbells hanging under your shoulders. Feet braced on the floor. Row them to your lower ribs, squeezing your shoulder blades.
seo.ex.dumbbell_incline_row.mistakes:
Lifting your chest off the bench — keep it down or it's just a bent-over row.
Rowing to your shoulders — pull to your lower ribs.
Flaring your elbows wide — for the back keep them at roughly 45 degrees.
Not letting your shoulder blades spread at the bottom — use the full range.
seo.exf.chest-supported-dumbbell-row.mus: mid back, lats, rear delts, biceps
seo.ex.straight_arm_dumbbell_pullover.le: The dumbbell pullover takes a dumbbell back over your head in an arc on nearly straight arms, stretching the lats and chest.
seo.ex.straight_arm_dumbbell_pullover.se: Lie along a bench or across it with your shoulder blades on it. Hold a dumbbell by the plate with both hands over your chest, elbows slightly bent. Lower it behind your head until you feel a stretch.
seo.ex.straight_arm_dumbbell_pullover.mi:
Bending your elbows and turning it into a skull crusher — keep the elbow angle fixed.
Lowering further than your shoulders allow — stop at a stretch, never pain.
Arching your lower back — ribs down, don't hike your hips.
Going heavy — a stretched shoulder needs a moderate weight.
seo.ex.thigh_abductor.lead: The hip abduction machine pushes your thighs apart while seated: it works the side of the glutes that squats barely touch.
seo.ex.thigh_abductor.setup: Sit with your back on the pad or leaning slightly forward, pads on the outside of your knees. Hold the handles. Push your knees apart as far as they go and bring them back slowly.
seo.ex.thigh_abductor.mistakes:
Letting the pads slam together — bring them back under control.
Short range with a heavy stack — go lighter and all the way.
Helping with your arms and torso — your hips do the work.
Only 6–8 reps — these muscles like 12–20.
seo.ex.thigh_adductor.lead: The hip adduction machine squeezes your thighs together while seated: it works the inner thigh, the adductors.
seo.ex.thigh_adductor.setup: Sit with your back against the pad and the pads on the inside of your knees. Set the starting width to a stretch you can feel, without pain. Squeeze your knees together and return slowly.
seo.ex.thigh_adductor.mistakes:
Setting too wide a start — the stretch should be comfortable.
Letting the weight fly back — open slowly.
Short jerky reps — use the full range.
Going heavy straight away — start with a light stack and 12–15 reps.
seo.ex.dead_bug.lead: The dead bug is a core-control drill on your back: one arm and the opposite leg reach away while your lower back stays pressed down.
seo.ex.dead_bug.setup: Lie on your back, arms reaching to the ceiling, hips and knees at 90 degrees. Press your lower back into the floor and exhale. Slowly lower your right arm behind your head and your left leg toward the floor, return and switch sides.
seo.ex.dead_bug.mistakes:
Your lower back lifts — only reach as far as you can keep it down.
Rushing — slow reps, or the drill does nothing.
Holding your breath — exhale as you reach.
Moving the same-side arm and leg — opposite pairs: right arm, left leg.
seo.ex.jm_press.lead: The JM press is a hybrid of the close-grip bench and the skull crusher: the bar comes down toward your chin, elbows move forward, and the triceps handle heavy weight.
seo.ex.jm_press.setup: Lie on a bench and grip the bar slightly narrower than your shoulders. Start as a close-grip bench, then let your elbows travel forward as you lower so the bar comes toward your upper chest and chin. Extend your elbows from the bottom.
seo.ex.jm_press.mistakes:
Starting heavy — the movement is unusual, learn it with an empty bar.
The bar drifting toward your face without control — go slow, with a spotter or safeties.
Elbows flaring — they point forward, toward your feet.
Turning it into a plain close-grip bench — the elbows should move forward, not down.
seo.ex.sit_up.lead: The sit-up takes you all the way to seated: more range than a crunch, and more work for the hip flexors.
seo.ex.sit_up.setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet on the floor — hook them under something or have a partner hold them. Cross your arms on your chest. Curl up from your head and shoulder blades, then sit all the way up.
seo.ex.sit_up.mistakes:
Yanking your head with your hands — arms on your chest, don't pull your neck.
Rising with a flat back from the hips — curl first, then sit up.
Flopping back down — lower one vertebra at a time.
Feet lifting — anchor them.
seo.ex.butt_lift_bridge.lead: The glute bridge lifts your hips from the floor with no weight: a first glute exercise and a good warm-up before a heavy leg day.
seo.ex.butt_lift_bridge.setup: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet hip-width near your glutes. Arms by your sides. Drive through your heels and lift your hips until your body is straight from shoulders to knees.
seo.ex.butt_lift_bridge.mistakes:
Arching your lower back at the top — stop when your hips line up with your body; past that it's your back.
Pushing through your toes — keep the weight on your heels.
Knees falling apart — keep them in line with your feet.
Not squeezing at the top — pause for a second.
seo.ex.glute_kickback.lead: The cable glute kickback swings one leg back from a low pulley: the glute extends your hip against the cable.
seo.ex.glute_kickback.setup: Strap a cuff around your ankle and face a low pulley. Hold the frame and lean forward slightly. Take your straight or slightly bent leg back until your thigh is just behind your body.
seo.ex.glute_kickback.mistakes:
Kicking high and arching your lower back — the range ends where the arch begins.
Swinging your torso — keep it still.
Fast swings — pause at the top.
Locking your standing leg — keep a soft bend in the standing knee.
seo.ex.bent_over_two_dumbbell_row.lead: The bent-over dumbbell row is a barbell row with dumbbells: each arm gets its own range and you can turn your hands to whatever is comfortable.
seo.ex.bent_over_two_dumbbell_row.setup: Hold the dumbbells and hinge to 30–45 degrees from the floor, back straight, knees soft. Let them hang under your shoulders. Row them to your waist, squeezing your shoulder blades.
seo.ex.bent_over_two_dumbbell_row.mistak:
Your torso rises with each rep — hold the hinge.
Rounding your back — keep it straight, eyes on the floor ahead.
Rowing to your chest — pull to your waist.
Yanking the weight — smooth up, slow down.
seo.exf.bent-over-dumbbell-row.muscles: lats, mid back, rear delts, biceps
seo.ex.zottman_curl.lead: The Zottman curl goes up palms-up and down palms-down: one rep works both the biceps and the forearms.
seo.ex.zottman_curl.setup: Stand with dumbbells, palms forward, elbows at your sides. Curl them up like a regular curl. At the top turn your palms down and lower slowly.
seo.ex.zottman_curl.mistakes:
Turning your hands at the bottom instead of the top — rotate at the top and come down palms-down.
Lowering fast — the slow palms-down lowering is the point.
Using your regular curl weight — you're weaker palms-down, pick the weight for that.
Elbows drifting forward — keep them at your sides.
seo.ex.standing_leg_curl.lead: The standing leg curl bends one leg at a time in a machine: each side works on its own, so a weaker side shows right away.
seo.ex.standing_leg_curl.setup: Step into the machine with the pad above the heel of the working leg and your knee in line with the pivot. Hold the handles, torso leaning slightly forward. Curl your heel toward your glute.
seo.ex.standing_leg_curl.mistakes:
Your knee drifting back or forward — the thigh stays still, only the knee bends.
Arching your lower back to finish the rep — drop the weight.
Letting it drop — lower slowly.
Doing more reps on your strong leg — same reps on both.
seo.ex.reverse_hyperextension.lead: The reverse hyperextension keeps your torso on the pad and lifts your legs: glutes and hamstrings work without compressing the spine.
seo.ex.reverse_hyperextension.setup: Lie face-down on the machine's pad with your hips at the edge and legs hanging. Hold the handles. Raise your straight or slightly bent legs back to body level and lower under control.
seo.ex.reverse_hyperextension.mistakes:
Swinging your legs above your body — stop in line with it; higher is just a lower-back arch.
Swinging like a pendulum — start each rep from still.
Bending your knees more and more — keep the knee angle fixed.
Loading it straight away — learn the movement unloaded first.
seo.ex.one_arm_kettlebell_swings.lead: The one-arm kettlebell swing is an explosive hinge: the bell flies forward from a hip snap, your arm just guides it.
seo.ex.one_arm_kettlebell_swings.setup: Stand with your feet a bit wider than your shoulders and the bell on the floor in front. Hinge with a straight back and take it in one hand. Hike it between your legs and snap your hips forward — the bell rises to chest height.
seo.ex.one_arm_kettlebell_swings.mistake:
Squatting instead of hinging — bend your knees only a little and push your hips back.
Lifting the bell with your arm and shoulder — the arm is loose, the hips do the work.
Leaning back at the top — stand tall with your glutes squeezed.
Your torso twisting after the bell — keep your shoulders square.
seo.exf.kettlebell-swing.muscles: glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors; shoulders guide the bell
seo.ex.bodyweight_squat.lead: The bodyweight squat is the first step toward a barbell squat and a way to warm up before a heavy day.
seo.ex.bodyweight_squat.setup: Stand with your feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out, arms forward for balance. Sit your hips back and down, knees tracking over your toes. Lower until your thighs are parallel or below, then stand up.
seo.ex.bodyweight_squat.mistakes:
Heels lifting — keep your weight mid-foot.
Knees caving in — push them out.
Rounding your back at the bottom — chest up, back flat.
Banging out a hundred fast reps — while it's easy, work on depth and tempo, then add weight.
seo.ex.barbell_walking_lunge.lead: The barbell walking lunge steps forward with a bar on your back: each leg works in turn and your core has to keep you balanced.
seo.ex.barbell_walking_lunge.setup: Put the bar on your upper traps as for a squat and step out to open floor. Step forward, lower until your back knee nearly touches the floor, then drive onto the front leg. Next step with the other leg.
seo.ex.barbell_walking_lunge.mistakes:
Steps too short — your front knee ends up way past your toes; take longer steps.
Torso tipping forward — chest up, back straight.
Front knee caving in — keep it in line with your foot.
Starting with a heavy bar — learn lunges with dumbbells first.
seo.ex.dumbbell_rear_lunge.lead: The dumbbell reverse lunge steps back instead of forward: easier on the front knee and easier to balance.
seo.ex.dumbbell_rear_lunge.setup: Stand with the dumbbells at your sides, feet hip-width. Step back with one leg and lower until your back knee nearly touches the floor. Drive back up through the front leg.
seo.ex.dumbbell_rear_lunge.mistakes:
Pushing off the back leg — the front leg stands you up, the back one only touches down.
Stepping back too short — let your front thigh reach parallel.
Torso folding toward the knee — keep your chest up.
Feet on one line — keep them hip-width apart for balance.
seo.ex.dumbbell_squat.lead: The dumbbell squat holds a dumbbell in each hand at your sides: no rack, no bar, and easier on your back than a barbell squat.
seo.ex.dumbbell_squat.setup: Stand with the dumbbells at your sides, feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out. Abs braced, chest up. Squat by sitting your hips back, dumbbells hanging straight down.
seo.ex.dumbbell_squat.mistakes:
Leaning forward to get the dumbbells lower — chest up, back flat.
Knees caving in — push them out.
Cutting depth — squat as deep as you normally would.
Your grip giving out before your legs — use straps or switch to a goblet squat.
seo.ex.deficit_deadlift.lead: The deficit deadlift is a deadlift standing on a low platform: the bar travels further and the start off the floor gets the hardest.
seo.ex.deficit_deadlift.setup: Stand on a platform or plates 2–5 cm high with the bar over mid-foot. Hinge, grip just outside your legs, back flat. Take the slack out of the bar and stand up like a regular deadlift.
seo.ex.deficit_deadlift.mistakes:
Too high a platform — 2–5 cm is enough; higher and you can't keep your back flat.
Your back rounding at the start — if you can't hold it, the deficit isn't for you yet.
Using your regular deadlift weight — drop it 10–20% for the deficit.
Jerking the bar off the floor — pull the slack out first, then push the floor away.
seo.ex.box_squat.lead: The box squat sits back to a box or bench: the depth is the same every rep and it teaches you to sit your hips back.
seo.ex.box_squat.setup: Set a box so your thighs are parallel when you sit on it. Unrack the bar and stand a little wider than usual in front of the box. Sit your hips back, touch the box, pause without relaxing, then stand.
seo.ex.box_squat.mistakes:
Dropping onto the box — touch down softly, never crash your tailbone into it.
Relaxing while seated — stay braced for the whole pause.
Rocking to stand up — rise without rocking your torso back and forth.
Box too low or too high — set it to parallel.
seo.ex.floor_press.lead: The barbell floor press is a bench press without the bench: your elbows stop on the floor, the range is shorter and the triceps work harder at lockout.
seo.ex.floor_press.setup: Lie on the floor in a power rack with the hooks set so you unrack with nearly straight arms. Grip as for a bench press, legs bent or straight. Lower until your triceps touch the floor, pause, press.
seo.ex.floor_press.mistakes:
Bouncing your elbows off the floor — touch and pause, no impact.
Elbows flared to 90 degrees — keep them at about 45 to your torso.
Unracking without a rack — on the floor it's hard to get the bar and there's nowhere to dump it; use a rack or a spotter.
Lifting your hips — glutes stay on the floor.
seo.ex.band_assisted_pull_up.lead: The band-assisted pull-up is a pull-up where a band helps at the bottom: the same hang and path while you can't do many on your own.
seo.ex.band_assisted_pull_up.setup: Loop a band over the bar and pull it through itself. Put a knee or foot in the loop and grip slightly wider than your shoulders. Drop your shoulders and pull until your chin clears the bar.
seo.ex.band_assisted_pull_up.mistakes:
Dropping into the band and bouncing — the band pulls hardest at the bottom, so lower slowly.
Staying on the same band forever — once you get 10–12 with it, switch to a thinner one.
Kicking your knees and swinging — keep your body nearly vertical.
Stopping short of the bar — use the full range, or your own pull-ups won't come.
seo.ex.stiff_legged_dumbbell_deadlift.le: The stiff-legged dumbbell deadlift is a hinge with nearly straight knees: the backs of your thighs stretch and do the work.
seo.ex.stiff_legged_dumbbell_deadlift.se: Stand with the dumbbells in front of your thighs, feet hip-width, knees slightly bent and staying that way. Push your hips back and hinge with a flat back, dumbbells sliding down your legs. Lower to a hamstring stretch and stand up.
seo.ex.stiff_legged_dumbbell_deadlift.mi:
Rounding your back to get the dumbbells lower — your depth ends where your back stays flat.
Bending your knees and turning it into a deadlift — keep the knee angle fixed.
The dumbbells drifting away — keep them close to your thighs and shins.
Leaning back at the top — just stand tall with your glutes squeezed.
seo.ex.weighted_pull_ups.lead: Weighted pull-ups add a belt with a plate or a dumbbell: the next step once you can do more than 10–12 with bodyweight.
seo.ex.weighted_pull_ups.setup: Put on a dip belt and hang a plate, or hold a dumbbell between your feet. Grip slightly wider than your shoulders, hang, drop your shoulders. Pull until your chin clears the bar and lower to straight arms.
seo.ex.weighted_pull_ups.mistakes:
Adding weight too early — get 10–12 clean bodyweight reps first.
Short range with weight — use a smaller plate and go all the way down and up.
The weight swinging — start each rep from a dead hang.
Jumping 5 kg at a time — step up by 1–2.5 kg if you have small plates.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.title: Compound vs isolation exercises: which to choose for strength and size — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.descript: How compound exercises differ from isolation, what research says about muscle growth, how much of each to put in a program and in what order.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.lead: The compound vs isolation argument never ends, and the answer is boring: you need both, for different jobs. Compounds build strength and save time; isolation reaches what compounds don't.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.card: Squat or leg extension: what you need and in what order.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.cta: Log both compounds and isolation — I'll count the weekly sets for each muscle myself.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.takeaway:
A compound works several joints and lots of muscle; isolation works one joint.
For beginners, compounds grow assisting muscles almost as well as direct work.
Side delts, hamstrings, calves and rear delts need their own isolation.
Compounds at the start of a workout, isolation at the end.
Count sets per muscle, not exercises.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s1_html:
In a compound exercise two or more joints move. A squat is hips, knees and ankles; a bench press is shoulders and elbows; a row is shoulders and elbows, and a deadlift adds the hips. Lots of muscle works at once, which is why the loads are the biggest.

In an isolation exercise one joint moves: a biceps curl, a leg extension, a lateral raise. Less muscle, less weight, but the load goes exactly where you aim it. In the diary and on this site I tell them apart by movement pattern: squat, hinge, presses and rows are compounds; everything else is isolation.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s2.h: What research says about muscle growth
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s2_html:
Direct comparisons are few, but they agree. In Gentil, Soares and Bottaro (2015), 29 untrained men spent ten weeks doing either only lat pulldowns or only biceps curls. Biceps thickness grew about 6% in both groups, with no difference in elbow-flexion strength either: for a beginner's biceps, the pulldown worked as well as direct work.

But those were beginners and a small muscle. The more experienced you are, the less an assisting muscle gets from a compound: in the large analysis by Pelland and colleagues, the data fit best when a set in another muscle's exercise was counted as half a set. That's why advanced lifters need isolation more than beginners do.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s3_html:
Compounds mean strength and time saved. One set of squats loads the quads, glutes and adductors; a bench press loads the chest, front delts and triceps. Three or four compounds cover almost the whole body, and they're where the weight climbs fastest — you can see it in the diary's estimated max.

For beginners compounds matter most: while technique is still settling, adding weight to the squat, bench and row is the progress. The starter programs — full body three days and 5×5 — are almost entirely compounds.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s4_html:
Some muscles compounds barely reach. The side delts do little in presses — they need lateral raises. The hamstrings hardly bend the knee in a squat — they need leg curls. Calves, rear delts and abs also grow better with their own work.

Isolation is also easy to take close to failure safely: missing a rep on a triceps pushdown is no big deal; missing one in a heavy squat is. And it barely tires the whole body, so it goes at the end of a workout when you have nothing left for another compound.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s5_html:
A simple rule for most people: two or three compounds at the start of a workout, then one to three isolation moves. Beginners do more compounds and less isolation; advanced lifters the opposite, with extra isolation for lagging muscles.

Count sets per muscle per week, not exercises: if your chest gets 10 sets from presses and 4 from flyes, that's 14 chest sets. Volume targets are in the sets-per-week guide, and you can check your own plan with the volume calculator.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s6_html:
Compounds go first while you're fresh: a heavy squat after three leg exercises means less weight and more risk. The exception is when a lagging muscle needs priority: then its isolation can come first, knowing the compound will suffer a little.

Rest differs too: 2–3 minutes for heavy compounds, 60–90 seconds for isolation — more in the rest guide. If a compound doesn't feel right, every exercise has substitutes — for example, bench press alternatives.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s7_html:
The upper day from "Upper / Lower" is a good model of the ratio. The barbell bench 4×6–8 and barbell row 4×6–10 — two heavy compounds first. Then the seated dumbbell press and lat pulldown — lighter compounds. Last, barbell curls and cable triceps pushdowns: isolation for the arms, which only assisted in the presses and rows.

Look at that day's volume by muscle: the chest and back get theirs from compounds, the biceps and triceps from their own exercises. Without the isolation, the arms would get zero direct sets by the diary's rule — and it would show in the program's volume table.
seo.guide.compound-vs-isolation.s8_html:
Can I do compounds only? As a beginner, yes, for the first months: the 5×5 program is built that way. In time the side delts, hamstrings and arms will lag — that's when to add isolation.

Can I do machines and isolation only? Your muscles will grow, but you'll be weaker in the big lifts and your workouts longer: one exercise per muscle.

What counts as a compound? The dumbbell press and lat pulldown are compounds too: two joints move. The pec deck and leg extension are isolation, even though they're machines. Each exercise page says what it loads and how — see exercises.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.title: Strength vs hypertrophy training: what's the difference — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.descri: How strength training differs from training for size: weights, reps, rest and exercises — what research says and how to combine both goals.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.lead: Strength and size grow together, but not the same way. Muscle grows from almost any hard set; strength grows from lifting heavy, often, in a specific movement.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.card: Reps, weights and rest: when they're different workouts.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.cta: Log your sets — I'll show whether your estimated max is rising and suggest a target for next time.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.takeaw:
Muscle grows with heavy and light loads alike — if sets go close to failure.
One-rep max strength grows more with heavy loads.
For strength: 1–6 reps, long rest and frequent practice of the lift.
For size: 6–15 reps and 10–20 sets per muscle per week.
Combining them is easy: the first exercise heavy, the rest for volume.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s1_htm:
Strength is how much you can lift once or a few times in a specific movement: squat, bench, deadlift. Size is muscle size — hypertrophy. They're directly linked: a bigger muscle has more strength potential. But strength is also a skill: your nervous system learns to fire muscles together, and technique learns to save every inch.

That's why someone with less muscle can bench more if they've trained the bench heavy for years — and why a bodybuilder with a huge chest can lose to them on a single.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s2_htm:
In the meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Grgic, Ogborn and Krieger (2017), training with heavy and light loads was compared. Muscle grew similarly with both — as long as sets went close to failure. One-rep max strength, though, grew more with heavy loads. That's the core difference: for size, load is a tool; for strength, it's the goal.

One more detail is volume: muscle growth depends more on the number of hard sets per week (Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger, 2017), while strength depends more on how heavy and how often you practise the lift.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s3_htm:
• Reps — 1–6 on the main lifts, at 80–90% of your one-rep max and above.
  • Rest — 2–5 minutes: a heavy set needs recovery.
  • Exercises — the lift you want to be strong in and its close variations.
  • Frequency — the lift two or three times a week: a skill likes repetition.

Failure isn't needed on heavy compounds: a set with 1–2 reps in reserve gives the same practice without the risk. The 1RM calculator will give you the percentages.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s4_htm:
• Reps — a wide range, usually 6–15, sometimes up to 20–30 on isolation.
  • Proximity to failure — 0–3 reps in reserve: that matters more than the exact rep count.
  • Volume — 10–20 hard sets per muscle per week for most people.
  • Rest — 1.5–3 minutes on compounds, 60–90 seconds on isolation: in Schoenfeld et al. (2016), three minutes produced more growth than one.

How many reps to do and why the range is so wide is in the reps for muscle growth guide.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s5_htm:
Most people don't need to choose. A working scheme: the first exercise of a workout is heavy, for 3–6 reps; the rest are for 8–15. That's how PHUL works with its power and hypertrophy days, and how most intermediate programs are built.

If you have one goal, pick for it: for strength, 5×5 or 5/3/1; for size, volume programs like "Upper / Lower" or push/pull/legs. They're all in the ready-made programs.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s6_htm:
For strength, watch the estimated max on your main lift: it should rise month to month. For size, watch the weight and reps on exercises for that muscle and, if you like, a tape measure: more reps with the same weight already means growth.

I track both myself: the estimated max for every exercise, records and weekly sets per muscle. If something stalls for a month, the chart shows it — and that's when to read the plateau guide.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s7_htm:
Take a bench press with an estimated max of 100 kg. For strength, the working sets are around 85 kg for 3–5 reps, three minutes' rest, three or four sets. For size, 70–75 kg for 8–10, two minutes' rest, also three or four sets, followed by another chest exercise.

In the first case you'll lift less total tonnage per workout, but every set is closer to your max — practice at heavy. In the second, more reps and more time under load. Both build strength and muscle, just in different proportions. The 1RM calculator works out the percentages of your own max.
seo.guide.strength-vs-hypertrophy.s8_htm:
Can you build muscle with light weights? Yes, if sets go close to failure: in the 2017 meta-analysis muscle grew similarly with light and heavy loads. But sets of 25–30 reps take longer and feel worse.

Do I need to test my max? No: the estimated max from your working sets tracks progress almost as well. If you really want to test it, the safe 1RM estimate guide shows how.

Why is my strength rising but not my muscle? That's normal for the first months: skill drives strength faster. If it's been six months, check your volume per muscle and your food — both are in the muscle gain program guide.
seo.guide.how-long-should-a-workout-be.t: How long should a workout be? — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.how-long-should-a-workout-be.h: How long should a workout be
seo.guide.how-long-should-a-workout-be.d: How long a good gym workout lasts: where the time goes, how many sets fit into an hour, and how to cut a session short without losing work.
seo.guide.how-long-should-a-workout-be.l: There's no correct workout length — there's a number of hard sets and the rest between them. Count those and the time follows. Usually it's 45–75 minutes.
seo.guide.how-long-should-a-workout-be.c: One hour or two: where the time goes and how to cut it.
Start the rest timer and log your sets — I'll show how long the workout took and how much you did.
seo.guide.how-long-should-a-workout-be.t:
The number of hard sets and the rest between them set your workout length.
15–25 sets with rest is roughly 45–75 minutes.
Rest 2–3 minutes on compounds and 60–90 seconds on isolation.
Antagonist supersets save time without losing work.
If the weights drop by the end and your log stands still, shorten or split the workout.
seo.guide.how-long-should-a-workout-be.s:
A workout has three parts: the warm-up, the working sets and the rest between them. A set lasts 30–60 seconds; rest runs from one to three minutes. So one working set with its rest is 1.5–4 minutes, and you spend most of your gym time resting.

That gives a simple sum: 15 working sets at 2.5 minutes each is about 40 minutes, plus 10 minutes of warm-up — 50. 25 sets is already more than an hour. So "how long should I train" is really "how many sets should I do".
How many sets you need per workout

For muscle growth what matters is weekly volume — hard sets per muscle per week. If you need 10–15 sets for each major group and train three times, that's 15–25 sets per workout. That's 45–75 minutes.

More sets give more growth, but with diminishing returns (Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger, 2017). And the last sets of a long workout are usually worse: fatigue builds and the weights drop. If a workout drifts toward two hours, it's usually better to split it in two than to finish it exhausted. See how many sets per session different splits give.

Short rest shortens the workout, but it also eats reps. In Schoenfeld et al. (2016), three minutes of rest gave trained men more growth and strength than one minute. In a newer review by Singer et al. (2024), going past 90 seconds added little for growth — but didn't hurt either.

In practice: 2–3 minutes on heavy compounds, 60–90 seconds on isolation. Rest without a timer is almost always longer than it feels, especially with a phone in your hand. Set the rest timer — it's the easiest way to finish in an hour without losing quality.
How to cut a workout without losing work

• Antagonist supersets — press and row, biceps and triceps in turn: while one muscle works, the other rests. More on what a superset is.
  • Fewer warm-up sets on the second and third exercises: you're already warm.
  • Machines at the end — moving a pin is faster than loading plates.
  • Fewer exercises, same volume — four sets of one exercise instead of two sets each of two.
When a long workout is fine

Strength programs with heavy sets of 1–5 reps take longer: 3–5 minutes of rest plus a long warm-up up to the working weight. Ninety minutes for a heavy squat and bench is normal. Same for leg day: squats, deadlifts and leg presses just take time.

The warning sign isn't length but that by the end you can't work with a normal weight, and the last exercises in your log haven't moved in months. Then shorten or split the workout instead of grinding through.
What to track in the log

Workout time on its own says nothing. What matters is how many hard sets you did and whether the weight or reps in them are rising. If you do in 50 minutes what used to take 80, that's progress in conditioning and rest discipline.

I time the workout, count sets and tonnage, and show for every exercise whether the estimated max went up. A short workout where everything grows beats a long one where nothing moves.

Take the "Push" day from push/pull/legs: six exercises, 19 working sets. The bench and overhead press — 7 sets at three minutes each with rest, about 21 minutes. Another 12 sets of isolation and dumbbell pressing at two minutes each — 24 minutes. Add a 10-minute warm-up and about five minutes moving between stations. Roughly an hour.

Done without a timer, with your phone and some chatting, the same workout easily stretches to ninety minutes — for the same work. If you need to finish in 45 minutes, it's easier to cut one exercise and add a set to the others than to shorten your bench rest.

Is a workout over an hour harmful? No. There's no 45-minute "window" after which muscles stop growing. The only question is whether you still have the energy for quality sets at the end.

What if I only have 30 minutes? Do 10–12 working sets, mostly compounds, plus supersets. Three short workouts a week beat one long one that never happens.

Should cardio go in the same workout? If the goal is strength and muscle, do cardio after lifting or on another day so you're not tired before the heavy sets. A five-minute warm-up on the treadmill doesn't count — it only helps. More in the warm-up guide.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.title: Your first week in the gym: where a beginner should start — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.h1: Your first week in the gym
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.descript: Where to start as a gym beginner: how many workouts in week one, which exercises, what weight to use, how to warm up, what to log and what not to worry about.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.lead: Week one isn't about results; it's about the habit and technique. The job is to show up three times, leave uninjured and want to come back. Everything else follows.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.card: Three workouts, light weights and a log from day one.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.cta: Log your first workout from the very first set — in a month you'll compare and see how much you've gained.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.takeaway:
Three full-body workouts a week with a rest day between them.
Five or six basic movements from a ready-made program.
Weight with three or four reps in reserve; technique beats kilos.
Warm-up: five minutes of cardio and two or three light sets.
Log every set from day one.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s1_html:
Three workouts a week with a day off between them — Monday, Wednesday, Friday or any three days with rest in between. Each one full body, 45–60 minutes. Two is enough too if that's all you can do: what matters is that next week looks the same.

Six workouts in the first week is a common mistake: you get so sore that week two falls apart. Muscle soreness in the first days is normal and fades in a couple of days; it gets milder every week.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s2_html:
Five or six movements that cover the whole body: a squat or leg press, a bench or dumbbell press, a lat pulldown or seated cable row, an overhead press, a Romanian deadlift, a plank. Machines and cables are a good start: the path is set and the weight changes with a pin.

Don't build a program yourself: take a ready one — full body three days or two days. Which one to pick is in the beginner program guide. Technique for every movement, with photos, is in exercises.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s3_html:
Light. Light enough that the last two or three reps of a set take effort but your form doesn't break. On the RPE scale that's 6–7: three or four reps left in reserve. Zourdos and colleagues (2016) built this scale so even beginners can use it: "how many more could I have done".

If you don't know where to start, begin with an empty bar or the lightest stack and work up until you hit that feeling. The weight in week one means nothing: a month from now it'll be different.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s4_html:
Five minutes on a treadmill or bike to get warm, then two or three light sets before the first exercise: an empty bar for 10, then half the working weight for 5. Warming up lowers the risk and helps you perform better — that's the average finding of the meta-analysis by Fradkin, Zazryn and Smoliga (2010).

Stretching before the workout isn't required. The warm-up calculator lays out the sets up to your working weight; more in the warm-up guide.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s5_html:
Every set: the exercise, the weight and the reps. That's it. In two weeks you won't remember what you benched last Tuesday, and without that you can't progress — progressive overload is built on comparing with last time.

In the bot a set is one line, "60 10" — I'll figure out the weight and reps, remember them and suggest a target next time. Voice works too if your hands are busy. How the diary works in Telegram is on the bot page.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s6_html:
• That everyone's watching. They aren't: everyone's busy with their own set.
  • Small weights. Everyone started with an empty bar. In a couple of months your weights will grow faster than they ever will again.
  • Asking. How to set up a machine or whether it's free are normal questions. Unsure about your form? Film a set and send it to me — I'll review it.
  • Missing a day. Missed one — do it tomorrow. A week away isn't a reason to start over; just come back near your previous weights.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s7_html:
Monday is day 1 of full body three days: squat, bench press, barbell row, overhead press, curls and a plank. Weight: an empty bar or a little more, three sets each. Wednesday is day 2: a light deadlift (or a Romanian deadlift if the deadlift still scares you), incline dumbbell press, lat pulldown, lateral raises, triceps and crunches. Friday is day 3: leg press, dips or push-ups, band-assisted pull-ups, seated cable row, hammer curls and leg raises.

Tuesday, Thursday and the weekend are for rest, walking and sleep. By next Monday the soreness will be milder, and you can add a little weight to every exercise.
seo.guide.first-week-in-the-gym.s8_html:
Do I need a personal trainer? Not necessarily. A ready program, technique photos and a video of your own set cover most questions. If you want someone to look at your form, send a video of a set — I'll review it.

What should I wear and bring? Comfortable clothes, flat-soled shoes (squats are unstable in running shoes), water and a towel. You don't need gloves or a belt in week one.

My muscles are really sore — should I go? If it's muscle soreness and bearable, yes — a light workout will even ease it. If a joint hurts or the pain is sharp, skip it and find the cause, with a doctor if needed. More on what to expect in the beginner gains guide.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.title: Common gym mistakes: why you're not making progress — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.descriptio: Ten mistakes that stall progress in the gym: no plan, weight for its own sake, junk sets, short rest, no log, no sleep — and how to fix each.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.lead: Almost every gym mistake isn't about one exercise's technique — it's that nothing changes from one workout to the next. These are the ones I see in logs most often.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.card: No plan, no log, no rest — what to fix first.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.cta: Start with the simplest fix — log your sets. The other mistakes will show themselves.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.takeaways:
One program for 8–12 weeks beats new exercises every week.
Without a log, progression is impossible — there's nothing to compare.
Add reps when the weight won't move with good form.
Most sets with 1–3 reps in reserve; failure only on isolation.
Sleep, protein and deloads are part of the program, not a break from it.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s1_html:
You walk in and do whatever's free — that's what a workout where nothing grows usually looks like. Bench today, dips next week, bench again with a different weight: nothing to compare, so nothing to build on.

The fix is simple: one program for 8–12 weeks. Not a perfect one — any reasonable one. Take a ready-made program and don't change it while the weights keep rising.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s2_html:
Without notes you don't know what you did last time, so you don't know what to do today. Progress in the gym is "one more rep or one more kilo than last time", and for that you need last time.

Log the weight and reps of every working set. How to do it quickly and what else is worth noting is in the workout log guide.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s3_html:
A heavy weight with half range and a swing looks impressive, but the muscle gets less than from an honest, lighter set. And the risk goes up: technique breaks exactly where the weight is at its limit.

Weight isn't the only thing you can add: in Plotkin et al. (2022), adding reps at the same weight produced similar muscle growth to adding weight. If the weight won't move with good form, add reps instead. Unsure about your form? Send a video of your set and I'll review it.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s4.h: Sets far from failure — and failure on everything
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s4_html:
Two opposite mistakes. The first is sets where you could do eight more: they hardly grow muscle — that's junk volume. The second is failure on every set, including heavy squats: fatigue climbs with no added benefit — in Refalo et al. (2023), failure showed no clear advantage for muscle growth.

The middle ground is 1–3 reps in reserve on most sets, with failure only on the last set of an isolation exercise.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s5_html:
Two minutes of rest turn into forty seconds ("I'm not tired") or seven minutes on your phone. In the first case the next set comes up a couple of reps short; in the second you cool down. In Schoenfeld et al. (2016), three minutes of rest gave more growth and strength than one.

Set a timer for 2–3 minutes on compounds and 60–90 seconds on isolation — the rest timer runs right in your browser.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s6.h: No sleep, no food, no deload
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s6_html:
Muscle doesn't grow in the gym; it grows afterwards. Six hours of sleep, skipped meals and little protein, and even a good program stalls. A protein guideline is about 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight per day — past that, the benefit barely grows (Morton et al., 2018).

And finally: months without a single easy week. If the weights are dropping and your joints ache, you need a deload first, not a new program. Details in the plateau guide.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s7_html:
• Skipping legs. Legs are half the muscle in your body. A week without squats, deadlifts and leg presses is half your volume gone.
  • Not warming up. Two or three light sets before a heavy weight lower the risk and help you perform — the warm-up calculator gives the weights.
  • Copying a pro's program. Twenty chest sets and six days a week is volume for someone with years of training and recovery behind them. Beginners don't need that much.
  • Comparing yourself to others. Someone else's weight says nothing about your progress. Compare yourself to yourself a month ago — that's what the log is for.
seo.guide.common-gym-mistakes.s8_html:
You don't need to fix everything at once. The order that works for almost everyone: first a log, then one program, then progression, then rest and sleep. The log comes first because without it the other mistakes are invisible: whether the weights are stuck, how many sets each muscle gets, how often you skip.

After a month of logging, look at three or four main lifts. Rising — fine, change nothing. Flat — check the list above for what applies to you. And if you're not sure you're doing it right, ask the coach: it sees your whole history and will tell you what to fix first. More on plateaus in the plateau guide.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.tit: Strength training after 40: how to start and how to train — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.des: How to train in the gym after 40 and 50: what research says about strength training with age, frequency, loads, warm-ups, recovery and progress.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.lea: It's not too late to start strength training after forty — or after sixty. Muscles respond to load more slowly with age, but they do respond. The principles stay the same; the margin for error shrinks.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.car: It's not too late: what changes with age and what doesn't.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.cta: Log your workouts — I'll show how your strength grows, and the coach will account for your limitations if you tell it about them.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.tak:
It's not too late to start at 40 or at 60.
The principles are the same: regular load that slowly increases.
Two or three full-body workouts; machines and dumbbells in the first weeks.
A longer warm-up, 8–15 reps, 2–3 reps in reserve.
With a chronic condition, talk to a doctor first.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s1_:
With age, strength and muscle mass decline if you don't train them, and that affects mobility and independence. The US National Strength and Conditioning Association's position statement (Fragala et al., 2019) names strength training as one of the most effective ways to counter this — while noting that few older adults actually do it.

The good news is you can start at any age. The question isn't "can I" but "how do I start without getting hurt or quitting".
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s2_:
The meta-analysis by Borde, Hortobágyi and Granacher (2015) pooled 25 randomised trials with participants averaging 65 or older. Strength training improved both strength and muscle measures, and the authors described which program variables worked best — frequency, volume and intensity close to ordinary adult programs.

The takeaway is simple: the principles are the same as at 25. Regular load that slowly increases is what counts. What differs is how fast you add weight and how much recovery you need.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s3_:
Two or three full-body workouts a week — two or three days. In the first weeks use machines and dumbbells: the path is simpler and the load is easier on your joints. The barbell will still be there once your technique is set.

If you have a chronic condition or issues with blood pressure, joints or your back, talk to a doctor first. They won't forbid training, but they can tell you what to avoid for now. Choosing your first program is covered in the beginner program guide.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s4_:
• A longer warm-up — 8–10 minutes of cardio and two or three light sets before each main exercise. The warm-up calculator lays out the sets.
  • Reps — 8–15 on most exercises: less joint stress for the same muscle growth.
  • Reserve — 2–3 reps short of failure, RPE 7–8. No need for failure on compounds.
  • Rest — don't skimp: 2–3 minutes on compounds. More in the rest guide.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s5_:
Recovery takes longer with age — that's normal. A rest day between full-body workouts is a must, and a hard week every 6–8 weeks should give way to an easy one. Sleep and protein matter at any age, but after forty a shortfall shows up sooner.

Achy joints the next day are a signal to lower the weight or swap the exercise: every exercise has substitutes, for example back squat alternatives. Sharp pain is a reason to stop and see a doctor.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s6_:
In the first months strength grows fast — like any beginner's, just a little slower than a twenty-year-old's. Then the pace levels off. Compare yourself only with yourself a month ago, not with the person on the next bench.

I track the estimated max for every exercise and chart it — progress shows even when the mirror doesn't show it yet. If you like, tell the coach about injuries and limitations — it'll take them into account when building your program.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s7_:
Two full-body workouts — Monday and Thursday — from the "Full body — 2 days" program. In the first month swap the barbell squat for the leg press or a goblet squat, and the deadlift for a light Romanian deadlift. Each exercise: three sets of 10–12, two or three reps in reserve.

After a month, if it's going well, add a third day or bring the barbell back for squats. Between workouts, walk: it speeds recovery and doesn't get in the way of lifting. Every exercise in the program has substitutes on its alternatives page, for example for the deadlift.
seo.guide.strength-training-after-40.s8_:
Is it too late to start at 50 or 60? No. The research above included people aged 65 and over, and strength training worked for them too.

Can I lift heavy? Yes, in time — once your technique is set and your body has adapted. Heavy sets of 5–6 reps are useful at any age; you just don't start there in the first month.

What about a bad back or knees? Don't train through pain. Find substitutes that don't bother you — every exercise on the site has an alternatives page. And talk to a doctor about what's fine to do. Tell the coach in the diary too — it will build that into your program.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.title: Beginner gains: how fast strength and muscle grow in your first year — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.beginner-gains.h1: Beginner gains: how fast you'll progress
seo.guide.beginner-gains.description: How fast a beginner's strength and muscle grow: why the first months are the fastest, when progress slows, how not to waste it and how to gauge your own pace.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.lead: Your first months in the gym are the most generous: the weight goes up almost every workout. That's not magic — your body is learning to lift heavy for the first time. The key is not to waste it.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.card: Why the first months are the fastest and when it ends.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.cta: Log from day one — those months of progress are better seen on a chart than remembered.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.takeaways:
In the first months strength grows mainly through skill; muscle follows.
In the first six months the weight on compounds rises almost every week.
Linear or double progression is the best use of this time.
The bench usually stalls first — that's a phase change, not failure.
Check the estimated max on your main lifts once a month.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s1_html:
In the first weeks strength grows mainly not from muscle but from skill: your nervous system learns to fire muscles together, and you learn to hold the path. That's why your bench can climb by tens of percent before your chest gets noticeably bigger.

Then muscle growth kicks in. It's slower, but for an untrained person any reasonable hard set is a strong stimulus: muscles respond to modest volume and a wide range of reps. Research shows it too: in beginners, different schemes produce similar results.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s2_html:
There are no exact numbers for everyone: the pace depends on age, sex, bodyweight, sleep, food and the program. There's a general pattern: in the first three to six months the weight on compounds goes up almost every week, by the end of the first year month to month, and after two or three years cycle to cycle.

My "when will I lift it" calculator works exactly this way: a beginner's estimated max grows faster than an intermediate's, and the rate fades over time. It's a forecast with two ends, not a promise — but it shows well why the first year matters so much.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s3_html:
Beginner progress is easy to waste: switching programs every week, training without a plan, quitting for a month. The best use of this time is linear progression: hit all your sets — add a little weight next time. That's how 5×5 works.
