Double progression in full-body programs works too: reps up to the top of the range first, then weight. In Plotkin et al. (2022), adding reps and adding weight grew muscle similarly, so pick whichever suits you.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s4_html:
The bench usually stalls first: the upper body grows slower, and a 2.5 kg jump is a big step for it. Then the squat and deadlift. That's not a plateau in the bad sense — it's a sign the beginner phase is ending. Don't scrap the program; change how you progress.

  • Add weight once a week rather than every workout.
  • Add reps: 3×5 → 3×6 → 3×7, then weight.
  • Move to a higher-volume program — "Upper / Lower" or push/pull/legs.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s5.h: Strength and muscle aren't the same
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s5_html:
The weight on the bar grows faster than the muscle in the mirror — especially in the first two or three months. Don't be discouraged if your measurements have barely changed: the skill is already working, and the muscle will catch up. In the meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Grgic, Ogborn and Krieger (2017), muscle grew similarly with heavy and light loads, while strength grew more with heavy ones: two linked but different things.

What matters for muscle is hard sets per muscle per week. Beginners need 6–10; details in the sets-per-week guide.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s6_html:
Once a month, look at the estimated max on three or four main lifts. Rising — all good. Flat for more than a month — check sleep, food and whether you're adding anything at all. Falling — time for an easy week.

I work out the estimated max from every set myself and chart it; you can also calculate it from any set with the 1RM calculator. A ready program for the first months is in the beginner program guide.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s7.h: What speeds it up and what slows it down
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s7_html:
• Speeds it up: consistency (three workouts every week, not six one week and none the next), 7–9 hours of sleep, enough food and protein, one program without constant changes.
  • Slows it down: missed sessions, short sleep, a calorie deficit, training "by mood" without a log, and ramping up volume so fast you can't recover.

Beginners can lose fat and gain muscle at the same time, but strength grows more slowly in a deficit. If the goal is to build strength and muscle faster, you need enough food. Food and protein are covered in the muscle gain program guide.
seo.guide.beginner-gains.s8_html:
How long do beginner gains last? For most people, six months to a year of regular training; then the pace drops noticeably. It's not a wall, it's a gentle slope.

Does fast progress come back after a break? Partly: after a pause strength usually returns faster than it grew the first time. Start 10–20% below your previous weights and work back up over a few weeks.

I'm not a beginner anymore but still progressing — is that normal? Yes: there's always progress, it's just slower. Look at the trend over two or three months, not a week. How to keep progressing is in the progressive overload guide.
seo.guide.junk-volume.title: Junk volume: the sets that barely build muscle — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.junk-volume.h1: Junk volume: sets that don't count
seo.guide.junk-volume.description: What junk volume is: sets far from failure, extra sets once you're exhausted and duplicate exercises — what research says and how to cut the excess.
seo.guide.junk-volume.lead: Junk volume is sets you do, log and count that give your muscles almost nothing. They're easy to miss: the workout is long and there's no progress.
seo.guide.junk-volume.card: Sets that eat time but barely grow muscle.
seo.guide.junk-volume.cta: Log your sets with RPE — it shows which ones are real work and which are just for show.
seo.guide.junk-volume.takeaways:
Junk volume is sets that give a muscle almost nothing.
A working set leaves 1–3 reps in reserve, not 6–8.
Each extra set on a muscle gives less than the one before.
Duplicates of the same movement in one workout are often wasted.
Fewer, harder sets usually win.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s1_html:
The term is informal, but the idea is clear: not every set is equally useful. What counts for muscle growth is working sets — hard ones, close to failure. A set after which you could have done eight more reps isn't really a working set, even if the weight is your "working" weight.

Junk volume comes in three kinds: sets too far from failure, extra sets once the muscle is exhausted and the weight is dropping, and exercises that duplicate each other without adding new load. Let's take them one by one.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s2_html:
Proximity to failure matters for muscle growth. In Refalo et al. (2023), sets to failure and sets stopped a little short grew muscle similarly. In Grgic et al.'s 2022 meta-analysis of 15 studies, failure and non-failure training also produced comparable results. But "a little short" means 1–3 reps, not 6–8.

How to check: at the end of a set, ask how many more reps you could do with the same form. More than four — raise the weight or the reps. The RPE scale makes this a habit.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s3_html:
More weekly sets give more growth on average — but with diminishing returns: that's what both Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (2017) and the large analysis by Pelland and colleagues show. The first sets give a lot, each one after gives less. At some point the return gets so small the set isn't worth the fatigue it adds.

The sign in a workout: your eighth chest set of the day comes in a third lighter than the first. It still does something, but those sets pay off better on another day of the week when your chest is fresh.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s4_html:
A barbell press, a dumbbell press, a machine press and push-ups in one workout are four exercises but one movement and one muscle in the same position. Sometimes that's fine, but often the third and fourth are just more sets on a tired muscle.

Different angles and movements work better: flat bench, incline press, flyes. Or different days: one exercise on Tuesday, another on Friday. Every exercise has substitutes at another angle — for example, bench press alternatives.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s5.h: How to spot it in your log
seo.guide.junk-volume.s5_html:
• Weight and reps on an exercise haven't moved for months while sets per muscle are high — the volume is there, the load isn't rising.
  • The last sets are much lighter than the first — fatigue ate the work.
  • RPE 5–6 on most sets — sets are far from failure.
  • The workout runs past ninety minutes and the last exercises don't progress.

The volume calculator counts your weekly sets per muscle, and the diary counts them from what you did.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s6_html:
Cut some sets and make the rest harder. Twelve sets per muscle per week with 1–3 reps in reserve almost always beat twenty with six in reserve. Split the volume across two workouts if one muscle gets more than 8–10 sets in a session.

And don't confuse junk volume with easy days: a deload week at low RPE is a plan, not a mistake. How many sets a muscle needs is in the sets-per-week guide.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s7.h: Example: cleaning up a chest day
seo.guide.junk-volume.s7_html:
Before: barbell bench 5 sets, dumbbell press 4, machine press 4, push-ups 3, flyes 4 — twenty chest sets in a day, and by the machine press the weight is already a third lower than usual. After: barbell bench 4 sets, incline dumbbell press 3, flyes 3 — ten sets, all with 1–3 reps in reserve. The other ten moved to a second chest day three days later.

The weekly volume is the same, but every set is harder and fresher. A month later the change usually shows in the log: the bench starts rising again. Check how many sets per muscle your plan gives with the volume calculator.
seo.guide.junk-volume.s8_html:
Are warm-up sets junk volume? No, they're separate work: they prepare you for the heavy sets and don't count toward growth volume at all. More in the warm-up guide.

What if I enjoy long workouts? Go ahead — junk volume doesn't hurt, it just barely helps and eats into recovery. If the weights are rising, you're fine.

How do I know how many reps I have left? Film a set, or every couple of weeks take the last isolation set to true failure — that calibrates the feeling. The RIR scale is the same idea: how many reps you left.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.title: Beginner gym workout program: where to start — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.descripti: Which program a gym beginner should pick: full body two or three days, or 5×5 for strength — how they differ, how many sets per muscle they give and how to progress in the first months.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.lead: A beginner doesn't need a complex program — they need a simple one they'll do for three months straight. There are three in my bot, and choosing between them takes a minute.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.card: Full body two or three days, or 5×5 — how to choose.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.cta: Take a program into your diary — I'll suggest the weight for every set from your last workout.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.takeaways:
Beginners need a simple full-body program, not a complex split.
Full body three days is the default; two days if time is short.
5×5 if strength is the goal: three lifts and more weight every session.
6–10 hard sets per muscle per week are enough to start.
Stay on the program while the weights rise — usually 3–6 months.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s1_html:
Three things: basic full-body movements, frequent practice of each, and a clear way to progress. Nothing else. Complex splits, supersets and ten chest exercises are for people for whom the simple stuff has stopped working.

Full body two or three times a week covers all three. Every muscle gets work several times a week, and in Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (2016), training a muscle twice a week grew more than once — largely because it's easier to get good-quality volume that way.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s2_html:
• Full body — 2 days — if you have two evenings. Two different workouts of six exercises.
  • Full body — 3 days — the classic start. Three workouts, basic lifts and a little isolation for arms and shoulders.
  • Strength 5×5 — if strength is the goal. Three lifts per workout, five sets of five, more weight every time.

If you're unsure, take full body three days. Each program's page shows the week day by day and sets per muscle, and three-day options are compared on the 3-day split page.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s3_html:
Beginners need 6–10 hard sets per muscle per week: they grow from almost any reasonable volume, and extra sets get in the way of learning technique. The programs above give roughly that — counted on their pages with the same rule the diary uses.

Reps: 5–12 on compounds and 10–15 on isolation. Reserve: 2–3 reps short of failure — in the first weeks, technique matters more than effort. More sets give more growth, but with diminishing returns (Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger, 2017), so starting at the low end is fine.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s4_html:
In 5×5 it's weight: hit five sets of five — next time add 2.5 kg on presses and 5 kg on squats and deadlifts. That's linear progression. In full-body programs it's double progression: in a "3×8–12" scheme, push the reps up to 12, then add weight. In Plotkin et al. (2022), adding reps grew muscle about as well as adding weight.

Don't add everything at once or skip steps: 2.5 kg a week is 30 kg in three months.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s5.h: How long to stay on it
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s5_html:
As long as the weights keep going up — usually 3–6 months. Don't switch after two weeks because you're bored: changing exercises wipes out the comparison with last time. Switch when the weight has stalled on two or three main lifts for 2–3 weeks and your sleep and food are in order.

Then comes the next step: "Upper / Lower" over four days or push/pull/legs. How to tell the beginner phase is over is in the beginner gains guide.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s6_html:
Take a program in the bot: {programs_btn} → {ready} → pick one → {add}. The days land in your diary, and at every workout I'll show what you did last time and what weight to use today. Do the first workout light: the job is to learn the movements.

What to bring, how to warm up and what not to worry about is in the first week in the gym guide.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s7_html:
"Full body — 3 days": Monday, Wednesday, Friday. Monday is squat, bench, barbell row, overhead press, curls and a plank; Wednesday is deadlift, incline dumbbell press, lat pulldown, lateral raises, triceps and crunches; Friday is leg press, dips, pull-ups, seated cable row, hammer curls and leg raises. Over the week the chest gets 9 hard sets, the back 13 and the quads 6 — counted on the program page with the same rule the diary uses.

Each workout takes 50–60 minutes with the warm-up, with a rest day between. If you miss Wednesday, do it Thursday and move Friday to Saturday: the sequence matters more than the weekdays.
seo.guide.beginner-gym-program.s8_html:
Can I start with push/pull/legs or a split? You can, but it's worse at the start: each movement comes up once a week, technique settles slower, and missing a day knocks a muscle group out for two weeks.

What if I can't do an exercise? Swap it for a variation on the same muscle: the squat for a leg press or goblet squat, pull-ups for lat pulldowns. Substitute lists are on the alternatives pages, for example for pull-ups.

Do I need cardio? For health, yes — at least walking. For strength and muscle it's optional. If you do it, put it after lifting or on another day.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.title: Muscle gain workout program: how to build muscle in the gym — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.h1: A workout program for muscle gain
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.descriptio: How a muscle gain program works: weekly volume per muscle, reps, proximity to failure, frequency, food and protein — and which ready-made programs suit building muscle.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.lead: A muscle gain program isn't special exercises — it's enough hard sets for every muscle every week, getting heavier over time. Plus enough food to grow on.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.card: Volume, reps, food and ready programs for size.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.cta: Log your workouts — I'll count the weekly sets for each muscle and show where you're short.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.takeaways:
Muscle grows from volume, proximity to failure and rising load.
8–16 hard sets per muscle per week for most people.
6–10 reps on compounds and 10–15 on isolation, 0–3 reps in reserve.
Protein around 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight, a modest surplus.
If the weights and reps in your log rise, so does your muscle.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s1_html:
Three things: volume — hard sets per muscle per week; proximity of those sets to failure; and progression — load that rises week to week. Specific exercises, their order and "secret" schemes matter far less.

Volume works dose-response: in the meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (2017), each extra weekly set gave a little more growth on average, and the large analysis by Pelland and colleagues showed the returns diminish with volume. So you need enough, not endless amounts.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s2_html:
• Starting out — 8–12 hard sets per muscle per week.
  • Intermediate — 10–16.
  • Lagging muscles — up to 16–20 if you're recovering.

Count sets by muscle: a deadlift is half back and half hamstrings and glutes, a bench press is chest. How to count precisely and where these numbers come from is in the sets-per-week guide, and you can split your own plan with the volume calculator.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s3_html:
A wide range works for size: muscle grew similarly with heavy and light loads in the meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Grgic, Ogborn and Krieger (2017) — as long as sets went close to failure. In practice 6–10 on compounds and 10–15 on isolation is convenient: heavy sets of 3 need lots of rest, sets of 30 need patience.

More important than the rep count is the reserve: 0–3 reps short of failure. Details in the reps for muscle growth guide.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s4_html:
Any program that gives every muscle enough sets and that you'll actually do. Of the bot's ready-made programs, these suit size well:

  • "Upper / Lower" over 4 days — every muscle twice a week.
  • Push/pull/legs over 3 or 6 days — flexible around your schedule.
  • The 3-day split — lots of sets per group in one go.

For a beginner, full body three days is enough for size too. How many sets each gives per muscle is on the program pages and in splits.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s5_html:
Muscle is built from what you eat. Gaining needs a small calorie surplus — a bit more than you burn — and enough protein. A protein guideline is about 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight per day: past that the benefit barely grows (the Morton et al. 2018 meta-analysis).

A big surplus doesn't speed up muscle growth; it adds fat. Check your bodyweight once a week: when gaining it climbs slowly, usually by fractions of a kilo a week. The weight diary is in both the bot and the app. The details are in the guides on protein per day and calories for muscle gain.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s6_html:
If the weight and reps on a muscle's exercises are rising, the muscle is growing. That's the best sign — better than the mirror: the mirror changes slowly, while the log shows every 2.5 kg. Once a month check the estimated max on two or three exercises for each major group.

If everything's been flat for a month, look at food and sleep first, then volume: add 2–3 weekly sets for what's lagging. If you're tired and the weights are falling, you need a deload, not more sets. Details in the plateau guide.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s7_html:
"Upper / Lower" over four days: Monday upper, Tuesday lower, Thursday upper, Friday lower. Upper: bench 4×6–8, barbell row 4×6–10, seated dumbbell press 3×8–10, lat pulldown 3×8–12, biceps and triceps 3 sets each. Lower: squat 4×6–8, Romanian deadlift 3×8–10, leg press 3×10–12, leg curls 3×10–12, calves and abs.

Over the week the chest gets 8 sets, the back about 14 and the quads 14 — that's what the volume table on the program page shows. It's enough for an intermediate; if something specific lags, add 2–3 sets for that muscle, not for everything at once.
seo.guide.muscle-gain-program.s8_html:
Should I change programs every 4–6 weeks? No. Change when it stops working: the weights have stalled for a month while sleep and food are in order. Constant changes make progress hard to see.

How much can I gain in a year? There's no exact number: the pace depends on training age, age, sleep and food. Beginners grow fastest, then slower. What matters is that the weights and reps in your log keep rising.

Is gaining without fat possible? A small surplus and enough protein is the closest you'll get. If your bodyweight climbs faster than fractions of a kilo a week, the surplus is probably too big. The weight diary shows the trend if you weigh in under the same conditions.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.title: Gym workout program for women: where to start — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.h1: A gym workout program for women
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.descript: How women should train in the gym: what's different and what isn't, what research says, a glutes-and-legs program and a full-body one, weights and progress.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.lead: Women in the gym don't need a "women's" program with pink dumbbells. Muscle grows by the same rules. What usually differs is the goal — and there are ready programs for it.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.card: Same principles, your own goal: glutes, full body and progress.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.cta: Log your workouts — I'll show how your weights grow in every exercise, without comparing you to anyone else.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.takeaway:
Women's muscles grow by the same rules as men's.
In relative terms women gain strength just as well, and even more in the upper body.
Light weights for high reps aren't required — proximity to failure is what counts.
For glutes and legs, take the "Glutes and legs — 3 days" program.
Compare yourself only with yourself a month ago.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s1_html:
The meta-analysis by Roberts, Nuckols and Krieger (2020) compared how men and women respond to the same strength program. Muscle growth and relative lower-body strength gains were similar, and women actually gained more relative upper-body strength. So one program works for everyone; nothing "women's" is required.

The difference is the starting point: on average women have less upper-body muscle mass, so pressing and pulling weights are lower. That's not a reason to train lighter — it's a reason to compare yourself only with yourself.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s2_html:
• "You'll get bulky." Muscle grows slowly for everyone, and for most women especially. Heavy sets make you stronger and more toned, not "huge" in a couple of months.
  • "Women should do lots of reps with light weights." Muscle grows with heavy and light loads if the set is close to failure (Schoenfeld, Grgic, Ogborn, Krieger, 2017). A light weight for 30 reps just takes longer.
  • "Ab work burns belly fat." Fat doesn't come off locally; you train abs for the abs.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s3.h: If the goal is glutes and legs
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s3_html:
It's the most common goal, and the bot has "Glutes and legs — 3 days" for it. The lower body gets three workouts, and the glutes work in two ways: bridges and abductions load them directly, Romanian deadlifts and lunges load them in a stretch. The upper body gets the minimum so it doesn't fall behind.

The key exercises are the hip thrust, Romanian deadlift, Bulgarian split squat and squat. How the glutes work and what else trains them is on the glutes page.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s4.h: If the goal is the whole body
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s4_html:
If you want strength and shape all over, take full body three days or two days — the same programs as for any beginner. After six to twelve months, move to "Upper / Lower".

Most people can't do a pull-up at the start — that's normal. Begin with lat pulldowns and band-assisted pull-ups: in a few months your first unassisted pull-ups become a real goal. Choosing a first program is covered in the beginner program guide.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s5_html:
Use a weight where the last 1–3 reps of a set are hard. In a "3×10–12" scheme, get 12 on every set, then add weight — that's double progression. On presses a 2.5 kg jump is big, so reps rise more often and weight less often; on hip thrusts and deadlifts the weight climbs faster.

Your cycle, sleep and stress can shift your strength from week to week — that's normal. Look at the trend over a month, not one workout: I chart every exercise.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s6_html:
Take a program in the bot or the app: {programs_btn} → {ready} → pick one → {add}. In the first week go light — the job is to learn the movements. Every exercise in the program, with photos and a technique breakdown, is in exercises.

If something in the program doesn't suit you, swap the exercise: each one has substitutes for the same muscle. Unsure about your form? Film a set and send it to the coach for review.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s7_html:
"Glutes and legs — 3 days": Monday is the heavy glute day (barbell glute bridge, Romanian deadlift, Bulgarian split squat, cable kickback, hip abduction machine), Wednesday is quads (squat, leg press, leg extensions and curls, calves), Friday is glutes plus light upper body (lunges, bodyweight glute bridge, back extension, lat pulldown, seated dumbbell press, plank).

Almost all the week's volume goes to the lower body: the quads and glutes get the most sets — you can see it in the volume table on the program page. If you want more upper body, add a fourth day — the upper day from "Upper / Lower" — or swap Friday for it.
seo.guide.gym-program-for-women.s8_html:
Should I train during my period? It's your call, based on how you feel. Many people train as usual; if you have less energy, do a lighter session with lower weights — that's normal, not a skipped day.

Are there special exercises "for women"? No. Hip abductions and bridges are just glute exercises; men do them too. You choose a program by goal, not gender.

Lose weight or gain? Strength training matters either way: when cutting it helps keep muscle, when gaining it builds muscle. The difference is food, not the program. More on protein and surplus in the muscle gain program guide.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.title: How to increase your bench press: technique, frequency and programming — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.h1: How to increase your bench press
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.descripti: How to raise your bench press: setup and technique, how often to bench, heavy sets and volume, accessory work, small plates and what to do on a plateau.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.lead: The bench press grows slower than the squat and deadlift: upper-body muscles are smaller and a 2.5 kg jump is big for them. But the bench has clear levers: technique, frequency, heavy sets and patience.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.card: Setup, frequency, heavy sets and small plates.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.cta: Log every bench session — I'll show your estimated max and suggest the weight for your next set.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.takeaways:
Setup: shoulder blades pinched, feet planted, bar to the lower chest.
Bench two or three times a week, not once.
A heavy bench for 3–5 first, then volume at 6–10.
Triceps and back hold up the bench — train them.
If +2.5 kg won't go, add reps or use small plates.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s1_html:
Most of the "free" kilos in a bench are in the setup: shoulder blades pinched and down, chest up, feet driving into the floor, the bar coming down to your lower chest. That keeps your shoulders safe and shortens the bar path. Detailed technique with photos is on the bench press page.

Grip a little wider than your shoulders, with vertical forearms at the bottom. Elbows at 45–70 degrees to your torso, not flared. Film a set from the side and behind: where the path breaks shows right away. You can send it to me — I'll review the set.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s2_html:
The bench is a skill, and skills grow with practice. Once a week is too little: most people do better with two or three sessions, one heavier and one lighter. In Grgic et al.'s 2018 meta-analysis, more frequent training produced more strength — largely because more sets were done per week; with volume equated the difference became small.

In practice: if you bench once a week for five sets, split them into two days of three. Slightly more sets, and each one is better quality. That's how "Upper / Lower" and full body three days are built.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s3_html:
Strength for a single needs heavy sets: in the meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Grgic, Ogborn and Krieger (2017), the one-rep max grew more with heavy loads, while muscle grew similarly with any. Hence the scheme: a heavy bench for 3–5 reps first, then volume at 6–10 so the chest and triceps grow.

Ready schemes: 5×5 to start and 5/3/1 for those no longer adding weight every week. The 1RM calculator gives you the percentages.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s4_html:
• Triceps carry the lockout: the close-grip bench, skull crushers, dips.
  • Chest in a stretch — the dumbbell press and incline press.
  • Back and rear delts keep your shoulder blades in place: rows, face pulls.
  • Weak points — the floor press if the middle and top are hard; a pause on the chest if you bounce the bar.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s5_html:
2.5 kg on the bench is 3% of 80 kg. A step like that every week doesn't last. If your gym has 0.5–1.25 kg plates, add 1–2.5 kg at a time. If not, grow by reps: 3×5 → 3×6 → 3×7, then weight. In Plotkin et al. (2022), adding reps grew muscle as well as adding weight.

Double progression and "as many as possible" sets are a normal way to grow once +2.5 kg a week stops working.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s6_html:
Check in order: sleep and food, technique on video, frequency (are you benching at least twice a week) and volume for chest and triceps. If it all checks out and the weight has stalled for 3–4 weeks, take an easy week and restart 10% lighter — the old record often goes after that.

The strength standards show where your bench sits among competitive lifters at your bodyweight. More on plateaus in the plateau guide.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s7_html:
Two bench days a week. Monday is heavy: bench 4×3–5 with three minutes' rest, then incline dumbbell press 3×8–10 and skull crushers 3×10–12. Thursday is volume: bench 3×8 at 15% less weight, close-grip bench 3×6–8, dips 3×8–12. In between, rows and pull-ups for your back.

Each week, try to add a rep on the heavy day, or 1–2.5 kg once every set hits the top of the range. After 6–8 weeks, an easy week, then start the cycle again. If you want a scheme that plans the weights a month ahead, try 5/3/1.
seo.guide.increase-bench-press.s8_html:
How much should a man or woman bench at their bodyweight? There's no single norm. The strength standards show how your bench compares with competitive lifters at your bodyweight — but remember those are people from the platform, not random gym-goers.

Do I need a big arch? A small arch from pinched shoulder blades is a normal part of the setup. A huge arch where your hips leave the bench is no longer a bench press and isn't needed in the gym.

Does a pause on the chest help? Yes: a paused bench teaches you not to bounce the bar and to stay tight at the bottom, where many people are weakest. Do it on the light day.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.title: How many reps to build muscle — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.h1: How many reps to build muscle
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.descrip: How many reps per set build muscle: what research says about light and heavy loads, why proximity to failure matters more, and which range suits each exercise best.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.lead: The short answer: almost any number from 5 to 30 — if the set is hard. The long answer is why it's still handier to stay at 6–15 in the gym, and where to go higher or lower.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.card: 6, 12 or 20: why the range is wide and what matters more.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.cta: Log your reps and RPE — I'll show whether the load is rising, whatever range you choose.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.takeawa:
Almost any range from 5 to 30 reps builds muscle.
What matters most is stopping 0–3 reps short of failure.
Heavy compounds 5–10, lighter compounds 8–12, isolation 10–20.
For strength on a single you also need heavy sets of 3–6.
A range is a plan: hit the top, add weight.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s1_html:
The meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Grgic, Ogborn and Krieger (2017) compared training with heavy loads (fewer reps) and light loads (more reps). Muscle grew similarly in both — provided sets went close to failure. One-rep max strength, though, grew more with heavy loads.

The takeaway: for size, the rep count on its own decides little. What decides is how hard the set was by the end. Twenty easy reps with ten more in the tank grow less than eight hard ones.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s2.h: Proximity to failure beats the number
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s2_html:
Failure isn't required: in Refalo et al. (2023), sets to failure and sets stopped a little short grew muscle similarly, and in Grgic et al.'s 2022 meta-analysis of 15 studies, failure and non-failure training also produced comparable results. A little short means 0–3 reps — in other words RIR 0–3.

With high reps, the reserve is harder to judge: at rep twenty the burn makes you think you're done when you have five left. That's why sets of 20–30 are harder to take honestly to the right effort, and most people are better off lower.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s3_html:
• Heavy compounds (squat, bench, deadlift) — 5–10. Below five it's more about strength and needs long rest; above ten your breathing and back give out before the target muscle.
  • Lighter compounds (dumbbell press, pulldown, leg press) — 8–12.
  • Isolation (raises, curls, extensions) — 10–20: a small weight for 5 reps is awkward and hard on the joints.
  • Calves, abs, rear delts — often 12–20.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s4_html:
If you also want strength for a single, do heavy sets of 3–6 as your first exercise. It doesn't hurt muscle growth and trains the skill of lifting heavy: one-rep max strength grows most with heavy loads. How to combine strength and size is in the strength vs hypertrophy guide.

The 1RM calculator gives you percentages of your max and the reps that go with them.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s5.h: How to progress within a range
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s5_html:
A range of "8–12" isn't just "somewhere in between" — it's a plan: start with a weight you can do for 8, work up to 12 on all sets, then add weight and start again at 8. That's double progression. In Plotkin et al. (2022), adding reps grew muscle about as well as adding weight — so reps count as progress too.

I suggest a target for each set from your last workout: "+1 rep" or "+2.5 kg", depending on where you are in the range.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s6_html:
• Stopping at the scheme's number when you have five more — the set got easy, time to add.
  • Chasing weight and losing range: 10 full reps beat 10 halves.
  • The same 3×10 on everything for years — your body adapts and the load stops rising.
  • High reps on heavy compounds — 20 squats run into your lungs, not your legs.

Sets that do almost nothing are covered in the junk volume guide.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s7_html:
A dumbbell press with an estimated max of 40 kg per hand. Option 1: 32 kg for 6 reps with one in reserve. Option 2: 26 kg for 12 with two in reserve. Option 3: 20 kg for 20 with two in reserve. According to the research, all three grow the chest similarly if they reach that reserve.

In practice the second is handiest: the first needs more rest and is harder on the shoulders, the third is long and unpleasant, and it's easy to stop too early. That's why most programs sit in the middle. The percentage table in the 1RM calculator helps you convert your weights for a different rep count.
seo.guide.reps-for-muscle-growth.s8_html:
Should I change the rep range? You don't have to, but you can: sometimes doing the same exercise heavier or lighter keeps progress from getting stuck on one number. Change it every few weeks, not every workout.

How many reps for "definition"? There's no separate range for definition: how visible your muscles are depends on body fat, which is about food. Reps build muscle; they don't "carve" it.

Is the number different for women? No, the rules are the same. More in the gym program for women guide.
seo.guide.training-frequency.title: Training frequency: how many times a week to train each muscle — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.training-frequency.h1: Training frequency: how many times a week
seo.guide.training-frequency.description: How many times a week to train a muscle: what research says about frequency for muscle growth and strength, why it barely matters at equal volume, and how to pick a schedule.
seo.guide.training-frequency.lead: How many times a week to train a muscle is one of the most studied questions in the gym. The answer is simpler than the arguments: weekly volume is what matters, and frequency is a way to get it in comfortably.
seo.guide.training-frequency.card: Once, twice or three times a week: what research says.
seo.guide.training-frequency.cta: Log your workouts — I'll show how many times a week you really train each muscle.
seo.guide.training-frequency.takeaways:
Frequency is how often a muscle works per week, not how often you're in the gym.
At equal volume, frequency barely affects muscle growth.
For strength, frequency matters more: skills grow with repetition.
Training more often makes good-quality volume easier.
More than 8–10 sets per muscle a week — split them into two workouts.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s1_html:
Frequency is how many times a week a muscle gets trained, not how many times you go to the gym. A five-day bro split trains your chest once a week; a three-day full-body program trains it three times. I counted what that looks like in real programs in the full body vs split comparison.

There's also frequency of a lift: benching twice a week is two skill sessions, even if your chest gets different volume on those days.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s2.h: What research says about muscle growth
seo.guide.training-frequency.s2_html:
An early meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (2016) found that training a muscle twice a week grew more than once. But most of those studies didn't equate volume: whoever trained more often also did more sets.

When studies with equal volume were compared, the picture changed: in the review by Grgic and colleagues (2019), frequency on its own barely affected muscle growth. In Šarić et al. (2019), trained men did the same volume over three or six sessions a week for six weeks — and gained similarly. The large analysis by Pelland and colleagues showed the same: at equal volume, frequency changes almost nothing for muscle.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s3_html:
Frequency matters more for strength. In Grgic et al.'s 2018 meta-analysis, more frequent training gave more strength, but largely because more sets were done per week; at equal volume the difference shrank. In the Pelland analysis, frequency affected strength more than muscle.

The logic is simple: strength is also a skill, and skills grow with repetition. That's why strength programs put the main lifts in two or three times a week, like 5×5 and full body three days.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s4_html:
Because it's easier to get good-quality volume. Twenty chest sets in one workout means the last ten on a tired muscle with less weight. Two workouts of ten each give twenty good sets. A practical rule: if a muscle gets more than 8–10 sets a week, split them across at least two workouts.

Also: at two or three sessions a week, missing one doesn't leave a muscle untrained for two weeks. How many sets you need overall is in the sets-per-week guide.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s5_html:
• 2–3 days a week — full body: every muscle two or three times.
  • 4 days — upper and lower twice: every muscle twice.
  • 5–6 days — push/pull/legs or upper/lower + PPL: twice; a bro split once, with many sets.

Every option, with the week day by day and sets per muscle, is in splits. Pick the schedule you can keep for months: at equal volume, that matters more than frequency.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s6_html:
Look at your log for the last month: how many times a week you actually trained each group — not by plan, but in fact. If the plan says twice and it comes out once every ten days, your frequency isn't what you think.

I count weekly sets for every group from what you did and show them on the main screen. You can lay out your plan by muscle in advance with the volume calculator, and the short definition of frequency is in the glossary.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s7_html:
Twelve chest sets a week can be done two ways. Once a week: bench 4, incline dumbbell press 4, flyes 4 — on chest day. Or twice: Monday bench 3 and flyes 3, Thursday incline dumbbell press 3 and dips 3. According to the research, the muscle will grow about the same.

But in the second version each set is fresher, and you practise the bench twice — a plus for strength. The first suits you if you love "chest day" and rarely skip. How this looks in ready programs shows in the frequency rows of the full body vs split comparison.
seo.guide.training-frequency.s8_html:
Can I train a muscle every day? You can, if the volume per session is small: studies with six sessions a week showed the same result at equal volume. But there's usually no point — recovery and planning get harder.

How long should a muscle rest between sessions? Usually a day or two after a hard session for that muscle is enough — check whether your weights have come back. That's why full body goes every other day and upper/lower trains different halves two days in a row.

Can abs and calves go more often? Yes, their volume per session is small, and many people train them three or four times a week. Just don't let them get in the way of the main work.
