seo.tool.protein.title: Protein calculator: how much protein per day to build muscle or cut — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.protein.description: How many grams of protein to eat a day for your bodyweight and goal — building muscle, maintaining or cutting — and how much per meal. Ranges from the Morton (2018) meta-analysis and the ISSN position stand, in kg or lb.
seo.tool.protein.lead: Enter your bodyweight and pick a goal — I'll work out how much protein you need a day and how much that is per meal.
seo.tool.protein.rate_kg: That's {lo}–{hi} g of protein per kg of bodyweight a day.
seo.tool.protein.rate_lb: That's {lo}–{hi} g of protein per lb of bodyweight a day.
seo.tool.protein.honest: A guide for healthy adults who train. Kidney disease or pregnancy — talk to a doctor first.
seo.tool.protein.log_cta: Log workouts and bodyweight — I'll show the trend
seo.tool.protein.cta: I don't track food — I track the weight on the bar and your bodyweight. Log your workouts and weigh in once a week: the diary shows whether your eating is working.
seo.tool.protein.how_html:
I multiply your bodyweight by a grams-per-kilo range, one per goal:

  • Build muscle — 1.6–2.2 g per kg. In the meta-analysis by Morton et al. (2018), muscle gain from protein rose up to about 1.6 g per kg a day and then levelled off; the top of the confidence interval was around 2.2 g.
  • Maintain — 1.4–2.0 g per kg: the range the ISSN position stand on protein (Jäger et al., 2017) gives for people who exercise.
  • Cut — 1.8–2.7 g per kg. Helms et al. (2014) recommend 2.3–3.1 g per kg of lean mass in a deficit; across total bodyweight, for a typical lifter, that's roughly this.

Per meal is the daily total divided by the number of meals. The ISSN position stand puts a meal at 20–40 g of protein: if a meal comes out well above that, add another one. If you carry a lot of extra fat, use the weight you're heading for, not your current one. The details are in the guide on protein per day, and the calorie calculator covers energy.
seo.tool.calories.card: Maintenance, bulking and cutting with the Mifflin–St Jeor formula.
seo.tool.calories.title: Calorie calculator: daily calories to bulk, cut or maintain — Athlete Diary
seo.tool.calories.description: How many calories a day you need to maintain, build muscle or cut: resting energy with the Mifflin–St Jeor formula, an activity factor and an honest check against the scale. In kg or lb.
seo.tool.calories.lead: Enter your sex, age, weight, height and activity — I'll estimate how many calories you burn a day and how much to eat for your goal.
seo.tool.calories.bmr: Resting energy — {bmr} a day: what you burn doing nothing.
seo.tool.calories.age_range: The formula was tested on adults — enter an age from {lo} to {hi}.
seo.tool.calories.honest: It's an estimate, not a measurement: two people with the same numbers burn different amounts. Eat like this for two or three weeks and watch your bodyweight — it's more accurate than any formula.
seo.tool.calories.log_cta: Weigh in in the diary — I'll show the trend
seo.tool.calories.cta: I don't track food, but I do track bodyweight and workouts. Weigh in once a week in the diary: after two or three weeks the trend shows whether the formula got you right.
seo.tool.calories.how_html:
First comes resting energy with the Mifflin–St Jeor formula (Mifflin et al., 1990): 10 × weight in kg + 6.25 × height in cm − 5 × age, plus 5 for men and minus 161 for women. That's what you burn at rest: breathing, heartbeat, body heat.

Then I multiply it by an activity factor — from 1.2 for a desk life to 1.9 for hard physical work plus training. That gives maintenance: the intake at which your bodyweight holds steady.

  • Bulk — 5–15% above maintenance: a slow gain where muscle grows, not just fat.
  • Cut — 10–20% below: a moderate deficit that makes it easier to keep your muscle and strength.

The formula is off for everyone in their own way: by a hundred or two calories, sometimes more. So treat it as a starting point, not the answer: eat like this for two or three weeks, weigh yourself under the same conditions and adjust by 100–200 kcal. How exactly is in the guides on calories for muscle gain and cutting without losing muscle. Daily protein is in the protein calculator.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.title: How much protein per day to build muscle — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.protein-per-day.h1: How much protein do you need a day to build muscle
seo.guide.protein-per-day.description: How much protein to eat for muscle growth: about 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight a day, with 2.2 g as the upper end. How to split it across meals, where to get it and when you need more — with research.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.lead: Short answer: about 1.6 g of protein per kg of bodyweight a day, up to 2.2 g to be safe. Below — where those numbers come from, how to spread protein across meals and where to get it without any magic.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.card: 1.6–2.2 g per kg a day, meals and sources.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.cta: I don't track food — I track the weight on the bar and your bodyweight. Log your workouts and weigh in once a week: the diary shows whether you're eating enough to grow.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.takeaways:
For building muscle, aim for about 1.6 g of protein per kg of bodyweight a day.
Above 2.2 g per kg, muscle barely gains anything more.
Split protein across 3–5 meals of 20–40 g.
Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans and protein powder all count.
Kidney disease or pregnancy — talk to a doctor first.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s1_html:
The biggest answer to this question is the meta-analysis by Morton et al. (2018): 49 studies in which people lifted weights and ate different amounts of protein. The muscle gained from protein rose up to about 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight a day and then levelled off. The top of the confidence interval was around 2.2 g: if you want a safety margin, aim closer to that.

The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand (ISSN, Jäger et al., 2017) gives a similar range for people who exercise — 1.4–2.0 g per kg a day. The numbers agree: for building muscle, 1.6 g is the working target and 2.2 g is the ceiling, above which you're paying for food, not growth.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s2.h: Work it out for your weight
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s2_html:
Multiply your bodyweight by 1.6 and by 2.2 — that's your daily range:

  • 60 kg (132 lb) — 96–132 g.
  • 70 kg (154 lb) — 112–154 g.
  • 80 kg (176 lb) — 128–176 g.
  • 90 kg (198 lb) — 144–198 g.
  • 100 kg (220 lb) — 160–220 g.

If you carry a lot of extra fat, use the weight you're heading for, not your current one: fat doesn't need protein, and a number based on full bodyweight comes out too high. Quicker still — the protein calculator, which also splits the day into meals.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s3.h: How to split it across meals
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s3_html:
The daily total matters more than the schedule, but spreading protein evenly is convenient and works at least as well. The ISSN position stand recommends 20–40 g of protein per meal, every 3–4 hours. For an 80 kg lifter building muscle, that's four meals of 32–44 g or five of 26–35 g.

Before bed you can add a serving of slow protein — cottage cheese or casein: the ISSN names 30–40 g. It's not required, just a handy way to close the day's gap.

Two big meals instead of four isn't a disaster. Your muscle won't melt in one uneven week; what matters is that the daily total adds up day after day.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s4_html:
Protein is ordinary food. Roughly this much per 100 g of food — the label has the exact figure:

  • Chicken breast, turkey, beef, fish — about 20–25 g raw.
  • Cottage cheese — about 11–12 g, Greek yogurt — about 10 g.
  • An egg — about 6 g each.
  • Canned tuna — about 23–25 g.
  • Lentils, beans, chickpeas — about 7–9 g cooked; tofu — 8–15 g.

Plant protein counts too; you just need a little more of it, ideally from several sources. If food alone doesn't get you there, protein powder helps — more on that in the guide on whey protein.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s5_html:
On a cut. When you eat fewer calories than you burn, your body is more willing to take energy from muscle too, and protein helps you hold on to it. Helms et al. (2014) recommend 2.3–3.1 g per kg of lean mass in a deficit — across total bodyweight, for a typical lifter, that's roughly 1.8–2.7 g per kg. The leaner you are and the deeper the deficit, the closer to the top end.

If you're coming back after a long break or started lifting after forty, extra protein won't hurt either: keep the day closer to 2 g per kg and don't skip meals. How a cut works as a whole is in the guide on cutting without losing muscle.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s6_html:
No. Protein powder is the same food, just in a tub: milk protein, dried and packed. Your muscles don't care whether 30 g of protein came from a shaker or a chicken breast.

In the Morton meta-analysis, supplemental protein helped people whose diet was short on it rather than acting as a growth trigger of its own. If you already reach 1.6 g per kg with food, the tub adds nothing. If you don't, a shake is the quickest way to close the gap.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s7.h: Is a lot of protein safe?
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s7_html:
In healthy people who exercise, these amounts haven't shown harm in research — that's the conclusion of the ISSN position stand. The "protein wrecks your kidneys" myth comes from advice for people whose kidneys are already sick.

Here's who should talk to a doctor first, not a calculator: kidney or liver disease, pregnancy and breastfeeding, a diet prescribed by a doctor. I'm a coach, not a doctor: these numbers are for healthy adults.
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s8.h: How to tell you're getting enough
seo.guide.protein-per-day.s8_html:
Look at your log, not your plate. If the weights and reps on your lifts go up week to week and your bodyweight creeps up slowly on a bulk, you're eating enough. If your strength has been flat for a month while you sleep well and train regularly, check calories and protein first, then the program.

I log your workouts and bodyweight for you — there's a weight diary in the bot and in the app, and I work out your progress on every lift after each workout. How to build a program for size is in the guide on a muscle gain program.
seo.guide.creatine.title: Creatine monohydrate: how to take it, how much and why — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.creatine.h1: Creatine: how to take it and what it does
seo.guide.creatine.description: What creatine monohydrate does, how much to take — 3–5 g a day, whether you need a loading phase, where the weight gain comes from and how safe it is. Based on the ISSN position stand (Kreider et al., 2017).
seo.guide.creatine.lead: Creatine is one of the few supplements that actually works: a few more reps at the same weight and a bit more strength over time. 3–5 g of monohydrate a day, and that's it.
seo.guide.creatine.card: 3–5 g of monohydrate a day, loading, water and safety.
seo.guide.creatine.cta: Log your sets — I'll show whether your reps at the same weight and your estimated max go up while you're on creatine.
seo.guide.creatine.takeaways:
Creatine helps you squeeze out a few more reps on heavy sets.
The dose is 3–5 g of monohydrate a day, any time of day.
Loading is optional: without it your muscles fill up in 3–4 weeks.
The 1–2 kg you gain in the first weeks is mostly water in the muscle.
Kidney disease, pregnancy or medication — see a doctor first.
seo.guide.creatine.s1_html:
Your muscles already hold creatine: as phosphocreatine it quickly restores energy for short, hard efforts — a set of 5–10 reps, a sprint, a jump. A supplement fills those stores more than meat and fish do.

In practice, that means a rep or two more at the same weight, and over weeks of training it adds up to slightly bigger gains in strength and muscle. The ISSN position stand (Kreider et al., 2017) calls creatine monohydrate the most effective over-the-counter supplement for lifters and one of the most studied.
seo.guide.creatine.s2_html:
The working dose is 3–5 g of monohydrate a day, every day, rest days included. Timing barely matters: morning, after training, with a meal — whatever makes it easy to remember. Mix it into water, juice or your protein shake.

It doesn't kick in after one serving like caffeine does. Creatine builds up in the muscle, so consistency matters, not timing. Missed a day? Just carry on — no need to double up.
seo.guide.creatine.s3_html:
A loading phase is about 0.3 g per kg of bodyweight a day — roughly 20 g split into four servings — for 5–7 days. Then the usual 3–5 g. That fills your muscles in a week.

Without loading, on 3–5 g a day, your muscles fill up in about 3–4 weeks, and after that there's no difference. Load if you want the effect sooner, say before a meet. The one downside: big servings more often cause stomach upset. If you're not in a hurry, start straight on the maintenance dose.
seo.guide.creatine.s4_html:
In the first weeks your bodyweight often goes up by 1–2 kg. That's water creatine pulls inside your muscle cells — not fat and not puffiness under the skin. Your muscles look a bit fuller and the scale jumps.

If you're cutting and tracking your weight trend, account for that jump: it happens once, at the start. After that, watch the trend, not the first week. If you stop taking creatine, that water leaves again over a few weeks.

There's no need to force down extra water — drink to thirst, same as without creatine.
seo.guide.creatine.s5_html:
In healthy people creatine has been studied more than most supplements: research lasting up to several years found no harm to the kidneys or liver — that's the conclusion of the ISSN position stand. Your blood creatinine may read higher than usual while you take it: that reflects more creatine in your body, not necessarily a kidney problem. Tell your doctor you take it if you're getting blood work done.

The link to hair loss rests on one small study that measured a hormone, not hair itself; it hasn't been confirmed.

Kidney disease, pregnancy, breastfeeding, regular medication — talk to a doctor first. I'm a coach: this is what's known about healthy adults.
seo.guide.creatine.s6_html:
Monohydrate. It's what nearly every study used, and it's the cheapest. Creatine HCl, "buffered" creatine, ethyl ester and fancy blends cost more and haven't done better than monohydrate.

Check the label: the tub should contain creatine monohydrate, without "proprietary matrices". Third-party lab testing is a plus — it matters if you compete and get drug tested.
seo.guide.creatine.s7.h: Who gets less out of it
seo.guide.creatine.s7_html:
Responses vary. People who eat lots of meat and fish already walk around with fuller stores, so they gain less. Vegetarians and vegans, on the other hand, usually notice it more.

Creatine doesn't replace training or food. Without progressive overload and enough protein it does almost nothing: its job is to let you get one more rep, and the sets are what make you grow. The order of priorities is in the guide on supplements that work.
seo.guide.creatine.s8_html:
Not by feel — creatine doesn't give you a buzz. By your log: after a month, compare how many reps you get at the same weight on your main lifts, and check your estimated max. If your reps went up and your bodyweight jumped a kilo or two at the start, it's doing its job.

I log your sets for you and work out your estimated max after every workout. How to keep a log so these things show up is in the guide on keeping a workout log.
seo.guide.whey-protein.title: Whey protein: what it is, why you'd use it and how to choose — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.whey-protein.description: What whey protein is, when it's handy, how isolate differs from concentrate, how much to take and why it's food, not magic. With research.
seo.guide.whey-protein.lead: Whey protein is milk protein in a handy tub. It's not a drug and not magic: it helps you hit your protein when food alone doesn't get you there.
seo.guide.whey-protein.card: Isolate or concentrate, how much and why at all.
seo.guide.whey-protein.cta: Log your workouts — I'll show whether your weights go up. That's the answer to whether you're getting enough protein, tub or no tub.
seo.guide.whey-protein.takeaways:
Whey is milk protein in powder form — in other words, food.
You need it only if food doesn't get you to about 1.6 g of protein per kg a day.
Concentrate is cheaper; isolate has less lactose.
A serving is 20–40 g of protein, and timing barely matters.
Look at the protein per serving and lab testing, not the marketing.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s1_html:
When milk is made into cheese, liquid whey is left over. It contains protein — quickly digested and with the full set of essential amino acids. That protein gets filtered out and dried into a powder. That's all "sports nutrition" is here.

It's closer to milk and cottage cheese than to pills. Your muscles can't tell protein from a shaker from protein from chicken — what matters to them is how much arrives over the day.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s2_html:
When food alone doesn't get you to your target. For building muscle, aim for about 1.6 g of protein per kg of bodyweight a day (the Morton et al. 2018 meta-analysis). For 80 kg that's almost 130 g, and not everyone wants to eat that much meat and cottage cheese.

  • No time for a proper meal — a shake takes a minute.
  • Dinner is still hours away after training.
  • You're vegetarian but eat dairy.
  • Your appetite is small, and a bulk needs more.

If you already hit your target with food, protein powder adds nothing. Work out your target in the protein calculator.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s3_html:
• Concentrate — the most common and the cheapest. It has a little lactose and fat and slightly less protein per serving.
  • Isolate — filtered further: more protein, almost no lactose or fat. It costs more. Pick it if milk upsets your stomach.
  • Hydrolysate — the protein is already partly broken down. The most expensive; no proven advantage for muscle growth.

For building muscle the difference between them is small. Take concentrate if you handle milk fine and isolate if you don't. If you can't do dairy at all, there are plant proteins — pea, soy, rice, ideally a blend.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s4_html:
One scoop usually gives 20–30 g of protein — check the nutrition label, not the front of the tub. The ISSN position stand (Jäger et al., 2017) puts a meal at 20–40 g of protein, so one or two scoops is already a serving.

How many servings a day depends on how much you're short. Add up the protein from your regular food, subtract it from your target — the difference is your protein powder. Most often that's one serving a day, sometimes two. Don't live on shakes: food brings fibre, vitamins and the stuff that keeps you full, not just protein.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s5_html:
Whenever it's convenient. The idea that you must drink it within 30 minutes of training or it's all wasted didn't hold up: in the review by Aragon and Schoenfeld (2013), the window around training turned out to be wide — what matters more is protein over the day and how much you ate before and after.

Handy moments: after training if your next meal is a couple of hours away; as a snack; at breakfast when it's low in protein. More on eating around training is in the guide on what to eat before and after a workout.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s6_html:
In the Morton meta-analysis, adding protein to training increased muscle and strength gains, but only a little, and mostly in people who weren't eating enough of it. Training with progressive overload is what makes you grow; protein is the building material.

If the tub says "10 lb of muscle in a month", that's marketing. If the weight on the bar has stalled, the cause is almost never your protein brand: more often it's sleep, calories or the program. Start with the guide on supplements that work.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s7_html:
• Look at the grams of protein per serving and the serving size — that's how you compare price per 100 g of protein, not per tub.
  • Ingredients: protein listed first, no "proprietary blends" that hide how much of what is inside.
  • Third-party lab testing — it matters if you compete and get drug tested.
  • Taste matters more than you'd think: protein you hate drinking will sit on the shelf.

"Growth" extras in protein powder — added amino acids, boosters — raise the price, not your muscle.
seo.guide.whey-protein.s8_html:
Is it bad for your kidneys? In healthy people, normal amounts of protein haven't shown harm. If your kidneys are sick, see a doctor first.

Is it for women too? Yes, it's just protein. You can't get "too bulky" from protein powder.

Can I take it without training? As food, sure, but training is what makes you grow, not the powder.

Should I take it before bed? You can; the ISSN names 30–40 g of slow protein before sleep as a handy way to close the day's gap — casein or cottage cheese fit that better than whey.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.title: How many calories to build muscle: a lean bulk without the fat — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.h1: How many calories you need to build muscle
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.descr: How many calories to eat on a bulk: a small surplus of 5–15% over maintenance, gaining about 0.25–0.5% of bodyweight a week, weighing in weekly and adjusting. With research.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.lead: To build muscle you need to eat a bit more than you burn. Not "eat everything in sight" — a small surplus, plus a weekly weigh-in that tells you whether you got it right.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.card: The surplus, the rate of gain and a weekly weigh-in.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.cta: Weigh in once a week and log your workouts — I'll show your bodyweight trend next to the weights going up on the bar.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.takea:
A bulk needs a small surplus — about 5–15% over maintenance.
The rate — about 0.25–0.5% of bodyweight a week.
The formula gives a start; two or three weeks on the scale give the truth.
Weight not moving — add 100–200 kcal; moving fast — take some away.
About 1.6 g of protein per kg and progressive training are a must.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s1_ht:
Building new muscle is work, and your body needs energy and material for it. When you eat exactly what you burn, muscle can grow, but slowly. When you eat less, your body saves energy, and growth almost stops.

There are exceptions: a beginner, someone coming back after a long break, or someone with plenty of fat to spare can build muscle at maintenance or even in a small deficit. But if you've been training for a couple of years and want to grow, you need a surplus — a small, controlled one.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s2_ht:
I go with 5–15% over maintenance: for someone with a maintenance of 2,700 kcal, that's about 2,850–3,100 kcal a day. It's easier to measure the rate of gain than the calories: the review by Iraki et al. (2019) recommends gaining about 0.25–0.5% of bodyweight a week. For 80 kg that's 0.2–0.4 kg a week, or about 1–1.5 kg a month.

A beginner can go closer to the top end: they grow faster, and the extra energy gets used. Someone who has trained for several years should go closer to the bottom: their muscle grows more slowly, and a big surplus turns into fat.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s3_ht:
Start with a formula: the calorie calculator works out your resting energy with Mifflin–St Jeor, multiplies it by your activity and gives you a bulking range right away. It's an estimate: two people with the same height and weight can burn hundreds of calories apart.

So the formula is a starting point, not the answer. Eat roughly the same for two weeks and weigh yourself. If your weight holds steady, that's your maintenance. If it drifts down, you were eating less than you thought. Add the surplus on top of that.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s4_ht:
Bodyweight swings by 1–2 kg in a day: water, salt, food in your stomach, yesterday's leg day. A single weigh-in tells you nothing. Here's what works:

  • Weigh yourself under the same conditions — in the morning, after the bathroom, before eating.
  • At least once a week, better 3–4 times.
  • Compare weekly averages, not single days.

There's a weight diary in the bot and in the app: log your weight and I'll show you the trend.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s5_ht:
Look at the trend over 2–3 weeks:

  • Weight not moving — add 100–200 kcal a day: a slice of bread with peanut butter, a glass of milk, an extra handful of rice.
  • Going up by 0.25–0.5% a week — leave it alone.
  • Going up faster — take away 100–200 kcal. The extra goes to fat, not muscle.

Change things a little at a time and wait two weeks: your body doesn't respond in three days. Big swings in your eating muddy the picture, and you can't tell what worked.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s6.h: Without training, a surplus is just fat
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s6_ht:
The surplus provides material; training provides the signal to grow. You need enough hard sets per muscle per week — in the meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (2017), growth followed volume — and a load that rises over time. How to put that together is in the guide on a muscle gain program.

And protein: about 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight a day (the Morton et al. 2018 meta-analysis). Calories without protein mostly build fat.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s7_ht:
"Eat everything you see" is old advice with a high price. A big surplus doesn't speed up muscle growth: growth has a limit, and everything above it goes to fat. Then you'll have to cut that fat, and a cut is months in a deficit, during which you grow more slowly.

If your bodyweight goes up by more than a kilo a week for longer than a couple of weeks, that's not muscle anymore. Cut back the extra, and in six months you'll have more muscle and less fat than after a "bulk at any cost". How to lose the fat later without losing your progress is in the guide on cutting without losing muscle.
seo.guide.calories-for-muscle-gain.s8_ht:
I can't eat that much. Drink your calories: milk, a shake with oats, banana and peanut butter. Add one more meal rather than eating huge portions.

How long should a bulk last? As long as your lifts are going up, your bodyweight is in range and your fat isn't visibly piling on. Usually that's months, not weeks.

Do I have to count calories? No. You can eat as usual and adjust by the scale — that's even more honest than trusting labels. I don't count food, but I'll show your weight trend and strength gains.
How to cut without losing muscle: deficit, protein and training — Athlete Diary
How to cut without losing muscle
How to lose fat and keep your muscle: lose 0.5–1% of bodyweight a week, keep a moderate deficit, eat more protein and keep lifting heavy. With research.
Three things keep your muscle on a cut: heavy training, enough protein and an unhurried pace. Everything else is detail.
The rate, the deficit, protein and the weight on the bar.
Weigh in and log your workouts — I'll show your bodyweight trend and estimated max side by side, so you can see whether it's fat or strength that's going.

Lose 0.5–1% of your bodyweight a week, no faster.
Start with a deficit of about 10–20% below maintenance, then adjust by the scale.
Train heavy, like on a bulk: the weights are what keep your muscle.
Protein higher than usual — about 1.8–2.7 g per kg of bodyweight.
Strength dropping fast means the deficit is too big.
What keeps your muscle

In a deficit your body looks for energy everywhere, muscle included. To make it take that energy from fat, you have to give it reasons to keep the muscle:

  • Load — heavy training tells your body the muscle is needed.
  • Protein — the material your muscle repairs itself with, even in a deficit.
  • Pace — the gentler the deficit, the less you lose.

The review by Helms, Aragon and Fitschen (2014) on natural bodybuilding contest prep comes down to these three points. Sleep and stress matter too, but nothing saves you without these three.
How fast to lose weight

Helms et al. recommend losing 0.5–1% of bodyweight a week. For 80 kg that's 0.4–0.8 kg a week. The leaner you are, the closer to the bottom end: when there's little fat left, a fast cut eats into muscle more often.

You'll always want to go faster, especially in the first weeks. But the difference between a two-month and a three-month cut is a few weeks, while the strength you lose stays with you much longer.
How big a deficit

Start at 10–20% below maintenance: the calorie calculator works out both your maintenance and a cutting range. For someone with a maintenance of 2,700 kcal, that's about 2,150–2,450 kcal a day.

After that, the scale is in charge. Weigh yourself under the same conditions and compare weekly averages: if you're losing less than 0.5% a week for two or three weeks running, take away another 100–200 kcal. Faster than 1% — add some back. In the first week weight often drops faster because of water — don't panic and don't draw conclusions from it.
Keep lifting heavy

The most common mistake is switching to "light weights and high reps for definition". Definition comes from low body fat, not from reps. Light weights take away the very signal that keeps your muscle.

Keep your main lifts and working weights the same as on a bulk. You can cut volume a little — by 2–3 sets per muscle per week if your recovery suffers. The goal on a cut isn't records; it's holding on to what you have. If your weights hold steady, you're doing it right. How to progress in general is in the guide on progressive overload.
More protein

In a deficit, protein matters more than on a bulk. Helms et al. recommend 2.3–3.1 g per kg of lean mass; across total bodyweight, for a typical lifter, that's roughly 1.8–2.7 g per kg. The ISSN position stand (Jäger et al., 2017) also says higher protein in a deficit helps preserve muscle.

Bonus: protein is filling, which makes a deficit easier to stick to. Work out your range in the protein calculator with the "Cut" goal. Kidney disease — talk to a doctor first.
What happens to your strength

On a cut, strength usually holds or dips slightly — especially near the end, when there's little fat left. That's normal. What's not normal is your estimated max on the main lifts dropping week after week right from the start.

That's a sign the deficit is too big, protein is too low or you're short on sleep. Add 100–200 kcal and check your protein. I see it in your log: I work out your estimated max after every workout, with your bodyweight trend right next to it.
Cardio and steps

Cardio helps with the deficit but doesn't replace lifting. The simplest option is steps: walking barely gets in the way of recovery. Hard leg-heavy cardio the day before squats or deadlifts steals strength from the bar.

The order goes: lifting first, then food, then steps, and cardio only if that's not enough. If there's so much cardio that your weights drop, it's not a cut anymore — it's marathon prep.

Keep your steps steady from day to day: if you start walking less, you burn less, and the scale will show it a week or two later.
Common questions

Can I lose fat and build muscle at the same time? Beginners, people coming back after a break and those with plenty of fat — often yes. People who've trained for years — slowly, which is why it's easier to alternate bulking and cutting.

How long should a cut last? Until you reach your goal — usually 8–16 weeks. Longer without a break is hard on your head and your body: you can spend a couple of weeks at maintenance and then continue.

How do I know it's time to stop? You've hit your goal in the mirror, or your strength keeps dropping despite every adjustment. Then ease back up to maintenance — see how to bulk after a cut.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.title: Caffeine before a workout: dose, timing and sleep — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.descri: How much caffeine to take before training — 3–6 mg per kg of bodyweight about an hour before, what it does for lifting, how not to wreck your sleep and what happens with tolerance. Based on the ISSN position stand.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.lead: Caffeine is the most accessible supplement that actually helps in the gym: a few more reps, heavy sets that feel a bit lighter. The trick is the dose and the timing, so you don't pay for it with your sleep.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.card: 3–6 mg per kg an hour before, sleep and tolerance.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.cta: Log your workouts — compare your sets on days with and without coffee: the diary shows whether it gets you more reps.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.takeaw:
The working dose is 3–6 mg per kg of bodyweight.
Take it about 60 minutes before training.
Start at the low end: the effect is already there.
Evening workout — a smaller dose or none: sleep matters more.
Heart issues, blood pressure, pregnancy, medication — see a doctor first.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s1_htm:
The ISSN position stand on caffeine (Guest et al., 2021) calls it an effective supplement for many kinds of exercise. For lifting, that means a few more reps to failure, a little more strength and power, and less sense of effort: the same set feels lighter.

The effect is small — it won't add 20 kg to your bench. But on a heavy day a couple of extra reps add up to extra volume, and on a max attempt to an extra chance.

Testing it on yourself is easy: add a note to the workout saying whether you had coffee, and after a couple of weeks compare your sets in the diary.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s2_htm:
In research, 3–6 mg of caffeine per kg of bodyweight works. For 70 kg that's 210–420 mg; for 80 kg, 240–480 mg. The ISSN position stand notes that lower doses, around 2 mg per kg, can work too, while very high doses bring side effects more often than benefits.

Start at the low end — 3 mg per kg or less — and see how your sets go. Raise the dose only if there's no difference and your heart, sleep and stomach aren't complaining. More isn't better: shaky hands and jitters hurt the bar more than the buzz helps.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s3_htm:
Usually about 60 minutes before training: that gives caffeine time to absorb by your first working sets. Caffeine gum kicks in faster than a drink.

A simple routine: coffee on the way to the gym or an hour before you leave, then your warm-up and working sets. If you drink it right before the bar, the peak lands at the end of the workout.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s4_htm:
• Coffee — a cup of brewed coffee has roughly 80–120 mg, but it varies a lot: the beans, the grind, the size of the cup.
  • Caffeine pills — an exact dose, handy if you want to know how much you took.
  • Pre-workouts — caffeine plus everything else. Check how much caffeine is in a serving: 300 mg or more isn't unusual.
  • Energy drinks — caffeine plus sugar; go by the label.

Don't stack sources blindly: coffee in the morning, a pre-workout before the gym and an energy drink after is already a lot.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s5_htm:
Caffeine stays in your blood for hours, and for many people an evening dose eats into deep sleep even if they fall asleep fine. And poor sleep takes more from your training than caffeine gives: recovery, strength next week, appetite.

Training in the evening? Take less, move your coffee earlier in the day or skip it. Test it on yourself: if you wake up wrecked after evening coffee, the honest answer is no.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s6_htm:
You get used to the buzz quickly: morning coffee stops hitting. The effect on training is a different story: the ISSN position stand considers that in regular coffee drinkers the performance boost usually remains, though the data here are mixed.

If your dose feels like it stopped working, don't keep raising it. A couple of weeks on less caffeine and your usual dose will feel like something again. Saving caffeine for heavy training days instead of three cups every day is a simple way to keep it working.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s7_htm:
For healthy adults, about 400 mg of caffeine a day is considered safe — that's the figure food safety agencies go by. Pre-workout doses for a heavier lifter easily get close to that ceiling, so count all the caffeine in your day, not just before the gym.

Heart disease, high blood pressure, anxiety, pregnancy, medication — talk to a doctor first. I'm a coach: these numbers are for healthy adults.
seo.guide.caffeine-before-workout.s8_htm:
Does it work for everyone? Responses vary: some people get a clear boost, others almost nothing. Test it on yourself with your log.

Can I take it with creatine? Yes, they work in different ways. You take creatine every day and caffeine before training. More in the guide on creatine.

Is a workout without caffeine a waste? No. It's a small boost, not the foundation. The foundation is your program, food and sleep — more in the guide on supplements that work.

Coffee or a pre-workout? For the caffeine itself there's no difference: the caffeine does the work, not the rest of the mix. Coffee is cheaper; a pre-workout is handier if you want to know the exact dose — check the label.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.titl: What to eat before and after a workout: protein, carbs and the anabolic window — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.h1: What to eat before and after a workout
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.desc: What and when to eat before and after training, whether there's a 30-minute anabolic window, how much protein per meal and what to do if you train fasted in the morning. With research.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.lead: The 30-minute window after training in which you have to down a shake is a myth. There is a window, but it's wide: what matters is the meal before, the meal after and protein over the day.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.card: The anabolic window, examples and training fasted.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.cta: Log your workouts — then compare your sets on days you ate beforehand and days you trained hungry: the diary answers more honestly than any plan.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.take:
There's no narrow 30-minute window — the window around training is wide.
Eat 1–3 hours before training: protein and carbs.
After training — 20–40 g of protein within the next couple of hours.
If you ate long ago, don't wait to eat after training.
Protein over the whole day matters more than exact timing.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s1_h:
The review by Aragon and Schoenfeld (2013) took apart the "anabolic window" idea and concluded there's no narrow 30–60 minute window. A meal before training keeps working during and after it, and the meal after adds to it.

The practical takeaway from the same review: don't space your meals before and after training too far apart — roughly 3–4 hours or less. If you ate an hour before the gym, a shake straight after isn't necessary. If you last ate in the morning and train in the evening, eat right after training without putting it off.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s2_h:
1–3 hours before training — a normal meal: protein, carbs, a little fat. Protein gives your muscles material; carbs give you fuel for the heavy sets. Save fatty, very filling food for 2–3 hours before: squatting on a full stomach is rough.

If you have less than an hour — something light: a banana, yogurt, a sandwich, a protein shake with fruit. The goal is to show up neither hungry nor heavy.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s3_h:
The ISSN position stand on protein (Jäger et al., 2017) puts a meal at 20–40 g of protein — and that's your post-workout serving. Add carbs, especially if the session was long or you train again the next day.

Timing — within a couple of hours. A normal dinner after an evening workout is perfect. A shake in the locker room only makes sense if a real meal is still a long way off. Work out the protein per meal for your weight in the protein calculator.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s4_h:
Training in the morning without breakfast is fine if you feel good and your weights don't drop. Many people find it easier. But then the meal after training matters more: it's been many hours since dinner, so don't put off your protein.

If you feel dizzy fasted or your sets are clearly worse, have at least a protein shake or a banana with yogurt before the gym. Check it in your log: your weights fasted versus after a light snack is an honest test.

The order of your meals matters less than the day's total: breakfast after training is still breakfast.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s5_h:
2–3 hours before:

  • Rice or potatoes with chicken and vegetables.
  • A three-egg omelette, toast and a piece of fruit.

An hour before:

  • Yogurt with a banana.
  • A protein shake with fruit, or a cheese sandwich.

After:

  • Pasta with meat sauce.
  • Cottage cheese with berries and bread.
  • Fish with potatoes.

These are examples, not a menu: any food with protein and carbs that sits well with you works.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s6_h:
For a regular hour of lifting, carbs before training help, but there's no rush to refill them after: your stores come back over the day with normal food. They matter more when sessions are long, frequent or twice a day.

If you run out of steam at the end of heavy workouts and you eat few carbs, try adding some to your pre-gym meal. Compare the last exercises of the workout in your log.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s7_h:
If you have coffee before training, it's easy to pair it with your meal an hour before the gym. The ISSN position stand on caffeine (Guest et al., 2021) names a working dose of 3–6 mg per kg of bodyweight about 60 minutes ahead. More in the guide on caffeine before a workout.

Drink water to thirst through the day and during training. Showing up dehydrated is as bad as showing up hungry: your strength fades sooner.
seo.guide.pre-and-post-workout-meal.s8_h:
Do I need a shake right after? No, if a normal meal with protein is coming in the next couple of hours. A shake is just convenience — more in the guide on whey protein.

Can I eat after training late at night? Yes. A meal after an evening workout is a normal dinner, not "midnight snacking".

What matters most? Protein over the day — about 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight, covered in the guide on protein per day. Timing around training is an add-on to that.

What if the session runs past two hours? Then carbs matter more: snack along the way — a banana, juice, a sports drink. For a regular hour of lifting, that's overkill.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.title: Supplements that work and the ones that don't: an honest guide — Athlete Diary
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.h1: Which supplements work and which don't
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.descript: An honest look at supplements: creatine, caffeine and protein work; BCAAs, testosterone boosters and fat burners don't. What the research says and what not to waste money on.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.lead: Three supplements have good evidence: creatine, caffeine and protein. The rest of the supplement shelf does nothing at best, and at worst costs you money and risks your health.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.card: Creatine, caffeine, protein — and what to skip.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.cta: Log your workouts — the weights going up in your diary are more honest than any tub. I'll show you whether what you're doing works.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.takeaway:
What works: creatine monohydrate, caffeine, protein as convenient food.
You don't need BCAAs if your diet has enough protein.
Testosterone boosters have no solid data on muscle growth.
Fat burners don't remove fat without a calorie deficit.
Sleep, training and food first — supplements last.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s1_html:
Reviews, before-and-after photos and "clinically proven" on the tub mean nothing. What's worth looking at is the position stands of professional societies and meta-analyses — summaries of many studies in people.

I sort supplements onto three shelves: they work, they work in specific cases, and they don't work. Spend your money and attention from the top down, not on whatever is advertised the loudest.

One more filter: an honest label. A supplement that "works like a steroid" sometimes turns out to contain one: something was mixed in. If the promised results are too loud, that's a reason to be suspicious, not to buy.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s2_html:
• Creatine monohydrate — 3–5 g a day. The ISSN position stand (Kreider et al., 2017) calls it the most effective over-the-counter supplement for lifters. More in the guide on creatine.
  • Caffeine — 3–6 mg per kg of bodyweight an hour before training, per the ISSN position stand (Guest et al., 2021). More in the guide on caffeine.
  • Protein — not a stimulant but food. The Morton et al. (2018) meta-analysis: supplemental protein helps people who aren't getting enough. More in the guide on whey protein.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s3_html:
• Vitamin D, iron and other vitamins and minerals — they help if you're low. You find that out from a blood test and a doctor, not from how you feel.
  • Beta-alanine — for efforts lasting one to a few minutes. In lifting sets of 5–10 reps the effect is modest.
  • Electrolytes — for long sessions in the heat when you sweat a lot.

If you're not sure you need any of these, you most likely don't. Or ask a doctor.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s4_html:
BCAAs — branched-chain amino acids — are three of the twenty amino acids that make up protein. They're sold as "muscle protection" and "recovery". But any complete protein — meat, fish, eggs, dairy, protein powder — already contains them, along with the other amino acids you also need to grow.

If you eat about 1.6 g of protein per kg of bodyweight a day, BCAAs add nothing. If you don't, buy protein powder: it has the same BCAAs plus everything else, and it's usually cheaper per gram.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s5_html:
Herbal "boosters" — tribulus, fenugreek and blends with loud names — promise more testosterone and muscle. There's no solid evidence that they build muscle or strength in healthy men. Where something does change, it's not a difference you'll see on the bar.

If you suspect your hormones really are off — fatigue, libido, mood — that's a question for a doctor and blood work, not a tub from the supplement store.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s6_html:
Most of them are caffeine plus plant extracts in a nice tub with a loud name. Fat comes off when you eat fewer calories than you burn — and no other way. Without a deficit a fat burner removes nothing, and with one it adds almost nothing beyond the caffeine.

The risk is real, though: strong stimulants, sometimes banned substances that aren't on the label. Spend the money on protein-rich food instead. How to cut without tubs is in the guide on cutting without losing muscle.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s7_html:
• Supplements are checked less strictly than medicines: what's inside may not match the label.
  • Pick products with third-party lab testing — especially if you compete and get drug tested.
  • A promise of "10 lb of muscle in a month" is a reason not to buy.
  • Health conditions, pregnancy, regular medication — talk any supplement over with a doctor first.

I'm a coach, not a doctor: this is what's known about healthy adults.
seo.guide.supplements-that-work.s8_html:
The order in which things actually pay off:

  1. A program with progressive overload and consistent training.
  2. Sleep — 7–9 hours.
  3. Calories for your goal and about 1.6 g of protein per kg of bodyweight — the protein calculator works it out.
  4. Creatine and, if you like, caffeine before training.

Until the first three are in place, no tub will help. The easiest way to check them is your log: are your weights and reps going up from month to month?

If you're not sure what to take, take nothing: it's free and it won't hurt.
